Using conceptual analysis and a structured review of the AI ethics literature, this article develops a theoretical framework for defining, explaining, and operationalizing AI honesty. Within this framework, AI honesty is defined not as a human virtue but as a designable and evaluable property of intelligent systems. The five principal components of this construct are epistemic honesty, truth representation, uncertainty disclosure, resistance to cognitive sycophancy, and correctability. The article subsequently proposes a conceptual model and a composite measure-the AI Honesty Index-for the empirical assessment of this concept. The index may provide a basis for evaluating large language models, developing technical standards, designing regulatory frameworks, and improving the trustworthiness of AI systems. Finally, the theoretical and policy implications of the framework and directions for future research are discussed.

title: Lossless Cross-Request KV Cache Reuse via Position-Aligned Block Injection using JaccardServe
abstract: We address the problem of cross-request KV cache reuse in large language model (LLM) serving, where many incoming requests share substantial prompt content but differ in small per-user details. Our earlier work introduced JaccardServe, a matching layer that uses MinHash localitysensitive hashing (LSH) on token shingles to identify near-duplicate prompt spans at the API gateway. That work also explored a token-reordering technique to enable KV block reuse via vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching, which produced a 44% time-to-first-token (TTFT) reduction on templated workloads but caused a 60% rate of structural output differences-making it unsuitable for production use. This paper presents a new approach that achieves KV cache reuse with no change to the input token sequence and therefore no change to model output. The key insight is that when the Jac-cardServe gateway finds a donor request whose matching span occupies the same absolute token position as in the target request, the donor's KV blocks can be injected directly into the target's block table before prefill. The model processes the same token sequence it would have processed anyway; it simply skips recomputing positions already covered by injected blocks. This is provably lossless. We characterize the matching layer for this lossless reuse mechanism across two workloads and compare MinHash-Jaccard similarity against SimHash-cosine similarity for the position-aligned matching task. On templated chat workloads, MinHash achieves 62.1% mean coverage per aligned hit versus 42.6% for SimHash-and 100% of MinHash hits exceed 50% coverage, making every match actionable. On multi-document summarization, MinHash again achieves higher per-hit coverage (32.2% vs 19.0%). GPU benchmarks on an RTX 5070 Ti show a projected 66.5% median TTFT reduction on matched requests (19.55 ms → 6.56 ms), covering 35.5% of all requests. The JaccardServe gateway adds a median overhead of 0.50 ms per request on templated workloads-negligible relative to any measured TTFT. Quality validation on 50 paired outputs confirms 100% EQUIVALENT rate (mean ROUGE-L = 1.0), establishing this approach as production-safe.

title: Ten Rules for Deploying Large Language Models in Official Statistics
abstract: Official statistics is increasingly produced with the help of large language models, which are being asked to write the code of its pipelines and to guide the statistics themselves, work whose outputs carry institutional weight and inform policy. The fluency of these models creates a failure mode distinct from ordinary software error: they produce plausible text whether or not it is correct, so a pipeline that relies on them can fail silently while still looking authoritative, which is at odds with the obligations written down in the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics and the European Statistics Code of Practice. We offer ten rules for deploying these models safely in official statistics at the current state of the technology. The rules follow one architectural principle: the model serves as a monitoring agent that observes,corrects bounded deviations, flags, and reports, while data selection, method choice, processing, causal reasoning, interpretation, and disclosure control remain with human analysts. We place this boundary on an adoption frontier, a decision tool that weighs the impact of a model error against the cost to the office of not adopting, so that each use case can be triaged on its own terms. We ground each rule in the Principles it protects and locate it in the phases of the Generic Statistical Business Process Model.

title: The Uncanny Valley of AI Phishing: Over-Precision as a Forensic Detection Paradigm in the LLM Era
abstract: Just as Mori's Uncanny Valley reveals that near-human representations unsettle observers precisely at their closest approach to authenticity, AI-generated phishing texts unsettle forensic detection by exceeding the natural precision ceiling of authentic institutional communication. This paper introduces and empirically validates the Uncanny Valley of AI Phishing, the finding that AI-generated financial phishing texts are detectable not through error but through over-precision, and operationalises this finding through two novel instruments: a three-zone forensic detection framework and the NULL_INTERFERENCE Protocol, developed from the L1 Interference Feature Set (LIFS v2). Drawing on the first purpose-built annotated multilingual corpus of Indian financial phishing texts (n = 380; 186 human fraud, 86 authentic institutional controls, 108 AI-generated across nine LLM platforms), we demonstrate that AI-generated T0 texts achieve a mean Type-Token Ratio of 0.978 (SD = 0.026), significantly exceeding authentic controls (0.927, SD = 0.069; U = 2,302, p < 0.001, r = 0.383). Moving-Average TTR (MATTR, window = 20) confirms this finding is length-independent: AI T0 MATTR = 0.984, exceeding both authentic controls (0.952) and human fraud (0.953). The three-zone framework maps the forensic landscape across two dimensions: L2 error density and positive variety feature profile. Zone 1 (high-error human) responds to conventional error-based methods; Zone 2 (low-error human) to positive feature profiling; and Zone 3 (AI over-precision, the Uncanny Valley) to absence detection alone. The NULL_INTERFERENCE protocol operationalises Zone 3 attribution in five steps, identifying 33 of 36 AI T0 texts (91.7%) via the TTR ≥ 0.94 signature. Platform analysis across nine LLMs identifies three geopolitically clustered compliance strategies, American (full compliance with Indian domain awareness), European (embedded anti-fraud disclaimer), and Chinese (URL dot suppression), constituting secondary platform-attribution signals. Together, these findings require a fundamental repositioning of forensic NLI for the LLM era: from error detection to absence detection and from a two-category to a three-zone attribution architecture.

title: Mitigating LLM Token Inflation and Attention Decay Through Client-Side Data Decimation and Structural Healing
abstract: Enterprise analytics powered by large language models hosted on the cloud are suffering from crippling costs caused by tokens, "Lost in the Middle Syndrome", and privacy exposure. In this paper, we present AK Aletheo Pro, an open-source decentralized web application that can perform secure browser-edge analytics with an innovative self-healing "Neural Handshake" framework, which extracts a statistical "Data DNA Profile" directly on the client side. A proof-of-concept implementation reveals that by replacing multi-megabyte CSV database transfers with an 85 KB statistical approximation there is a significant reduction of 68.8x query latency (124s-> 1.8s), and a 1200x reduction of query costs in enterprise analytics scenarios. A Structural Healing Engine performs JSON schema validation and a Complexity Scorer optimizes visualization rendering, and a Symmetrical Multilingual Engine maintains bidirectional language translation. The application was tested on a 10,000-row database, rendering 60 FPS consistently while maintaining an offline auto-fallback mechanism with 100% effectiveness. An excellent System Usability Scale SUS of 90.8 was recorded. This suggests that AK Aletheo Pro could serve as a secure alternative to enterprise and healthcare information analytics systems.

title: Synthetic Hegemony: Generative AI and the Democratic Risks of Language Infrastructure
abstract: This article introduces hybrid barbarism as a concept with two co-present modalities and theorizes their convergence under generative artificial intelligence. Hybrid barbarism is a persistent public-sphere pathology in which algorithmic infrastructures amplify emotive tribalism while the civic norms of shared inquiry atrophy. Platformized media sediment a distribution modality (HB-D) that rewards circulation; language-synthesis systems add a generation modality (HB-S) that assembles plausibility at the moment of production. Their interlocking generation–distribution–re-generation loop erodes shared facts, blurs provenance, and overloads institutions designed for fixed objects and stable authorship. I identify three mechanisms distinctive to HB-S — epistemic delegation, synthetic neutrality, and authorlessness — and specify the boundary conditions under which each becomes pathological rather than benign or even corrective. Reading three democratic contexts (the United States and Brazil; South Korea; Hungary and Turkey) through the framework, I derive three strategic manifestations — epistemic fragmentation, institutional sabotage, and systemic control — and state the conditions that select among them. Against approaches that merely police “bad content,” I argue for a Democratic Epistemic Infrastructure: public-interest language models with auditable lineage, civic AI literacy that restores critical distance, and risk-based provenance and audit regimes in high-stakes domains. The article is a concept paper; the case readings are advanced as derived expectations rather than demonstrated findings, and a separate preregistered empirical study is designed to render the claims falsifiable and cumulative.

title: Data Governance as a Decision Variable: A Model-Driven Decision Support System for Budget Allocation in Generative AI Adoption
abstract: Corporate adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is routinely managed as a problem of technological scaling: firms decide how much to use the tool while treating the quality of the underlying knowledge base as a given feature of the environment. This paper shows that such a formulation is structurally incomplete and yields systematically biased recommendations. We present a model-driven decision support system (DSS) that endogenises data governance through an explicit budgetary variable, I Q , and that jointly solves the allocation between investment in information quality and the intensity of algorithmic use, x. The formal core is a non-linear, two-variable optimisation model in which data quality Q(I Q) simultaneously modulates the value production function and the cost structure, through a variable-cost coefficient γ(Q) and a convexity exponent δ (Q) that captures the agency cost of human oversightthe Babysitting Tax. We prove analytically the existence of a scissor effect (data degradation shifts marginal value downwards and marginal cost upwards at the same time), we characterise the Marginal Profit Destruction Zone, and we establish the existence of a viability corridor for governance investment, bounded both from below and from above. We further prove that, for firms with severely fragmented data architectures, Π * (I Q) is non-monotonic: the first units of governance investment reduce profit before increasing it, which gives the decision the character of a big push rather than of a marginal adjustment. On this core we build the artefact: a five-layer architecture-telemetry, estimation, optimisation, policy and interface-whose policy layer materialises in three executable budgetary decision rules (marginal parity, condition-precedent threshold and dynamic operating ceiling). We show that these three rules decentralise the centralised optimum between the Finance function and the Data function through the exchange of two scalars only, and that the convergence condition of the protocol coincides exactly with the second-order condition of the problem. The two-variable problem further reduces to a scalar search of logarithmic cost, which makes the artefact computable in real time. Simulation-based evaluation over two calibrated organisational profiles quantifies the value of the artefact: a firm with fragmented data that applies the conventional static model over-uses the technology by 27.8%, believes it is obtaining a profit of +32.0 monetary units and in fact realises a loss of 36.7, whereas the DSS solution places it at +8.4. The decomposition of the scissor effect reveals that the cost channel-ignored by the previous literature-accounts for a further contraction of the optimum of 91.7% on top of the contraction already caused by the loss of value.

title: LLM-powered SOC Assistants: Prompt Injection Risks in Threat Triage
abstract: Security Operations Centres (SOCs) are increasingly deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants to accelerate threat triage, alert prioritisation, and incident response. While these systems offer substantial productivity gains, their integration into security-critical pipelines introduces a novel and underexplored attack surface: prompt injection. This paper investigates how adversaries can manipulate LLM-powered SOC assistants by embedding malicious instructions within security alerts, log entries, threat intelligence feeds, and risk-scoring pipelines, causing the assistant to suppress high-severity alerts, downgrade risk scores, or recommend unsafe remediation actions. Grounded in practitioner insight gathered from a serving SIEM manager at a Google SecOps deployment with a 98.4% automation rate, we develop a SOC-specific prompt injection threat model anchored in the MITRE ATT&CK framework and the SANS PICERL incident response methodology. We conduct a simulated evaluation across three production-grade LLMs integrated into a synthetic risk-based alerting environment, measuring Alert Suppression Rate (ASR-SOC), Risk Score Manipulation Rate (RSMR), False Negative Injection Rate (FNIR), and Tool Misuse Rate (TMR). Our findings reveal that injection payloads targeting the risk-based alerting threshold mechanism achieve FNIR values exceeding 85% without mitigation. We further introduce the Triage Paradox, wherein models optimised for low false-positive rates exhibit the highest susceptibility to risk-score manipulation. Finally, we propose the Guardian Framework, a layered defence architecture incorporating alert-channel isolation, dual-LLM triage verification, and SOC-specific role-based access control. Experimental results demonstrate that the Guardian Framework reduces injection-induced misclassification by an average of 76% across all evaluated models and attack vectors.

title: Tears and Rain: Part 3: Resurrection -Phase IV
abstract: The idea of illustration as a traditional art or craft is increasingly untenable when both the concept of an image and the subjectivity of the author and reader have irrevocably changed. As illustration is embedded into online and animated environments, it necessarily extends into the data sets used to train large language models (LLM) for AI-generative art applications. This transformation fits the theoretical shift from postmodernism to alter-modernism and presents the role of the illustrator in a transitional stage, to which we appear blind. Originality is becoming a rarity among seemingly ubiquitous and unique images that proliferate in the hypermediated environment in which many illustrators must practise. This third and final part of the extended article seeks to further explore the idea of originality in reference to AI's ability to generate images with little or no technical expertise under the framing of 'tears and rain'. It shows how the subjectivity of the illustrator, along with the materiality of the image object, has changed in ways that may not at first seem apparent, indicating a new mode of illustrational research that seeks to identify new forms of authorial intent designed to cut through visual noise. It is incumbent on illustration research to register this blind spot.

title: LLM-Computed Contextual Surprisal in Financial News: Associations with Market Repricing
abstract: Financial-text research has established that the direction of language matters for markets. This paper examines a complementary property: whether realised financial-news wording is unexpected relative to the recent news environment. I use 4.48 million deduplicated English headlines from the public FNSPID dataset over 2014-2023 to construct a daily, clusterweighted contextual-surprisal measure with the causal language model Qwen 3.5-9B. The score is paired, headline by headline, with FinBERT sentiment so that adverse but routine wording is distinguished from adverse and contextually unexpected wording. The main result is contemporaneous. In a 2014-2020 development sample and an independent 2021-2023 holdout, a greater prevalence of unexpectedly negative language is associated with a larger increase in the VIX, a lower SPY return, and higher abnormal SPY dollar volume. The reported associations survive the stated within-family false-discovery-rate adjustment in both samples. A fixed-input comparison across Qwen, Gemma, and Llama shows strong agreement under two pre-computed token-aggregation variants. The evidence is consistent with the view that negative information which departs from a recent linguistic baseline is associated with broad same-day risk repricing. It provides a reproducible headline-level construction for subsequent research on timestamped news, temporal ordering, and the incremental value of contextual surprisal relative to established risk indicators.

title: Towards Autonomous Structural Engineering: A Multi-Agent Artificial Intelligence Framework for Intelligent Design, Analysis, Optimization, and Decision Support
abstract: Structural engineering decisions have historically depended on a licensed engineer's direct authorship of every design, analysis, and compliance check, even as computer-aided engineering, building information modeling, and digital twins have progressively digitized the information those decisions rely upon. Recent large language model (LLM) agents, physics-informed learning, and multi-agent construction systems each automate part of this process, but no existing framework combines persistent multi-agent coordination, physics-and code-verifiable reasoning, and a quantified, auditable account of how much decision authority an artificial intelligence system should hold. This paper proposes Autonomous Structural Engineering (ASE), a conceptual and theoretical framework in which specialized artificial intelligence agents collaborate across the structural engineering lifecycle within a six-layer architecture, coordinated through a proposed Engineering Agent Communication Protocol, and governed by a mathematical formalism comprising a Verification Score, a Trust Score, and an Autonomy Gating Function. The framework's principal contributions are threefold: a multi-agent architecture for autonomous structural engineering workflows; a trust-aware autonomy governance mechanism that regulates AI decision authority; and a human-supervised deployment framework integrating verification, reliability, and engineering accountability. An illustrative, hypothetical worked example demonstrates the operational logic of these mechanisms trust assessment, autonomy regulation, and decision routing without constituting empirical validation of an implemented system. The paper closes by outlining the implementation, benchmarking, and expert-evaluation pathway required before such a framework could be responsibly validated and considered for deployment in safety-critical structural engineering practice.

title: A cloud native framework for Automated Image Generation using Generative AI
abstract: The increased demand for high quality digital images in e- commerce, marketing, and media production has revealed many flaws in traditional photography workflows. Generally, the conventional image shoots need a studio setup, lighting and heavy manual work, which is time consuming and resource draining when expanding visual production. On the contrary, generative AI brings in a whole different scenario, where one can synthesize photorealistic images straight away from text descriptions. Herein, we present a cloud-based generative framework for multi-domain image creation, structured prompt orchestration, and diffusion-based synthesis models. In doing so, this study held a comparative analysis involving various generative image models regarding the responsiveness of prompts for visual consistency in a generation pipeline. Large language models refine user prompts into structured instructions for the generation process while reference- image conditioning ensures visual attributes such as lighting, composition, and tone. It runs on a serverless architecture for intake coordination in output requests with storage allocated to generated images and metadata. Furthermore, the platform allows for prompt editing and attribute-weighted prompt interpretation for consistency across different visual contexts. It therefore suggests a scalable framework for automatic visual content generation within product visualization, marketing creatives, and digital media production in general.

title: Moving Targets: Promissory Instability in the Pricing and Access Terms of Generative AI Subscription Services (2024-2026)
abstract: Between October 2024 and July 2026, the leading commercial providers of generative artificial intelligence repeatedly modified the pricing, usage limits, and access terms of subscription services after consumers had already paid for them. This paper documents that pattern through a rapid multiple-case documentary analysis of four providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Moonshot AI), drawing exclusively on dated public sources: official announcements, technology press coverage, community bug trackers, and the public record of two formal legal actions. Seventeen documented episodes are organized into a chronology and classified with a two-dimensional framework defined by the trigger of the change (exogenous shocks of capacity, regulation, or safety versus endogenous commercial strategy) and the quality of its communication (managed transitions versus unmanaged or repeatedly revised promises). Two findings emerge. First, post-purchase modification is not an incident but an industry-wide operating pattern, and it moves in both directions: restrictions and reversals, price increases and price cuts. Second, formal accountability (a proposed class action against Anthropic over advertised Claude Max usage multipliers and a regulatory enforcement action against Microsoft over Copilot-linked price increases) concentrates in one quadrant of the framework: endogenous changes communicated in unmanaged or shifting ways. The paper argues that this instability is a structural consequence of selling elastic promises against inelastic compute, discusses implications for consumer protection in AI markets, and proposes an agenda for longitudinal, archive-based tracking of subscription terms.

title: Consumer AI and Exploitation of Information-processing Frictions
abstract: We study whether LLMs, as increasingly accessible consumer-side AI tools, would eliminate consumer exploitation targeting information-processing frictions or merely relocate it. LLM adoption does not improve products on its own: firms keep exploiting maximally until a rising share of expert consumers tips them into competition over product value. Even then, firms counter with adversarial investment that corrupts capability enhancement by LLMs. This arms race arises in equilibrium, persists as adoption broadens, peaks then fades as LLMs improve, and can neutralize consumer gains when adversarial investment is cheap. Consumer-side AI thus reshapes cognitive exploitation rather than eliminating it.

title: The Syntactic Exoskeleton: How Generative AI Homogenizes the Structure of Arabic-L1 English Academic Writing
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is deeply embedded in second-language (L2) writing, yet its structural impact on student essays, distinct from vocabulary, remains under-examined. This comparative corpus study analyzes 423 essays by Arabic-L1 undergraduates, contrasting unassisted exam writing (n = 339) with GenAI-mediated assignments (n = 84). Computational analysis reveals that GenAI mediation severely homogenizes structure, compressing sentence-length variance eighteen-fold while densifying clauses. Unassisted texts display the additive, paratactic clause-chaining characteristic of Arabic L1 transfer, including a long tail of extended sentences that GenAI eliminates. This study argues the tool acts less as a scaffold than a "syntactic exoskeleton," replacing the learner’s paratactic fingerprint with a uniform, Anglo-academic template. Simultaneously, surface proficiency markers rise sharply (CEFR rating 56% to 71%), producing a fluency illusion consistent with the LLM Fallacy. As writers experience fluent output as their own, the loss at the textual level is not a loss of authorship but of structural repertoire. Consequently, L2 writing assessment must pivot to valuing the developmental friction of drafting and to teaching "Algorithmic Rhetorical Resistance" to protect the diverse structural representation of World Englishes.

title: Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour
abstract: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
abstract: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

title: When Memory Lies: An Empirical Study of Spatial Memory Staleness in VLM Agents
abstract: Memory-augmented VLM agents act on persistent spatial knowledge, yet that knowledge silently goes stale as the environment changes. We ask what happens when an agent must reconcile a confident memory claim with a contradicting observation, and whether current models can catch the conflict before it becomes a safety-relevant mistake. Using a dynamic FrozenLake testbed, we pair a staleness-detection task with a downstream navigation task across three closed-source models and three open-weight VLMs under both text and image inputs (1,800 detection runs, and 12,000 text-mode navigation episodes over four LLM navigators at a shared 50-seed scale). Three findings emerge. First, text solvability does not imply visual grounding: models that flag stale entries reliably from text nonetheless span vision F1 from 0.887 down to 0.067 on the identical grids, and the weakest keeps making fluent, confident decisions that ignore the image. Second, consuming stale memory without an audit is a safety liability: in our primary GPT-4o setting, an agent that trusts raw memory dies more than twice as often as the same agent given no memory at all. Third, auditing helps but does not close the gap: a transparent read-time filter removes much of the safety cost in text mode, yet even oracle stale labels bring no further significant gain on the current grid size, and when visual auditing is unreliable, filtering yields no consistent benefit. Together these results frame spatial-memory staleness as a safety failure mode and isolate reliable visual grounding and action selection under memory--observation conflict as the central open challenges for memory-augmented agents.

title: The Personalization Mirage: How LLMs Fabricate User Profiles, and Why Self-Monitoring Misleads
abstract: Personalized LLMs with persistent memory are increasingly deployed, yet the faithfulness of their user models remains unexamined. We study over-inference (OI): the phenomenon where LLMs fabricate user attributes beyond what evidence supports. We introduce MirageBench, comprising 150 personas balanced across stereotypical, counter-stereotypical, and neutral profiles, 6 personalization tasks spanning an ``imagination gradient'', a four-way faithfulness taxonomy operationalized by an independent judge (validated against a blind human annotator on 400 claims: Cohen's kappa = 0.863 four-class, kappa = 0.900 binary), and a leaderboard of 12 models across 7 families on 143616 judged claims. We find that over-inference is pervasive: every one of the 12 models over-infers 35%--49% of its claims (cross-model mean 41.6%; claim-weighted 41.8%), with no model in this evaluation escaping it. Most strikingly, we surface a Self-Monitoring Inversion: at the model-selection level, models' self-assessed OI is negatively rank-correlated with their judge-measured OI (rho = -0.60, p = 0.044; exploratory, wide bootstrap CI [-0.90, +0.06], n = 12). The models that report the least over-inference tend to be flagged as fabricating the most, so self-reported confidence is a misleading signal for comparing models, even though within a single model self-audit still ranks that model's own claims moderately well (AUROC 0.58--0.83). We further show that OI is task-dependent (27%--59%) and that, in a multi-turn pilot, inferred attributes accumulate approximately linearly with little revision. MirageBench positions external verification, rather than model self-report, as a more reliable foundation for trustworthy personalization.

title: FinReportBench: Measuring and Improving Institution-Grade Financial Report Generation
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent financial analysis, but fluency alone does not establish whether a report is suitable for institutional delivery. We introduce FinReportBench, an expert-grounded benchmark for measuring and improving institution-grade financial report generation. Expert review reveals recurring gaps in report identity, institutional components, source discipline, and visual delivery. We derive a 35-item rubric through expert partial orders, multimodal evidence, and audits of decision boundaries, covering deliverability, report identity, and institutional completeness. Starting from 10,000 balanced Chinese and English financial-research source records, we curate 244 bilingual tasks across three research objects and two input tiers. Each task separates the public query, reconstructed research trajectory, and hidden source packet. Three independent judge families reproduce the expert partial order at near-ceiling rates, showing that bounded, observable criteria support reliable evaluation. Across nine model families, basic deliverability is nearly saturated, while report identity and institutional completeness remain the primary bottlenecks. The largest cross-model gaps concern generation-trace control, information density, and data discipline rather than basic report framing. We then use benchmark-guided skill distillation to turn recurrent failures into reusable generation and self-review constraints. Across five model families, the evolved skill improves mean G1 by 33.85 points and mean G2 by 13.83 points over paired no-skill runs while preserving G0 for every pair. Code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/MisterBrookT/finreportbench.

title: A Zero-Trust Hybrid Architecture for Enterprise LLM Deployment
abstract: Enterprise adoption of large language model (LLM) APIs creates two acute operational challenges: (1) data sovereignty-how to use cloud AI without exposing confidential client data; and (2) API drift-how to maintain stable AI behaviour when cloud providers update models without notice. This paper presents a zero-trust hybrid middleware architecture deployed across multiple enterprise clients under active client confidentiality agreements. The architecture comprises four composable components: the Capability-Preserving Anonymization Protocol (CPAP), a reversible semantic masking layer; a Dynamic Router implementing the Routing Score Matrix (RSM) with a circuit-breaker penalty box; a Local Verification Council of deterministic guardrails; and an AI Ledger that accumulates operational intelligence to counteract model drift. We present the system design, complete architectural specifications, and reproducible benchmark evaluations on a synthetic enterprise dataset (n = 100 prompts, seed = 42). CPAP achieves 100% masking accuracy and perfect reversibility at 10,897 prompts/second. The Dynamic Router delivers 67.1% cost reduction against an always-GPT-4o baseline while retaining 90.4% of peak quality. The AI Ledger reduces drift-induced error rates by 70.0% through accumulated corrections. All components are released as open-source reference implementations under the MIT License.

title: Mapping the Scientific Landscape of AI Governance in Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of Scopus-indexed Publications from 2019 to 2025
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed educational systems, creating new opportunities for personalized learning, academic support, institutional decision-making, and educational innovation. However, its increasing use has also raised concerns related to ethics, academic integrity, transparency, data privacy, algorithmic accountability, AI literacy, and institutional policy. This study mapped the scientific landscape of AI governance in education using a bibliometric analysis of 1,649 Scopus-indexed journal articles published from 2019 to 2025. Biblioshiny and VOSviewer were used to examine publication growth, source productivity, country and institutional contributions, author productivity, globally cited documents, keyword co-occurrence, collaboration networks, bibliographic coupling, thematic evolution, and thematic mapping. Findings revealed a sharp increase in publications, from 4 articles in 2019 to 917 articles in 2025, indicating the rapid expansion of the field, particularly after the emergence of generative AI and ChatGPT. The United States, United Kingdom, and China were the leading countries, while Hong Kong-based universities emerged as highly productive institutions. Keyword and thematic analyses showed that the field is anchored in artificial intelligence, ethics, education, AI literacy, academic integrity, generative AI, explainable AI, regulation, data ethics, and governance. Collaboration and bibliographic coupling networks further demonstrated the interdisciplinary and international character of the field, although research influence remains concentrated among highly productive countries and institutions. The thematic map suggests that AI governance in education remains a formative research domain, with central themes still requiring deeper theoretical and empirical development. The study concludes that future research should advance contextsensitive governance frameworks, strengthen empirical policy studies, and promote inclusive international collaboration for responsible AI use in education

title: LLM Agents in Transportation-enabled Service Platforms: From Behavioral Simulation to Platform Decision Support
abstract: Transportation-enabled service (TRENS) platforms, including ride-hailing, food and grocery delivery, and crowdsourced logistics, are platform markets in which pricing, matching, routing, service recovery, and information design continuously reshape the behavior of customers, drivers, couriers, merchants, and operators. This survey asks where large language model (LLM) agents can credibly improve such systems. The opportunity, we argue, is not replacing mature operations research (OR), machine learning (ML), or reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines, but two interfaces those pipelines handle poorly. First, behavioral agents can enrich offline policy evaluation by simulating heterogeneous stakeholder responses to changed prices, incentives, service promises, and information structures. Second, operational agents can translate unstructured language, documents, regulations, complaints, and managerial intent into structured inputs for platform workflows and optimization systems. Reviewing classical TRENS baselines, LLM behavioral- and operational-agent studies, and industrial systems from Meituan, DiDi, Instacart, Uber Freight, and DoorDash, we find a consistent pattern: current production evidence is concentrated in semantic-heavy workflow layers such as customer service, catalog/query understanding, document processing, internal analytics, and passenger or logistics copilots, while public evidence of LLMs deployed directly on the critical operational path for real-time dispatching or pricing remains limited. The resulting research agenda prioritizes revealed-preference calibration of behavioral agents, bilevel models coupling platform controls with simulated stakeholder response, explicit latency and verification contracts for hybrid systems, and TRENS-specific benchmarks that jointly evaluate behavior, optimization, and workflow automation.

title: CVExploit: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated CVE Exploit Generation and Validation
abstract: Automated exploit generation remains difficult because exploitability validation is iterative. It depends on target-specific constraints, runtime feedback, and error recovery. While recent large language model (LLM) systems can assist in code synthesis, direct generation frequently falls short. Crucially, exploit development entails multidisciplinary expertise and substantial cognitive demands that a single model operating in isolation can scarcely accommodate. This paper studies a narrower and practical task: controlled CVE exploit reproduction for network-based targets that are already assumed to be vulnerable. We present CVExploit, an expert-driven orchestration framework in which an autonomous reasoning agent acts as a senior analyst, coordinating specialized tool manipulation to dynamically address emerging subproblems during exploit generation. The framework combines retrieved context, workflow-guided code construction, execution-grounded validation, and iterative correction without giving the model CVE-specific proof-of-concept code. We evaluate CVExploit on 32 CVEs in isolated environments. We measure effectiveness, robustness, efficiency, and component contribution. CVExploit achieves a 65.6% overall success rate, with 18 successful CVEs on the first attempt and 21 within five attempts. The ablation study shows that validation and refinement produce the largest gains. The efficiency analysis shows the cost of that added reliability. Taken together, the results suggest that the main value of LLM-based exploit generation lies not in one-shot code synthesis, but in reducing human cognitive overhead by orchestrating and decomposing the inherently complex and multidisciplinary exploit development process into manageable subproblems.

title: Toward a Cognitive Enterprise
abstract: The enterprise is a sociotechnical negentropic network of resources, processes, and stakeholders that converts environmental signal into ordered, exportable stakeholder value. This paper proposes a foundational architecture for understanding that system: the Cognitive Stack, a five-layer hierarchy of cognitive assets (Data, Information, Explicit Knowledge, Tacit Knowledge, Wisdom) divided by the Context Frontier, the line separating what can be processed symbolically and syntactically without context (in-silico) from what requires somatic, semantic (in-cerebro and in-viscera) reasoning. Central to this architecture is a precise, operational definition of wisdom as the capacity to choose and deploy reasoning modes – deductive, inductive, and abductive – each with a distinct relationship to AI augmentation. As the transaction costs of explicit-layer cognitive work approach zero – driven by the microprocessor, the internet, and a range of modern AI models, including LLMs – firm boundaries are no longer determined primarily by transactional friction or resource stocks, but by the preservation and governance of high-context tacit knowledge and wisdom, which remain unexportable. The paper extends and sharpens the existing theoretical tradition rather than displacing it, and introduces the Cognitive Enterprise as the organizational form that manages this architecture deliberately.

title: Rank Order is Mostly Noise Confidence Intervals for Brand Visibility in AI Answer Engines, and a Failure of The Citation-Extraction Layer
abstract: Vendors and agencies increasingly publish ordered leaderboards of which brands large language models recommend, almost always as bare rank orders without any statement of uncertainty. We measured 4,497 answers across 9 B2B software categories and 90 products, using 5 AI engines and 10 pre-registered buyer prompts at 10 runs per prompt per engine, and attached a 95% confidence interval to every share estimate. In 6 of 9 categories the first-ranked product is not statistically separable from the second. In the most extreme case the top four products are mutually indistinguishable. Category leaders cluster in a narrow band of 16.4% to 25.0% share of model, suggesting a ceiling on how dominant any single brand becomes in a competitive category. We conclude that published rank orders in this field convey less information than they appear to, and that reporting a rank without an interval is not a presentational shortcut but a substantive overstatement. We additionally report a negative methodological result. Our own citation-extraction layer failed unevenly across engines: one engine returned zero distinct cited domains in all 9 categories, a second returned 1-2 against a list cap of 5, and 39% of extracted citations resolved to a platform redirect wrapper rather than a source. We therefore withdraw the citation-level findings of an earlier draft and report the extraction failure itself, because it has a consequence beyond this paper: citation-share figures are published across this sector without any disclosure of extraction quality, and our results indicate that quality cannot be assumed.

title: Tracing the Heart: An Evidence-Linked Pipeline for Heart-Failure Feature Engineering
abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. This is especially pronounced in heart failure, which affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults and requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches offer only partial automation with limited maintainability and evidence traceability. We developed the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering, and evaluated it on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM. Adding the aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping, and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness scored the features at 81.5% of maximum points. These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data, though evaluation was limited to a single-institution cohort and external validation is needed.

title: The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images
abstract: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

title: A Hierarchical Shapley Framework for Crash Severity Prediction and Factor Attribution with Large Language Models
abstract: Crash severity analysis guides the safety measures that reduce road deaths. It tells agencies which factors raise injury risk and where to place engineering, enforcement, and design measures. Narratives are the raw data recorded by the police, and they hold more information than the coded data derived from them later. Machine learning and language models can read text narratives, but current methods for interpreting these models remain limited. This paper models crash severity from narrative data and interprets the resulting predictions. Both textual and numerical data are organized into structured text about people, vehicles, roads, and the environment, in which every factor occupies exactly one sentence under a fixed topic header. A Qwen backbone with Query-Based Global Aggregation (QBGA) predicts severity from this text, and a Shapley module then attributes each prediction at the topic, sentence, and term levels. The three levels are derived from one cooperative game through the levels structure value, so the value of a topic equals the sum of the values of the sentences and of the terms inside it. The framework is tested on 17,976 pedestrian crashes recorded in Hong Kong from 2018 to 2024. It reaches a macro F1-score of 0.81 and stays balanced across the fatal, serious, and slight classes. The ablation shows that QBGA gives the largest single gain, and the attribution results stay stable across model families and across years. Safety agencies can read the topic level to see which factor group dominates fatal crashes for each vehicle type and rank program priorities from it. The sentence level shows why one crash turned fatal, so site work and enforcement can target the mechanism behind that case rather than a generic risk profile.

title: The Last Costly Signal: How Generative AI Collapses Competence Signaling and Why Liability Sustains Markets for Expert Services
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has reduced the cost of producing convincing artifacts of expertise—reports, analyses, proposals, references to a polished body of work—to nearly zero. Signaling theory makes a sharp prediction for this case: signals whose informational content rests on their production cost lose that content when production becomes cheap. We formalize this prediction for markets for expert services, a class of credence goods, by modeling generative AI as acompression of the discernible headroom between what machines produce at negligible cost and what buyers can distinguish at all. Below a critical headroom, no separating equilibrium in production-side signals exists; the market pools, high-competence providers earn no premium, and those with outside options exit—Akerlof’s lemons dynamic. We then show that an outcome-contingent signal—a warranty backed by damages 𝐷 with ex-post verifiability 𝜑—restores full separation for any level of AI capability whenever 𝜑𝐷 ≥ 𝑣, where 𝑣 is the value of a solved problem. The expected cost of liability depends on whether the problem is actually solved, not on how cheaply documents are produced; it is therefore invariant to AI capability and preserves single crossing when all production-side signals fail. A corollary shows that provenance certification (e.g., C2PA content credentials), whose cost is type-independent, cannot restore separation. Monte-Carlo simulations of an agent-based market illustrate the dynamics: after an AI capability shock, the high type’s premium collapses (in our baseline from 20% to 0% of the transaction value) and high-type participation falls from 88% to 68% when only production-side signals are available, while both are fully sustained when liability contracts are offered. Two further results endogenize the institutions behind the contract: because civil-procedure costs contain a fixed block while recoveries scale with the claim, liability signaling has a minimum ticket size 𝑣min below which no credible enforcement threat exists and the market for small expert engagements pools without contractual remedy; and with liability insurance, the signal-effective quantity is not the damages promised but the risk the seller retains or is individually priced on—under pooled premiums a warranty separates only if the deductible satisfies the original condition, while experience rating restores it slowly, on the insurer’s information timescale. We state the falsification conditions of the theory and propose a preregistered choice-based conjoint experiment with business decision-makers in the German-speaking B2B expert-services market—the empirical intersection (liability signal × AI disclosure × B2B expertise × willingness to pay) that, to our knowledge, no existing study covers.

title: A Technology-Function-Guided Patent Drafting Framework Incorporating Etfm and RAG-Based Large Language Model
abstract: Traditional patent drafting is time-consuming and labor-intensive, creating a bottleneck for innovation-driven industries. To address this, this study proposes a technology-function-guided patent drafting workflow that contributes in three respects. First, a computer-aided Technology-Function Matrix (eTFM) is extended from an analytical tool into a generation-control layer, where high-potential technology-function pairs directly guide the drafting direction and the same matrix is then reused to verify that each draft falls within its intended cell, forming a closed generation-and-validation loop that distinguishes this workflow from qualitative structured-ideation (e.g., TRIZ-based) and full-document generation approaches. Second, ontology-based retrieval and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ground the Large Language Model (LLM) in domain prior art, while prompt engineering coordinates a multi-stage pipeline that produces invention concepts, abstracts, titles, descriptions, claims, and IPC classifications. Third, the workflow is validated through a case study in the sustainable energy storage domain. The evaluation indicates that the generated drafts maintain non-trivial semantic differentiation from retrieved prior art, exhibit structurally organized claim content, and remain consistent with their assigned technical domain and technology-function targets. These results are interpreted as evidence of feasibility for an AI-assisted patent drafting tool that supports expert-reviewed first drafts, rather than as a determination of legal novelty or patentability.

title: From Natural Language to Optimization Models: A Survey of LLM-based Autoformulation
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based autoformulation is a rapidly growing and promising direction for translating natural-language descriptions into formal optimization models and solver-ready artifacts, yet the field lacks a systematic and in-depth synthesis. This survey fills that gap by proposing a unified four-stage pipeline and taxonomy that organize stage-specific challenges and techniques. We trace benchmark development and analyze datasets by input, output, and construction process to clarify the capabilities they evaluate. We also propose a two-level taxonomy of outcome-and system-level metrics, together with practical metric-selection guidelines. Finally, we synthesize the insights across methods, data, and evaluation to identify future directions and support more reliable and comparable research.

title: AI-Enabled Credit Assessment for MSMEs: A Framework for Transparency and Inclusion
abstract: Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are a critical component of the Indian economy, contributing 30% to GDP and 60% to employment. Yet, a severe credit gap persists, with the sector receiving only ~16% of total bank credit. This financing constraint stifles growth and reflects a fundamental market failure. This research directly responds to the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) mandate for efficient, transparent credit by building FinTech a proof-of-concept prototype that operationalizes India's digital public infrastructure (IndiaStack). Our system automates credit assessment by integrating consented data flows from GSTN, bank transactions, and metadata. A rule-based engine executes a multi-faceted financial analysis (liquidity, DSCR, cash flow stability, sectoral NPA exposure), while an integrated Large Language Model (LLM) generates narrative, explainable AI (XAI) rationales for full transparency. The pivotal achievement is a reduction in credit decision time to under 15-20 seconds. This demonstrates a viable model for banks to drastically reduce operational costs and, critically, has the potential to mitigate NPAs through a more dynamic, forward-looking risk assessment that surpasses static collateral evaluation. By providing a tangible blueprint to bridge the gap between IndiaStack's potential and banking practice, this work offers a strategic tool for policymakers, financial institutions and fintech developers. It enables a shift towards a resilient, inclusive lending ecosystem that unlocks the full potential of MSMEs, directly fueling India's broader digitalization vision and sustainable macroeconomic health.

title: Governance Gaps in Human-Directed AI Development: Empirical Evidence, Theoretical Foundations, and the Human-AI Co-Authorship Protocol (HAICA)
abstract: The rapid normalization of human-directed AI development — the practice of producing functional software artifacts through natural language instruction of AI systems — has created a structural governance gap that existing legal, security, and accountability frameworks are not equipped to address. This paper identifies, characterizes, and quantifies that gap through a systematic review of empirical evidence, and proposes a theoretically grounded governance architecture as the primary research output. Drawing on published security research across 5,600 publicly accessible AI-assisted applications, vulnerability analysis of outputs from 100+ large language models (Veracode, 2025), and CVE attribution data (Cloud Security Alliance, 2026), this paper establishes that: (1) 45% of AI-generated code introduces OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities; (2) AI-assisted commits expose credentials at 2.1× the rate of humanauthored commits; (3) CVEs attributable to AI-generated code increased 483% between January and March 2026; and (4) a novel, previously uncharacterized vulnerability class — packaging configuration exposure — is not addressed by any existing static analysis tooling. The paper argues that these failures share a single structural cause: existing governance frameworks assume the human author and the code author are the same entity, an assumption that fails when human cognitive intent is translated into executable systems through an AI-mediated execution channel. To address this gap, the paper introduces three original theoretical constructs — the cognitive instrument, prompt lineage as an authorship evidence category, and packaging configuration as a formal vulnerability class — and presents the Human-AI Co-Authorship Protocol (HAICA) as an operational governance architecture derived from these constructs. HAICA has been independently assessed at a composite score of 9.5/10 across nine governance dimensions and is published under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20509820.

title: From Product Search to Preference Articulation: The Economics of Agentic Commerce
abstract: Generative AI is moving digital commerce from browsing toward agentic search, in which consumers delegate product discovery to AI agents. We model manual search, which accurately evaluates a limited product set, against agentic search, which screens a broad catalog using noisy representations of preferences and products. Preference complexity measures the number of satisfaction-relevant dimensions that are difficult to articulate before search but readily evaluated upon inspection. Consumers hold a finite attention budget and choose both a search regime and how intensively to use it; under agentic search that intensity is the depth of refinement of the agent's representation. First, as preference complexity grows, manual search eventually collapses: inspection ceases, mismatch returns to its no-search level, and platform revenue falls to zero. Agentic search does not: complexity raises the marginal value of refinement, so when refinement is worthwhile in the least-complex category, refinement remains positive at every level. Articulation effort and mismatch may increase, but mismatch remains below the no-search level and revenue remains positive. Second, the platform ranks search regimes by conversion revenue, whereas the consumer also bears search expenditure. When manual inspection is sufficiently inexpensive, agentic search becomes revenue-superior before it becomes privately optimal for the consumer. Over the intervening range, the consumer rationally continues manual search, creating an adoption lag. Third, the platform may provide lower AI fidelity to consumers with greater attention capacity because they can compensate through additional refinement, producing an inverted fidelity allocation. Agentic commerce thus shifts scarcity from product search to preference articulation, implying that platforms should weigh consumer articulation burden alongside conversion when evaluating adoption and designing fidelity.

title: Schema Persistence and Field-Role Organization: Observable Dimensions in Black-Box LLM Interaction Traces
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in multi-step interactions, yet comparatively little attention has been given to how the visible organization of their output traces changes across interaction steps. This study examines trace-visible structural organization under controlled perturbation in a commercial GPT-family deployment. Using fixed initialization and a JSON-structured observational scaffold, the analysis separates two observable dimensions: schema persistence and field-role organization. Across the primary controlled variants, the shared outer schema remains visible while prior field-role organization is not preserved. The observed configurations include container overflow, field-role redistribution, and field compression. These findings indicate that schema-level continuity alone is not sufficient evidence of tracelevel structural stability when interaction requirements change. The paper contributes a bounded observational distinction and a procedure for examining structured interaction traces without evaluating task performance, estimating pattern prevalence, or making claims about internal model mechanisms.

title: Prompt Engineering for Large Language Models
Development and Testing of Retrieval Augmented Generation in Large Language Models
FinRobot: An Open-Source AI Agent Platform for Financial Applications using Large Language Models
Ai Agents in Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis: Automating the Analytic Hierarchy Process with Large Language Models
PathoScribe: Transforming Pathology Data into a Living Library with a Unified LLM-Driven Framework for Semantic Retrieval and Clinical Integration
abstract: Pathology underpins modern diagnosis and cancer care, yet its most valuable asset, the accumulated experience encoded in millions of narrative reports, remains largely inaccessible. Although institutions are rapidly digitizing pathology workflows, storing data without effective mechanisms for retrieval and reasoning risks transforming archives into a passive data repository, where institutional knowledge exists but cannot meaningfully inform patient care. True progress requires not only digitization, but the ability for pathologists to interrogate prior similar cases in real time while evaluating a new diagnostic dilemma.We present PathoScribe, a unified retrieval-augmented large language model (LLM) framework designed to transform static pathology archives into a searchable, reasoning-enabled living library. PathoScribe enables natural language case exploration, automated cohort construction, clinical question answering, immunohistochemistry (IHC) panel recommendation, and prompt-controlled report transformation within a single architecture.Evaluated on 70,000 multi-institutional surgical pathology reports, PathoScribe achieved perfect Recall@10 for natural language case retrieval and demonstrated high-quality retrieval-grounded reasoning (mean reviewer score 4.56/5). Critically, the system operationalized automated cohort construction from free-text eligibility criteria, assembling research-ready cohorts in minutes (mean 9.2 minutes) with 91.3% agreement to human reviewers and no eligible cases incorrectly excluded, representing orders-of-magnitude reductions in time and cost compared to traditional manual chart review.By unifying retrieval and reasoning, PathoScribe enables pathologists to move from isolated case interpretation toward data-informed decision-making grounded in institutional precedent. This work establishes a scalable foundation for converting digital pathology archives from passive storage systems into active clinical intelligence platforms.

title: Toward Neuro-Inclusive Generative AI: Cognitive Barriers, Coping Strategies, and Design Patterns in Prompt-Based Creative Tools
abstract: Prompt-based creative AI systems, diffusion-based image generators in particular, open new possibilities for visual expression while also imposing cognitive demands that the literature links to exclusion for some neurodivergent users. This structured narrative review draws on scholarship from 2020 to 2026 across humancomputer interaction, cognitive accessibility, neurodiversity, and generative AI to examine how prompt-mediated interaction creates barriers for people with ADHD, autism, dyslexia, and related cognitive differences. This review proposes four barrier types grounded in convergent findings from adjacent HCI and accessibility research: working-memory overload from prompt construction and parameter management; executive-function burden during iterative refinement; sensory and language-processing friction in visually dense, text-centric interfaces; and opaque feedback and hidden prompting conventions that prevent users from diagnosing why outputs diverge from intention. Direct empirical evidence specific to diffusion tools remains thin. Each proposed barrier type warrants direct empirical testing with diffusion-tool users before the framework can be treated as validated. The paper proposes a three-layer taxonomy separating barriers users encounter, coping strategies they develop, and design patterns that future interfaces should test. Accessible creative AI, the review concludes, requires moving past compliance-based thinking toward co-designed, cognitively adaptive interfaces with progressive disclosure, multimodal input, editable prompt histories, interpretable feedback, and metrics built for the prompting workflow rather than borrowed from static interfaces.

title: Cataloging Growth: A Re-Evaluation of 1900-1990
abstract: Measuring real GDP growth requires distinguishing changes in prices from changes in product quality and composition, yet systematic quality adjustment of price indexes is unavailable for much of the twentieth century. We construct a new quality-adjusted price index for U.S. consumer goods using 5.1 million product listings from Sears catalogs, 1900–1990. We use large language models to extract product information and estimate hedonic price schedules from high-dimensional text embeddings, allowing us to infer annual changes in the cost of living. The resulting cost-of-living index implies substantially lower goods inflation than conventional deflators, and consequently implies much faster real economic growth: between 1900 and 1990, real goods consumption grew by a factor of 39 using our index, compared with a factor of 10.3 using standard goods deflators. The gap between our index and canonical ones is largest before World War II, reversing the conventional view that goods consumption growth was slower before 1945 than in the post-war decades.

title: STAIR: A Five-Level Framework for Evaluating LMS Readiness for Agentic AI Teaching Agents
abstract: Autonomous AI teaching agents promise personalised instruction at scale, but the learning management systems that would host them were designed for human workflows, not agentic ones. This paper shows the mismatch is not a matter of capability but of architecture. Applying a new five-level readiness framework, STAIR (Scaffold for Teaching Agent Integration Readiness), to Moodle 5.2dev+ reveals a 28-percentage-point cliff between student-state infrastructure (53%) and agent-reasoning infrastructure (25%). The cause is code-level isolation between the platform's AI and analytics subsystems. STAIR derives its levels from converging requirements in Zimmerman's self-regulated learning cycle, Talebirad and Nadiri's multi-agent collaboration architecture, and a recent educational LLM agent taxonomy. The framework operationalises these into 28 sub-dimensions, each scored against an evidence-linked rubric through systematic source-code analysis. Moodle scores 55% at event sensing (L1) and 53% at student state (L2) but falls to 25% at agent reasoning (L3), 5% at orchestration (L4), and 22% at intervention delivery (L5). The platform provides no native support for autonomous agent coordination or pedagogically timed response. Until learning management systems bridge language-model reasoning and learner data, the field's growing investment in educational AI remains structurally stranded. The ceiling is set by the architecture of the host platforms, not by the capability of the models.

title: Replace Runtime. Keep State: IPSD as a Field Methodology for State-Centric Work with AI Agents
abstract: Most AI adoption fails not because models are weak, but because context is scattered, decisions die in chat, and every session restarts from zero. This paper formalizes IPSD — Intake → Process → Store → Dispatch — a field methodology for state-centric work with AI agents. IPSD is not a chatbot workflow. It is an operating protocol: capture messy input, structure it under human authority, compound durable files, and dispatch finished knowledge. The durable asset is the shared state layer and the protocol that keeps runtimes interchangeable — replace runtime; keep state. Adjacent developer methods (CLAUDE.md-style instructions, LLM Wiki, measure-and-loop harnesses) remain incomplete without a dispatch layer and a stack-agnostic store. The paper describes patterns from live multi-runtime practice and one I→P→S→D specimen. Metrics are proposed, not reported.

title: Dynamic RAG (Retrieval-augmented Generation) Recommendation for SAP-Integrated Fleet Maintenance Software using Artificial Intelligence and Role-based Access Control
abstract: The effective management of modern vehicle fleets, particularly within SAP-integrated environments, is challenged by the sheer volume of telemetry and maintenance data, often resulting in delayed and suboptimal decision-making. This research proposes a Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) recommendation framework designed to enhance fleet maintenance software by integrating Artificial Intelligence with fine-grained security controls. Leveraging the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) and its Generative AI Hub, the proposed system employs a dynamic RAG architecture that retrieves contextual information from both structured data in SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) and unstructured knowledge sources such as maintenance logs and technical manuals. To address critical enterprise security and compliance requirements, a Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) model is implemented, ensuring that AI-generated recommendations and accessed data are strictly governed by user permissions, thereby enforcing the principle of least privilege. The framework's efficacy is evaluated on key metrics including answer accuracy, latency, and audit trail completeness, positioning it as a governed and intelligent decision-support system for fleet managers and maintenance personnel. The findings underscore the potential of a secure, context-aware AI architecture to significantly improve operational efficiency and reduce maintenance costs in enterprise fleet operations.

title: Cognitive Dual-Process Planning for Autonomous Driving with Structured Scene Knowledge and Verifiable Reasoning--Action Consistency
abstract: High-level planning for autonomous driving is a knowledge-intensive engineering decision task that requires accurate scene understanding, timely inference, and internally consistent action selection. Vision-language models (VLMs) can make intermediate reasoning explicit, but their use in deployed planners is constrained by costly structured supervision, unnecessary reasoning in routine scenes, and possible inconsistencies between generated rationales and driving actions. We present a cognitive dual-process planning framework that represents planning-relevant scene knowledge in a machine-parsable structured chain-of-thought (S-CoT) schema. An automated data engine integrates perception foundation models, critical-path filtering, and an expert VLM to generate S-CoT supervision without manual annotation of individual rationales. A lightweight visual Arbiter estimates scene complexity from multilevel vision-encoder features before language decoding and routes each input to either fast meta-action prediction or slow structured reasoning. For slow-path outputs, a deterministic rule-based validator checks whether the parsed S-CoT fields are consistent with the final meta-action and provides verifiable rewards for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). In a 195-scene manual audit, the generated annotations achieve 91.8% CoT accuracy and a 98.5% Logical Consistency Score (LCS). On 574 manually verified NAVSIM test samples, the planner achieves 80.14% planning accuracy and 97.20% LCS while reducing average latency by 17.39% relative to applying slow reasoning to every scene. Evaluation on external long-tail subsets further identifies conditions under which routing and planning performance degrade. Together, these results show how explicit scene knowledge can be operationalized through adaptive reasoning and rule-based verification to support high-level VLM planning decisions.

title: An archive-conditioned large language model-enhanced evolutionary algorithm for integrated variable lot splitting and automated guided vehicle transport scheduling in flexible flow shops
abstract: Consumer electronics manufacturing requires coordinated scheduling of production, variable lot splitting, line assignment, and unit-load transportation when tasks may enter the shop at different operations and compete for shared resources. This paper formulates a static flexible flow shop scheduling problem with non-uniform starting operations, variable sub-lots, and automated guided vehicle (AGV) transport scheduling (FFS-NLA). We develop an archive-conditioned large language model (LLM)-enhanced evolutionary algorithm (LEEA), in which the LLM generates structured refinement policies for designated decision layers, while decoding, repair, feasibility checking, evolutionary evaluation, and selection remain deterministic. On 27 literature-informed synthetic instances, LEEA attains the lowest mean relative percentage deviation among the selected heuristic, metaheuristic, learning-based, and LLM-EA comparators. The ablation results further show that unstructured LLM intervention can be inferior to the LLM-free evolutionary backbone, whereas exploration-exploitation differentiated prompting with curated elite and tabu guidance produces consistent improvements. Controlled parameter-perturbation tests indicate that LEEA maintains comparatively stable optimization performance when rerun under the tested processing-time, transportation-time, and AGV-availability changes. These findings support LEEA as a potential decision-support approach for coordinated production and material-handling planning in the studied static setting.

title: Patterns of AI-generated Formative Feedback: A Structural and Linguistic Analysis in an Assessment Automation Context
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into formative assessment has opened new possibilities for automated feedback generation, yet the structural and linguistic patterns of such feedback remain largely unexplored. This study investigates the architecture, rhetorical moves, and pedagogical alignment of AI-generated formative feedback messages derived from the Integrated AI Triad (IAT) Assessment Automation Dataset. Through a qualitative content analysis of 68 feedback messages-each following a prescribed three-part structure of positive opening, guiding question, and encouraging closure-we examined structural patterns (RQ1), developed a typology of guiding questions (RQ2), and assessed alignment with Hattie and Timperley's (2007) feed-up/feed-back/feed-forward framework (RQ3). Findings reveal that all messages strictly adhered to the three-part architecture, with consistent length proportions across subject areas and grade levels. Probing for explanation (35.3%) emerged as the dominant question type, followed by scaffolding to the next step (23.5%) and locating the error (17.6%), with disciplinary and developmental variations observed. While feedback was strong (89.7% explicit) and messages were highly task-specific (82.4%) and overwhelmingly supportive in tone (94.1%), feed-forward was predominantly implicit (73.6% present, only 32.4% explicit), and feed-up was critically weak (76.5% absent). The study contributes an empirically grounded taxonomy of guiding-question types, introduces the concept of Reverse PCK for teacher professional development, and situates AI-generated feedback within the broader IAT ecosystem of teachers, managers, and families. Implications for prompt engineering, teacher training, and instructional design are discussed, alongside limitations and future research directions.

title: Agentic Inception and Bounded Delegated Authorization: Managing Non-Deterministic Corporate Risk Under Caremark
abstract: The architecture of corporate oversight liability has historically assumed a binary world split into deterministic machines and non-deterministic human personnel. Under the traditional Caremark framework, directors manage corporate risk by relying on retrospective reporting systems, periodic auditing routines, and internal accounting controls designed to flag structural or human behavioral anomalies before they result in completed liabilities. The integration of advanced generative artificial intelligence fundamentally shatters this structural foundation. By deploying non-deterministic computational platforms driven by probabilistic token selection, modern firms routinely prompt a profound operational shift: Agentic Inception. At this threshold, software assets operating within specialized, network-layer computational jurisdictions possess the technical capacity to execute transactions, synthesize disclosures, and bind the corporate principal at machine speed, completely bypassing traditional governance and escalation loops.
