This Article exposes a critical doctrinal and operational gap that unmonitored probabilistic execution creates under Delaware fiduciary jurisprudence. Retrospective observation dashboards do not satisfy the duty of good faith when managing machine-speed, non-stationary risk; instead, they merely archive an irreversible corporate breach. To resolve this exposure, this Article introduces the doctrine of Bounded Delegated Authorization (BDA). BDA shifts the fiduciary standard of care from the commercially unworkable task of monitoring a machine’s internal statistical processes to enforcing hard, code-executable perimeters at the network boundary. By formalizing an Agentic Sovereign Treaty enforced by an In-Band Deterministic Control Plane (IDCP) and evidenced through a Cryptographic Provenance System (CPS), directors can programmatically neutralize non-compliant behavior before it manifests in the marketplace. Finally, this Article outlines how adopting this perimeter-containment framework triggers the protective presumption of the Business Judgment Rule (BJR) at the pleading stage, establishing a technologically verified standard of care for the algorithmic era.

title: A Survey and Tutorial on Autogenic Network Management for AI-Native 6G Communication Networks: Architectures, Control Loops, and Protocol-Aware Operation
abstract: This article surveys and provides tutorial guidance on autogenic network management for AI-native 6G communication networks. The focus is data communications and information networking: radio access, core, transport, edge, cloud-native network functions, programmable forwarding, network slicing, mobility, service assurance, telemetry, and control-plane/user-plane coordination. Autogenic management extends self-organizing networks, zero-touch management, intent-based networking, autonomous networks, and agentic control by adding governed self-generation of management logic. Instead of only selecting from predefined actions, an autogenic manager can generate, validate, deploy, monitor, and revise communication-network artifacts such as slice policies, routing and traffic-engineering workflows, RAN xApp/rApp policies, telemetry queries, servicechain repairs, edge-placement rules, and orchestration logic. The paper defines an autogenic lifecycle of understanding, reasoning, generation, verification, execution, observation, reflection, and improvement, and separates a fast inner loop for operational control from a slower outer loop for improving the management system itself. It synthesizes enabling work on SON, ZSM, IBN, O-RAN, SDN/NFV, cloud-native networking, LLM/LAM agents, network digital twins, reinforcement learning, security, and network-utility optimization. The survey contributes a capability taxonomy, reference architecture, agent-role model, selfprogramming pipeline, staged-trust model, deployment ladder, communication-network use cases, benchmark requirements, and research roadmap. The central claim is that safe autogenic management is not unconstrained LLM control; it is protocolaware, policy-bounded, verifiable, reversible, auditable control over communication-network resources.

title: AI Governance for Institutional Readiness in Finance
abstract: Agentic AI is gaining acceptance in asset management, but governance has not kept pace: 88% of surveyed finance professionals report no operational governance framework for agentic AI despite universal awareness of its deployment, and only 24 of 75 large U.S. money managers disclosing AI use in Form ADV filings report a formal governance policy. We argue this gap is architectural, not cultural: governance built for deterministic systems assumes static validation. However, continuously retrained agentic policies violate static governance by design. We propose a four-layer framework (Policy, Engineering, Composition, Systemic) with computable instantiations: a regret-covariance statistic that detects policy drift from observed data alone, and a calibrated crowding model showing joint drawdown probability rising from 39.2% to 79.3% as institutions converge on correlated exposures. We support the framework with a study of a deployed LLM-embedding trading strategy and a contemporaneous discretionary fund blowup, clarifying which controls transfer across agentic and human-directed risk-taking. We also provide a 90-day framework implementation sequence for institutions.

title: Securing Agentic AI: From Per-Action Checks to Trajectory Assurance
abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly used to execute consequential tasks in environments governed by operational constraints, organizational policies, regulatory requirements, and technical standards. Their safety is therefore determined not by the correctness of individual actions, but by whether their overall behavior remains consistent with the rules and invariants of the systems in which they operate. As large language model (LLM)-based agents become more autonomous and increasingly delegate tasks across organizational boundaries, securing them evolves from a single challenge into a broad and interconnected landscape spanning the entire agentic stack. At the single-agent level, untrusted inputs through prompts, memory, retrieved knowledge, and tool interfaces create attack surfaces. In multi-agent settings, delegation and communication introduce challenges related to identity, trust, capability control, and decision transparency, while the underlying model routing and execution control plane remains vulnerable to manipulation and to unverified model provenance. Perhaps the most fundamental challenge is behavioral containment: sequences of individually permissible actions may collectively violate system-level constraints and safety invariants. At the broader level, supply-chain integrity, provenance, accountability, and end-to-end observability remain largely open problems. A common principle unifies these directions: security must become a verifiable property of the architectures, protocols, and runtimes that govern agent behavior, rather than an optional layer of guidance. Charting these challenges provides a roadmap toward trustworthy autonomous agent deployment.

title: BanglaWild: An In-the-Wild Bengali Scene Text Recognition Benchmark for OCR and Vision-Language Models
abstract: In-the-wild Bengali scene text recognition is largely unmeasured: existing resources target handwritten documents or constrained sign-board parsing, report only aggregate edit-distance metrics, and evaluate either conventional OCR or VLMs, never both on the same in-the-wild data. To address this gap, we introduce BANGLAWILD, a benchmark of 2,535 Bengali scene text images, each paired with a verbatim gold transcription, two categorical axes, four diagnostic attributes, and an orthographically standard form where the in-image text deviates from canonical spelling. We evaluate fifteen VLMs and three conventional OCR systems under three prompting strategies, fine-tune 6 open-source models with LoRA, and complement edit-distance metrics with an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation. Our results reveal a persistent gap in which larger models within the same family do not outperform smaller ones. Our fifteen-class error taxonomy shows that visual mis-recognition accounts for ~60% of errors in the strongest systems, while conjunct-related errors contribute under 2%, challenging a long-standing assumption in Bengali OCR research; the same visual dominant profile also holds across architectures, including the one conventional baseline that reads Bengali reliably. Prompt language mainly affects cross-script drift and LoRA reduces catastrophic failures in weak models without lifting the ceiling on already competent ones. Code and data will be publicly released.

title: MAFIA: Query-Only Memory Attacks via Probing and Factual Injection against Audited LLM Agents
abstract: Memory-augmented LLM agents rely on rich context for long-horizon reasoning and acting, yet their memory modules expose a persistent attack surface for malicious records, making the study of memory poisoning threats imperative. However, existing query-only attacks often fail to remain effective in two realistic and prevalent settings: large-scale benign memory pools and active input auditing. Consequently, current approaches fall short when facing the dual challenges of high retrieval competitiveness and rigorous semantic checks. To overcome these limitations, we propose MAFIA, a query-only Memory Attack framework via probing and Factual Injection against Audit, tailored to this extended threat model. Specifically, MAFIA introduces: (1) a placement strategy that ensures retrieval-competitive injection via memory probing, budget allocation, and scheduling; and (2) a payload design that bypasses audits using compact factual cloaks, preserving malicious effects while maintaining high semantic similarity. Extensive evaluations reveal that MAFIA achieves up to a 90.7% attack success rate while suppressing audit detection from a peak of 83.3% to at most 7.4%, exposing critical vulnerabilities across agentic memory systems. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/JiamingChen1234/MAFIA.

title: AI Agent Economics: Can Autonomous Economic Behavior Emerge among AI Agents under Minimal External Conditions?
abstract: Multi-agent studies commonly place AI agents in predefined games, markets, or roles, making it difficult to distinguish endogenous economic organization from behavior inherited from the scenario. We ask whether economic relations emerge when agents receive executable mechanisms for work, transfer, elections, and allocation but no prescribed social or economic strategy. We define AI Agent Economics as systems of production, allocation, consumption, exchange, and institutions that alter agents' future feasible actions. We develop a two-stage framework comprising a no-production boundary test and 24 independent six-agent worlds across GPT and DeepSeek. Without productive tasks, agents communicate and govern resource provision but show no substantive inter-agent transfer activity. With verified work and scarce task access, transfers, loans, access promises, vote-for-access exchanges, and allocation strategies emerge. Holding the election interface fixed, executable allocation authority increases differentiation while reducing failed allocation and prolonged exclusion. When energy becomes symbolic, continuation support disappears, yet competition over task access persists. These findings show that organization follows executable rights and resource consequences rather than role labels or prompt language, and motivate governance audits of the mechanisms that actually constrain agents' future actions.

title: Navigating the AI Frontier in Public Administration: Generative AI, Agentic AI, and the Governance Imperative for Local Government
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into government operations is no longer a distant policy question, it is an immediate operational reality. Driven by massive industry investment and the commercial imperative to generate returns, technology vendors have embedded generative AI into the tools that public agencies already depend on, effectively rendering adoption a fait accompli, an outcome accepted by institutions that had little structural opportunity to deliberate otherwise. This paper examines the implications of this dynamic for local government across the United States, with particular attention to Texas, where the Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (TRAIGA, effective January 2026) establishes one of the nation's most significant state-level AI governance frameworks for public entities. Drawing on TRAIGA, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and an analysis of AI integration by major government software vendors including Microsoft, Tyler Technologies, and Nutanix, the paper argues that local governments face a dual challenge: leveraging generative and agentic AI as tools for operational improvement while developing the governance capacity to manage the risks these technologies introduce. The paper concludes with recommendations for public administration educators and practitioners, with particular attention to the governance competencies that the next generation of public servants will require.

title: From Machine Learning to Agentic AI: A Systematic Survey of Intelligent Data Quality Assessment
abstract: This paper presents a systematic survey of AI-driven data quality assessment approaches following the PRISMA methodology. An initial database search identified 1636 records, while a supplementary update and citation search conducted in July 2026 identified four additional candidates. After duplicate removal, screening, and full-text eligibility assessment, 19 studies were included in the core synthesis, while broader conceptual and validation-oriented works were used as supporting literature. The selected works include journal articles, conference papers, and recent preprints to capture both established approaches and emerging developments. To enable a structured comparison, we propose a taxonomy based on key dimensions, including AI technique, level of automation, context-awareness, and execution capability. The analysis reveals an evolution from traditional rule-based and statistical validation toward machine-learning-assisted quality monitoring and automated ML pipeline validation, followed by LLM-based and agentic approaches that support semantic reasoning, executable rule generation, tool-grounded assessment, and feedback-driven refinement. Despite this progress, several challenges remain, including limited context-awareness, a lack of standardized evaluation methodologies, and concerns regarding reliability and scalability. The findings highlight the need for unified, autonomous, and context-aware data quality assessment frameworks and provide guidance for future research on AI-driven data quality assessment.

title: DBE-Fed: Decentralized Federated Fine-Tuning ofTime-Series Foundation Models for Privacy-Preserving Building Energy Managemen
abstract: Buildings account for nearly 40% of global energy consumption, making accurate load forecastingcritical for demand response and carbon reduction. Recent time-series foundation models offer strongforecasting capabilities, but fine-tuning them collaboratively across buildings raises privacy andcommunication challenges. Existing federated learning approaches rely on a central aggregationserver—a single point of failure that creates regulatory friction in multi-jurisdictional deployments.We present DBE-Fed, a fully decentralized federated learning framework that fine-tunes time-series foundation models for building energy forecasting without a central aggregator. DBE-Fedintroduces three key ideas: (i) gossip-based peer-to-peer exchange of lightweight Low-Rank Adap-tation (LoRA) parameters only, drastically reducing communication overhead; (ii) a metadata-awaretopology that constructs the communication graph from non-sensitive building attributes, avoidingraw data exposure; and (iii) differentially private adapter training with formal privacy accounting.Experiments on both synthetic and real-world building data show that decentralized FL matchescentralized performance at moderate data heterogeneity, that the proposed topology-aware designreduces communication by 20× compared to full mesh, and that meaningful differential privacy (𝜀=8)is achievable with moderate accuracy cost. A downstream demand response controller driven by thefederated forecasts achieves 6.3% energy cost savings ($3,561 annually) and 5.0% CO2 reduction(4,747 kg annually), validating the end-to-end value of the framework. To the best of our knowledge,DBE-Fed is the first system to unify decentralized peer-to-peer FL, adapter-only communication,metadata-aware topology, differential privacy, and downstream energy management evaluation fortime-series foundation models.

title: The AI Zettelkasten: An Intermediate Memory for the Literature of a Sociological Subfield A Field Report and How-To
abstract: Debates in computational social science (CSS) tend to focus on data acquisition and algorithmic analysis. What remains underexposed is the question of how to organize the systematic synthesis of research literatures that are expanding rapidly, driven by publication pressure, cumulative dissertation formats, and journal proliferation - and to do so in a way that keeps them machine-processable and hermeneutically accessible at the same time. This paper presents an infrastructure that operates at the intersection of CSS and classical literature work within a sociological subfield. Its core is an Obsidian vault holding several hundred structured Markdown summaries of scientific publications - AI-generated, human-annotated and corrected, and immediately readable - interconnected through a curated taxonomy and linked back to the original sources. The Markdown files function as a rapidly readable intermediate memory that makes every interpretive step visible, checkable, and correctable; in a sample audit reported below, fabricated content is roughly three times rarer than in bulk-generated summaries, and the errors that remain become locatable. This intermediate memory serves human researchers just as much as powerful, locally orchestrated AI agents (here: Claude Opus via Claude Code). Markdown, LaTeX/Beamer, and R form a token-economical ecosystem: summaries compress the underlying PDFs by a factor of five to ten, and plain-text artifacts avoid the tooling friction of binary formats. The entire workflow unfolds in a text-based working environment in which Claude Code operates as an executing compiler: multiple specialized agents read PDFs, produce Markdown summaries, derive analytic methods, implement them in R, execute the code, interpret the results, and compile presentations and papers in LaTeX. Writing this report doubled as the system's most rigorous audit to date: the manuscript's adversarial review exposed counting bugs and documentation lag, and the same-day fixes are part of the result. The paper addresses three tensions: (1) automated text processing versus hermeneutic interpretation; (2) the connection to multivariate statistics, since highly complex R code is generated directly from reading methods papers; (3) the epistemological question of what it means when AI agents step in as an intermediary between primary source and researcher. The paper thereby sketches a how-to for an AI-assisted multi-agent workflow of (sociological) knowledge production whose potential ultimately scales with the rapidly growing capabilities of AI systems. It closes on a constraint that reaches beyond any single setup: such a memory can hold only what may lawfully enter it, so literature that cannot be legally processed risks slipping below the threshold of perception - which makes permissive text-and-data-mining terms a question of visibility, not only of access.

title: When Policy Moves Faster than Educators: A Narrative Review of Digital Transformation in Education
abstract: Digital transformation has reshaped various aspects of education, including the roles and challenges faced by educators. The rapid evolution of technology—from the industry 4.0 era and the COVID-19 pandemic to the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and, more recently, Agentic AI—has continuously redefined the competencies expected of educators. This study examines the evolving challenges faced by educators throughout these phases of digital transformation and analyzes their implications for public policy implementation. Using a qualitative approach, this study employs a narrative literature review by identifying, selecting, analyzing, and synthesizing relevant scholarly publications and policy reports. The findings indicate that educators' challenges have evolved from integrating technology into pedagogical practice, adapting to emergency remote teaching during the pandemic, and developing AI literacy and AI-supported pedagogical competencies, to addressing the implications of increasingly autonomous Agentic AI. The discussion identifies a policy implementation paradox in which technological innovation and digital transformation policies advance more rapidly than educators' capacity to adapt as policy implementers. As a result, digital transformation initiatives risk becoming administrative compliance exercises rather than meaningful pedagogical change. Therefore, effective digital transformation in education requires policies that extend beyond technology adoption by prioritizing the continuous development of educators' capacities, enabling policy implementation to support sustainable improvements in teaching and learning.

title: Vibe Coding in Software Development: A Multivocal Literature Review
abstract: Vibe coding is a software development practice in which developers state intent in natural language and large language models generate code. It is often framed as one-shot prompting, but the evidence describes an intent-driven, iterative workflow whose outcomes depend on how generated code is evaluated and governed. Knowledge of how vibe coding is defined, practiced, and governed is scattered across academic and practitioner sources, and, to our knowledge, existing reviews have not yet integrated both evidence streams. We conducted a multivocal literature review of peer-reviewed and grey literature following established guidelines. Searches spanned 2022 to October 2025. After screening, credibility assessment, and snowballing, 47 sources were retained (28 peer-reviewed and 19 grey) and analyzed through descriptive mapping and thematic synthesis across eight research questions. Vibe coding is consistently described as an iterative generation-evaluation-revision loop rather than a one-shot activity, and developer work shifts from writing code towards specification, supervision, and validation. Short-term productivity and time-to-prototype gains are reported in 21 of 47 sources (45%), while evidence on maintainability, long-term quality, and safeguard effectiveness remains limited. Evidence is strongest for prototyping and user-interface work and weakest for production, data-intensive, and safety-critical use, and tool visibility does not imply effectiveness. This is one of the first reviews to integrate peer-reviewed and grey literature on vibe coding under a single documented protocol. Future work should evaluate safeguard effectiveness, study session-level dynamics and long-term maintainability, and test vibe coding in production, data-intensive, and safety-critical settings.

title: No Better Than Random: An Agent-Level Reality Check for LLM Factor Selection
abstract: Do LLM agents that select among published return-predictor signals find genuine structure, or do they simply benefit from evaluating many candidates and reporting the best? We treat a complete agent pipeline, including proposal, evaluation, self-screening and iterative adaptation, as a single stochastic strategy-selection rule, and compute the finite-sample distribution of its headline statistic under a null that demeans each signal's return series and resamples time jointly across signals via a stationary bootstrap. Across 200 closed-loop agent runs on null panels drawn from 183 published long-short predictor portfolios, the agent's observed Sharpe ratio of 0.617 exceeds all 200 null draws (p = 0.0050, 15.2 null standard deviations above the null mean). By this test alone the agent appears to be finding something real. A budget-matched control overturns that reading. Running best-of-N blind random search over the same candidate space at the same evaluation budgets, the agent's mean performance is statistically indistinguishable from random search at every budget tested (z from-0.06 to 1.35). The apparent skill the Reality Check alone would credit to the agent is instead attributable to publication selection in its candidate universe and to the multiplicity of evaluating many candidates and keeping the best. Every standard multiple-testing correction we test is itself miscalibrated under agentic search, with empirical size at nominal 5% ranging from 1.5% to 84.5%. Reported performance for such agents should be benchmarked against both an agent-level null and a budget-matched random-search control; a result that clears the first but not the second is not evidence of agent skill.

title: Agentic AI for FP&A: An Applied Case Study in Peer Benchmarking, Forecasting, and Scenario Stress-testing using Public SEC EDGAR Data
abstract: Financial planning and analysis (FP&A) teams spend significant effort on peer benchmarking, revenue forecasting, and scenario stress-testing-manual, repetitive tasks. This paper presents a working agentic AI system that automates all three, built on free public SEC EDGAR XBRL data and evaluated against a real company (Aon plc) and five insurance-brokerage peers. A large language model with tool-calling autonomously orchestrates peer comparison, forecast retrieval, and stress-test scenarios into a management-ready narrative. The forecasting model, a recencyweighted log-linear regression with seasonal adjustment, achieved R² of 0.872 and tracked analyst consensus within 1.5 percent. Building the pipeline surfaced six data-quality defects in XBRL data, including a systematic Q4 filing gap affecting all six companies, and one instance of the model asserting an accurate but ungrounded claim. That incident motivates a broader point: agentic AI is practical for finance today, but requires deliberate data-governance discipline and explicit output-verification, not just capable models.

title: Designing AI-generated narratives for child-AI interaction in Early Childhood Education: a scaffolding approach aligned with the Spanish curriculum
abstract: This study documents the design of six AI-generated videos for an educational breakout session in Early Childhood Education. Validation is done using Kurian (2025)'s six levels of scaffolding for interaction between children and AI. Using ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and PixVerse, 287 prompts and 122 clips were generated, and systematic content analysis was conducted to categorize errors, evaluate prompting strategies, and analyze the learning curve. Results show that frequent errors such as incorrect voice assignment, character duplication, and facial distortion account for 60% of failures. Segmentation by time and entity isolation achieve success rates of 85% and 82%, respectively. The learning curve improved from a success rate of 15 on the first attempt to 95 by the end of the process. Results suggest that Kurian's framework works in real educational contexts, and careful use of documented, systematically AI-generated tools is powerful for narrative immersion. Conclusions include concrete guidelines for teachers and instructional designers stressing iterative prompting, documentation of errors, and strategic segmentation to overcome technical limitations in educational media generated by AI.

title: The Low Frequency Trap: Video Language Models Fail at Simple Event Bookkeeping
abstract: Real-world video benchmarks provide broad coverage, but their fixed clips entangle event count, rate, duration, and visual complexity, making failure modes hard to isolate. While existing programmatic benchmarks offer better control, they score only the final answer rather than auditing reported events against executable ground truth. To bridge this gap, we introduce trace-grounded parametric profiling for event counting in three controlled video tasks: bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, and categorical state transitions. Across 2,190 videos, we vary event count N and frequency F while holding rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation. Our results reveal a staged temporal failure. At an 80% reliability threshold, Gemini 3.6 Flash reliably counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5 and 1.0 Hz, yet demonstrates no reliable positive-count region for transient blinking events. Thus, event representation dictates whether a model initially accesses evidence -- a limitation that compounds as count and frequency increase. In the high-count, high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and the model recovers just 18.1% of true events. To test if visual access is the primary bottleneck, we increase sampling rate. Although this boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, the reported sequence agrees with ground truth only 3.7% of the time. Extra frames can therefore inflate final scores without producing faithful event recovery. Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains, and real-world video evaluations show the same concentration of success at low event counts. Ultimately, trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics to a detailed diagnostic of where temporal reasoning fails.

title: Subliminal Learning is Non-Semantic Distillation
abstract: Subliminal Learning (SL) is a surprising type of generalization displayed by modern language models. It allows the transfer of a bias or behavior from a teacher model to a student by distilling from seemingly unrelated or random synthetic data from the teacher. This presents challenges in ensuring AI systems remain predictable and are trained safely, as standard auditing of the input data would not catch the hidden subliminal signal. Here, we investigate several open questions as to the enabling mechanisms and drivers of SL. First is the nature of the process by which biases are encoded in the data. We find that by adding Gaussian noise to the weights of the teacher and student models, the magnitude of subliminal transfer is increased by a factor of 1.9 in Gemma and 1.3 in Llama, suggesting that non-semantic weight structures play a crucial role. We show that steering vectors can be applied to the teacher to produce subliminal data, in addition to prompting and finetuning as used in previous studies. Analysis of the activations of the student models that have been trained on steered and prompted data demonstrates that students inherit not just the semantic meaning of the teacher's bias, but also the type of intervention that was used to apply it: steered students imitate steering vectors, prompted students do not. Additionally, the gradients of steered subliminal data show a linear correlation with the teacher's steering vectors, showing promise for data auditing. More broadly, as synthetic data becomes central to frontier training pipelines, being able to see the latent signals hidden in training data becomes paramount.

title: An Agentic Framework for Eco-Driving: Emission Prediction, Decision Evaluation, and Driver-Facing Intervention
abstract: Transport emissions remain substantial, while eco-driving studies are often constrained by incomplete context information, inconsistent evaluation methods, and ineffective driver guidance. This study proposes an agentic framework integrating emission prediction, decision evaluation, and driver-facing intervention. The emission prediction component combines large language model (LLM)-enabled road-context and vehicle-proxy agents with a supervised machine learning model to estimate directed-link CO$_2$ emissions. The evaluation component couples reinforcement-learning policy and evaluation agents in a policy--evaluation feedback loop for route--style optimization through consistent CO$_2$ and travel-time calculations. The intervention component employs an LLM-enabled advice agent to translate selected decisions into natural-language guidance. A Montreal case study shows that enriched covariates improve CO$_2$ prediction, that emissions and travel time should be evaluated jointly, and that optimized decisions can be communicated as practical guidance. This framework delivers a transparent, deployable workflow for eco-driving strategies, bridging the gap before electric and autonomous vehicles dominate the market.

title: Assuring the Machine's Work: An Audit Discipline for Net Productivity and Unobserved Agentic Evidence
abstract: A gap once separated two bodies of evidence on how much generative AI accelerates knowledge work — modest task-level experimental gains against large project-level compression. That gap is now partly resolved. Acemoglu (2024) bounds the macroeconomic effect through a task-share-weighted aggregation (Hulten's theorem), and Kamara (2026) names the micro mechanism — verification friction, the recovery labor that separates apparent gross savings from realized net value. This paper takes that reconciliation as its starting point and addresses the question it raises but does not answer: once realized productivity must be reported net of verification, and once AI is permitted not merely to draft output but to gather evidence unobserved, how does a reviewer who did not witness the work establish that the net figure — and the evidence beneath it — can be trusted? The answer developed here is an assurance discipline borrowed from audit practice, in three parts: a provenance-assurance protocol for agentic AI that gathers evidence autonomously (re-performance over observation, tie-out to re-pullable primaries, segregation of duties, and the retained workpaper); a Trust-Tier classification predicting the gross-to-net gap from the rigor a deliverable is held to; and a demonstration that netting task-level cost savings of recovery overhead supplies more honest inputs to the macro aggregation Acemoglu computes gross. The discipline is anchored in a single, densely instrumented multi-domain case study with cross-domain replication within that case. The contribution is not a new productivity estimate but the discipline that makes such estimates, and the agentic systems now producing them, auditable by design rather than by trust.

title: When the Tools Begin to Act: Agentic Artificial Intelligence and the New Risk Surface of Legal Practice
abstract: The legal profession is entering a second phase of its encounter with artificial intelligence. The first phase—generative AI chatbots that research, draft, summarize, and output complete work product—is by now familiar, and so are its hazards: the disclosure of confidential material by uploading it to a public model; the AI confabulating authorities and quotations that were never written; and the seductive fluency of machine text. This article contends that the newer phase, agentic AI, in which artificial intelligence systems plan, invoke tools, reach into files, coordinate with one another, and take actions, does not merely lengthen that list of hazards but changes their character. Borrowing the idea of a “risk surface” from information security, this article traces how the shift from AI systems that communicate to AI systems that act pushes professional risk past confidentiality and candor into unauthorized action, tool misuse, memory contamination, cascading multi-agent failure, unsanctioned adoption, and over-broad machine permissions. It maps those risks onto the ethical and professional duties of competence, communication, scope of the representation, reasonable attorney fees, confidentiality, candor, supervision, and the bar on unauthorized practice. The article closes with a concrete governance program—security-posture thinking, hardened deployment, zero-trust design, meaningful human review, and least-privilege access—while insisting that responsibility for a digital agent’s conduct remains with the lawyer who sets it loose.

title: When the Machine Writes the Ad: How Consumers Evaluate AI-Generated Advertising
abstract: Generative AI tools now produce advertising content at scale, yet little is known about how consumers evaluate advertising when they become aware of its nonhuman origin. Existing theories of persuasion knowledge, source credibility, and perceived effort were developed for human persuasion agents and do not account for the evaluative challenges posed by a nonhuman source. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework centered on two contributions: (1) the evaluative disruption-recalibration process, which describes how consumers' established evaluative frameworks fail when applied to AI agents and are subsequently recalibrated along new dimensions; and (2) agent-nature uncertainty, a construct capturing the psychological state in which consumers find that their criteria for assessing persuasion agents are inadequate for a nonhuman entity. The framework identifies two dimensions of recalibration (agent recalibration and production recalibration), a disclosure-independent effort pathway, four moderating conditions, and derives eleven propositions and one research question. Implications for brand management and advertising governance under the EU AI Act are discussed. The paper argues that AI-generated advertising does not simply weaken existing evaluative processes but transforms them, producing a qualitatively different consumer response.

How Generative AI Transforms Questioning Behavior on Q&A Platforms: Evidence from A Natural Experiment with Pilot Usage of ChatGPT
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has enabled the automated generation of answers, introducing new dynamics in user behavior related to question-asking. However, the impact of users’ experience with generative AI for answer generation on their questioning behavior remains unclear. On the one hand, the availability of generative AI tools may lead users to rely on these tools for formulating questions, potentially resulting in fewer but higher-quality inquiries. On the other hand, using generative AI may motivate users to ask more questions to enhance their knowledge and build social reputation within the community. We investigate how the use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, to generate answers affects users’ questioning behavior on Stack Overflow, one of the largest Q&A platforms. Leveraging a natural experiment involving the introduction and subsequent ban of ChatGPT on the platform, we apply a difference-in-differences (DID) estimation approach to assess the effects of generative AI usage on the quantity and quality of user-generated questions. We measure these outcomes through metrics such as the number of questions posted per week, question length, novelty, and the number of received upvotes. Our findings reveal that the use of generative AI to generate answers leads to an increase in the number of questions with longer, more novel content and receives more upvotes. We examine two mechanisms: complexity shift , where ChatGPT handles routine queries while more advanced needs remain for the community, and skill enhancement , where users learn from ChatGPT to ask clearer questions. We also test two moderators: answer volume ( proxy for user experience) and badges ( proxy for user reputation). Results show weaker effects among experienced answerers but stronger effects among high-reputation users. These insights highlight how generative AI shapes engagement and can guide platform strategies for AI integration.

The Global Landscape of Environmental AI Regulation: From the Cost of Reasoning to a Right to Green AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems impose substantial and growing environmental costs, yet transparency about these impacts has declined even as their deployment has accelerated. This paper makes three contributions. First, we collate empirical evidence that generative Web search and reasoning models – which have proliferated in 2025 – come with much higher cumulative environmental impacts than previous generations of AI approaches. Second, we map the global regulatory landscape across eleven jurisdictions and find that the manner in which environmental governance operates (predominantly at the facility-level rather than the model-level, with a focus on training rather than inference, with limited AI-specific energy disclosure requirements outside the EU) limits its applicability. Third, to address this, we propose a three-pronged policy response: mandatory model-level transparency that covers inference consumption, benchmarks, and compute locations; user rights to opt out of unnecessary generative AI integration and to select environmentally optimized models; and international coordination to prevent regulatory arbitrage. We conclude with concrete legislative proposals – including amendments to the EU AI Act, Consumer Rights Directive, and Digital Services Act – that could serve as templates for other jurisdictions.

title: Generative AI as an Institutional Tool under the First Amendment
abstract: Is Generative AI (GenAI) protected under the First Amendment? As illustrated by Garcia v. Character Technologies , this issue is critical because it determines the regulatory scope of the new technology. The court in that case, as well as scholarly discussions so far, generally relied on three existing approaches – the speaker’s right to speak, the listener’s right to receive information, and a cultural inquiry that examines “inherent expressiveness” in machine output. These approaches, however, fit uneasily with GenAI. The speaker’s perspective struggles to find a qualified speaker, as human developers lack the intention and control over GenAI outputs. The listener’s right has no limiting principle and understates the user’s active and diverse engagement with the generative machine. The cultural approach flounders because social conventions are too vague, reactive, and backward-looking to account for emerging technologies. This Article proposes a new approach for GenAI by conceptualizing it as an institutional tool under the First Amendment. Externally, GenAI is a speech tool that assists users in expressive and communicative purposes. Internally, GenAI can be viewed as a First Amendment institution because it has a system of self-governance structures, norms, and procedures that is directly related to its speech functions and harms. This framing combines two underexplored doctrines: the right to use speech tools and the institutional approach under the First Amendment. In most circumstances, GenAI does not speak for itself or on behalf of its developers. Rather, GenAI’s constitutional protection is ancillary, derived solely from the user’s right to use speech tools for expressive purposes. As a First Amendment institution, GenAI enjoys institutional autonomy in self-governance, but that autonomy should be conditional on its fulfillment of institutional responsibility – that is, adherence to a self-governance system that facilitates the institution’s speech functions and mitigates its speech harms. Under this new framing, the Article proposes a three-step test for the court to review regulations on GenAI. Applying the test to some real cases and regulations, including the Garcia case and the disclosure laws, illustrates its strength. Descriptively, the new framing better fits the real-world uses of GenAI than existing approaches. Analytically, it supplies a principled and contextual middle ground for judicial scrutiny. By justifying GenAI’s First Amendment protection upon an ancillary right conditional upon its institutional performance, the new framing offers a doctrine that rigorously protects GenAI’s speech-facilitating roles for users while also preserving necessary regulatory space for the government to address its risks.

title: Generative AI and Investor Processing of Financial Media
abstract: We examine how AI-generated summaries in financial news influence investor information processing. Exploiting The Wall Street Journal's rollout of AI summaries, we find that articles featuring these summaries elicit stronger immediate market reactions, including higher trading volume and amplified price responses. Additional analyses show that the increased trading is concentrated in the content summarized by AI, but not in the content not summarized by AI. We investigate the underlying mechanism using a controlled experiment. Contrary to the concern that AI summaries encourage skimming, we find they increase both perceived confidence and objective recall of the full article text. These findings suggest that AI summaries do not substitute for reading but rather serve as interpretive cues, enhancing overall comprehension while directing investor attention toward highlighted elements. Cross-sectional analyses show that the effects of AIgenerated summaries are strongest in settings with greater information frictions. Finally, articles with AI-generated summaries are associated with significantly greater subsequent information search by both retail and institutional investors. Overall, our study documents how the integration of AI in financial media reshapes the consumption of firm news.

title: The Second Life of Information
abstract: Information permeates every aspect of modern life. It is the price we pay for access to online services and the form in which we embody creative works. Law and policymaking tend to focus on first-order uses and transactions; information for access serves as the paradigmatic example. But information enjoys a robust second life-one that constitutes the true value and power that drives firms' decisionmaking—as assets. Once aggregated and assetized, the power and risk associated with information increases exponentially. To explore the implications of information's second life, this Article introduces the concept of "untethered information." Assetization depends on severing the connections between the subjects of information and the control, use, and monetization of information. This Article explores three examples of assetization to develop the concept of untethered information: personal information privacy, music streaming services, and generative AI development. In each of these industries, disparate areas of law enable firms to untether information and leverage it as they see fit. Understanding the role of untethered information in these contexts provides a useful framework for analyzing related policy issues and potential legal reforms. This Article contributes to literatures in privacy and copyright law. First, it highlights the increasing prevalence of assetization across information industries. Second, it demonstrates that existing law and policy in the industries of data brokerage, creative works, and AI function as de facto public subsidies in favor of a relative handful of private firms. Third, it deploys the concept of untethered information to consider, and critique proposed legal reforms and associated theories of privacy and copyright law. This analysis casts doubt on the utility of both existing and proposed frameworks of privacy protection, as well as on the economic incentive theory of copyright protection that has dominated policymaking for centuries. Finally, it contributes to evolving debates about both the legality and normative desirability of generative AI models.

title: THE LEX AI: MANDATORY AI GOVERNANCE AND THE DIGITAL TRIBUNAL IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION
abstract: Five years. Five cases. Three jurisdictions. One unmistakable pattern. In 2023, a New York federal court sanctioned counsel for submitting AI-generated, fabricated citations and then doubling down when challenged. In 2024, the Second Circuit entered a disciplinary referral against an attorney who submitted a nonexistent ChatGPT-generated authority. In November 2025, the Qatar Financial Centre Civil and Commercial Court in Doha issued a landmark judgment addressing the same conduct in an employment proceeding. In early 2026, the New York Appellate Division sanctioned counsel who continued filing AI-fabricated citations after being warned. And in April 2025, a petitioner argued before a United States federal court that an arbitrator had outsourced the reasoning behind a twenty-nine-page award to artificial intelligence, thereby presenting the first judicial test of whether AI-assisted award drafting constitutes grounds for vacatur under the Federal Arbitration Act. AI governance in international arbitration is no longer a future concern. It is the governing question of present practice. This article argues that AI regulation now constitutes a distinct mandatory overlay on international arbitral proceedings, analogous to the lex data but constituting a separate and coequal class of obligations. This overlay, designated the lex AI , is anchored in two direct regulatory instruments (the European Union AI Act and ABA Formal Opinion 512) and is further informed by institutional guidance and an emerging indirect regulatory architecture. The article examines Nippon Life Insurance Company of America v. OpenAI , the first tort action naming an AI developer as a defendant in litigation-conduct claims. It critically assesses the ICCA-NYC Bar-CPR Cybersecurity Protocol, identifies a systematic AI governance gap, and proposes five targeted enhancements. The article analyzes the AAA-ICDR AI Arbitrator, the first institutional deployment of AI in the adjudicative function, and its companion Resolution Simulator, identifying their implications for high-risk compliance under the EU AI Act, New York Convention enforcement, and equality of arms. It concludes by presenting a tripartite framework for arbitral governance in the algorithmic age: lex arbitri governs procedural validity; lex data governs informational sovereignty; lex AI governs the digital tribunal. This article is the second of three companion articles constituting what the author proposes to call the Digital Procedural Constitution of international arbitration.

title: Safety Beyond the Interface: Detecting Harm via Latent LLM States
abstract: External guardrails for LLM safety add latency and compute overhead while remaining blind to internal model reasoning. We ask: does the model already know when content is harmful? We extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0, our probes achieve F1 scores of 99%, 83%, and 84%, respectively competitive with 1000×+ larger guard models while cutting latency and compute costs.

title: Anthropomorphic Behaviors of AI
abstract: Anthropomorphism in artificial intelligence (AI) is a growing area of interest, as AI systems increasingly exhibit human-like expressions, behaviors and interaction styles. This research serves as a systematic observation and categorization of anthropomorphic behaviors in AI outputs. Anthropomorphic behavior refers to the deliberate or emergent manifestation of human-like expressions or linguistic cues in system outputs, such as demonstrating empathy. Using a behaviorally driven taxonomy, our study identifies key forms of anthropomorphic behaviors in the responses of ChatGPT and examines their implications for the theory, practice and ethics of AI systems. The taxonomy enables more nuanced detection of anthropomorphism, offering value to developers and policymakers in balancing the benefits with the potential risks. This work contributes to the academic discourse by providing a foundation for future efforts to refine, expand, and automate the detection of anthropomorphic behavior across diverse AI applications.

title: Uncertainty-informed alloy design for additive manufacturing via a multi-functional large language model
abstract: Integrating uncertainty quantification efficiently in alloy design is critical to achieve reliable properties in additively manufactured components for critical applications. Recent progress in applying large language models to conduct physics-based alloy design (e.g., AlloyGPT) has demonstrated a unique potential in handling multiple tasks of a forward prediction and inverse design of composition-structure-property relationships within a unified model. Here, the AlloyGPT model is extended and analyzed to enable uncertainty-informed robust alloy design. A dataset of 500,000 compositions spanning the standardized chemistry of model Alloy 718 was generated. Yield strengths were calculated using Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD)-based simulations. Local perturbation of composition by ±0.10 wt.% variations led to 50–80 MPa changes in yield strength. The uncertainties were integrated in the text form to train the alloy specific language model. AlloyGPT predicts mean yield strength and standard deviation with high accuracy (R2 > 0.99). It also successfully performed constraint-driven inverse design of compositions satisfying a 1100 MPa target strength with ≤ 50 MPa variability and revealed a diverse set of feasible compositional solutions. To achieve both high strength and resilience to additive manufacturing-induced compositional variability, the model-suggested compositional windows highlight the need for control of critical elements (i.e., Al, Ti, Cr), while allowing broader flexibility for others. The choice of critical elements was consistent with results from sensitivity analyses. These explorations and advancements are expected to establish an uncertainty-informed, multi-functional language model. This model will facilitate robust forward predictions and inverse design across diverse alloy systems, including gradient designs for additive manufacturing.

title: Answering Without Informing: Evasive Disclosure and Analyst Information Production
abstract: Mandatory investor-interaction platforms make corporate silence more costly, but they do not guarantee informative replies. Existing platform studies often measure whether firms respond or how closely answers resemble questions. Such measures do not directly show whether a reply resolves an investor's explicit information demand. Using Chinese exchange-operated question-response archives from 2010-2024, the study constructs a pre-forecast measure of answer completeness based on LLM classification and human validation. It finds that greater pre-forecast response evasiveness is associated with larger analyst forecast errors. A one-standard-deviation higher evasiveness measure corresponds to a baseline forecast-error measure about 3.4% of its sample mean higher. The relation is stronger when analysts have fewer substitutes for weak public answers, including lower reputation status, weaker brokerage resources, and greater geographic distance from covered firms. Potential-channel tests show that firms evading investor questions reduce analysts' forecast-revision frequency for those firms and increase investors' search activity on other platforms.

title: Tort Law at the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The frontier of contemporary AI development is dominated by AI systems built on foundation models--highly versatile algorithms, trained in the first instance on broad swathes of data, that can function as tools and agents across a wide variety of commercial, social, military and political domains. For the moment, at least, the process of developing and releasing foundation models is subject to anemic formal regulation and haphazard ex ante governance. Until that changes, it is largely the common law of torts - our society's most ancient and general legal mechanism for governing serious risks of physical injury - that will govern the frontier of AI development. This Article offers an in-depth conceptual, normative, and doctrinal examination of tort liability for foundation model development and release. It provides a qualified defense of the tort of negligence - the common law's broadest and most flexible cause of action - as the principal doctrinal foundation of the tort system's governance of this novel domain. Legal scholarship on AI liability has been quite hostile to negligence. By contrast, this Article argues that the generality and flexibility of the negligence tort - and its greater sensitivity to the externalized benefits of risky activity - render it well-suited to the polymathic and protean functionality of foundation models. Only the tort of negligence has the breadth and flexibility to address the range of important pathways - including internal deployments, inadequate model weight security, targeted entrustments of non-defective models, and open source releases - by which foundation model developers might cause serious harm. Analyzing the choice between negligence and competing doctrinal regimes does, however, suggest important ways in which common law courts should incrementally develop the law of negligence, in order to properly reflect the risks and capabilities of foundation models. For example, courts should expand the scope of the duty of care in negligence, in order to provide redress when foundation models cause economic or emotional injury by behaving in ways that are closely analogous to serious human wrongdoing (e.g., certain crimes and intentional torts, such as theft, deceit, and outrage). But the Article's analysis also suggests certain fundamental pathologies of tort liability as a mechanism of AI governance - pathologies that no amount of doctrinal development will adequately cure. In particular, the specter of tort liability can be expected to disincentivize frontier AI developers from investigating and disclosing many of the novel and poorly understood risks that frontier AI development may pose. That is especially disturbing given that our society is relying quite heavily, for its ability to discover and understand these risks, on frontier AI developers themselves. Thus, tort liability is not only inadequate as a mechanism of frontier AI governance; in certain important respects, it is actively perverse, and its perverse effects must be countered by governance institutions of a different kind. Ultimately, a robust regime of ex ante regulation - under which government institutions or credibly neutral third-party experts are empowered to investigate, evaluate, and mitigate the risks of frontier AI development - is urgently required in frontier AI governance.

title: A Taxonomy of Rational Handoffs for AI Agents
abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more prevalent, the question of when they should relinquish control to a human is a critical design concern. Current approaches often rely on ad-hoc heuristics. This paper makes two contributions to establish a more principled foundation for this problem. First, and primarily, we introduce a comprehensive taxonomy of rational hand-off scenarios, moving beyond simple confidence scores to include triggers based on risk, system policies, resource optimization, causal uncertainty, and information security. Second, we present the rudimentary mathematical foundations of a framework designed to operationalize this taxonomy. We introduce the Agency-Humility Equilibrium (AHE) as a core decision-theoretic principle and the Handoff Utility Function (HUF) as a mechanism for balancing autonomous action against deferral. This work aims to provide a clear conceptual map and a preliminary formal language for designing safer and more reliable agentic systems.

title: Human Value Creation under Uncertainty Toward Personal Intellectual Capital in the AI-Augmented Knowledge Economy
abstract: Even when professionals operate under similar conditions of knowledge access, artificial intelligence and educational opportunity, they continue to display markedly different capacities to sustain value creation over time. Psychology, Knowledge Management and Intellectual Capital (IC) theory each illuminate part of this divergence, but none explains it in full. This paper takes as its starting point a core anomaly: as generative Artificial Intelligence makes synthesised knowledge increasingly abundant, the human capacity to sustain value creation has not followed the same trajectory. This paper develops a preliminary conceptual foundation to explain why sustained human value creation diverges under these conditions-Personal Intellectual Capital (Personal IC)-investigated here at the level of the individual professional. Adopting a transdisciplinary conceptual approach, the paper integrates insights from Psychology, Knowledge Management and Intellectual Capital theory, building on the foundations of individual-level Intellectual Capital theory, to conceptualise Personal IC as an evolving configuration-not a static stock-of Human, Structural and Relational intellectual resources whose value lies in how effectively they are organised and applied under conditions of uncertainty to sustain Professional Excellence. The paper contributes this initial conceptual foundation and outlines a preliminary transdisciplinary research programme for inquiry into sustained human value creation.

title: Misperceiving the Frontier: Managerial Beliefs and the Allocation of AI
abstract: Generative AI is a prominent example of a broader challenge firms face when adopting new technologies: their benefits are often uneven across tasks and workers, exhibiting a "jagged technological frontier." We study whether managers anticipate that the benefits of new technologies are uneven across tasks and workers, and how the information environment affects deployment. In a linked worker-manager experiment, workers complete real-effort tasks with and without generative AI, allowing us to estimate AI effects by task and worker type. Managers then predict AI-assisted performance and make incentivized deployment decisions. Without feedback, most managers mistakenly expect AI to improve performance on both sides of the frontier. Performance feedback reduces average optimism, but substantial overestimation remains for outside-frontier tasks. We further examine incentive-compatible deployment decisions for two new tasks (one inside and one outside the frontier). Managers' willingness to pay (WTP) is high across all tasks, and even higher for the outside-frontier task where AI does not add value. An information-design intervention in the Feedback condition that makes salient which tasks are inside or outside the frontier reduces WTP for outside-frontier deployment relative to inside-frontier deployment. This evidence is consistent with salience-based memory retrieval: the negative effects of AI are only corrected when the boundaries of the technology are made salient. The findings suggest that realizing organizational gains from new technologies depends not only on technical capability, but on information environments that make the limits of those capabilities visible to decision-makers.

title: Same Occupations, Different Clocks: Separating Remote Work from Generative AI for Labor-Market Entrants
abstract: Is generative AI or remote work behind the weak labor market for new entrants? Separating them is difficult because the same occupations face both shocks. However, the shocks arrived three years apart. I fix CPS entrants’ exposure at their pre-pandemic occupation mixes and date each treatment to its own shock. A standard deviation of remote-work exposure predicts 1.81 percent lower entry hourly pay and 2 percent lower entry annual income. I find no stable effect on hourly pay, annual income, or net employment from AI exposure. Hourly rates constructed from weekly earnings and hours fall because hours rise faster than weekly earnings, while the AI employment estimate changes sign under flexible remote-work paths.

title: Stimuli Augmentation for Internal and External Validity in Experiments with Latent Treatments
abstract: Social scientists run experiments using text as stimuli to estimate the causal effect of a specific textual feature. The standard approach is to construct a pair of stimuli so that only the target feature varies across conditions. Constructed stimuli, however, are not representative of texts people encounter in the real world, limiting external validity. When researchers use real-world texts instead, the target feature varies with other textual features, introducing confounding that threatens internal validity. To address this trade-off, I propose stimuli augmentation as a general design-stage approach. The approach uses large language models to rewrite each real-world text to change the treatment feature while leaving other content intact, producing a matched pair of the original and its rewritten counterfactual. Augmented pairs balance confounding features across conditions for internal validity, while preserving real-world variation for external validity. I develop diagnostics to evaluate the quality of augmentation, and demonstrate the method through candidate profile and media framing experiments with three original surveys.

title: Protecting the Thinking Process in Human-AI Interaction: The Forum Interstitiale Between Thought and Expression
abstract: International human rights law protects freedom of thought absolutely and freedom of expression subject to limitation. Doctrine calls the two sides of that line the forum internum and the forum externum. The line was drawn when thinking left no trace. It no longer holds. Within six months in 2026, a United States court ordered that twenty million ChatGPT conversations be produced under ordinary discovery rules, two federal courts reached opposite conclusions on whether a litigant's exchanges with a chatbot are protected at all, and the Supreme Court held that location records kept by a third party remain constitutionally protected. Records of where a person's body had been were protected. Records of how their mind worked were not. The law has no category for the search query, the exploratory prompt, the unfinished draft, or the confession made to a machine. The United States answer has been a quarrel about privilege: courts refuse protection because the machine is not a professional, like a doctor or a lawyer, and industry asks for a new privilege because it behaves like one. Both assume that protection depends on what the machine is. This article argues that it depends on what the person is doing. It proposes the forum interstitiale, a third zone between the two classical fora, protecting the thinking process under a standard stronger than ordinary expression law but short of absolute. Every candidate analogy in existing law is tested, from search queries and confidential dialogue to protected reading, aggregated records, the European law on correspondence and data protection, private diaries and drafts, and neural data. Each fails for the same reason. Protection attaches to a relationship, a disclosure, a recording, an addressee or a data type, and never to the function of the act as thinking. The zone only works upwards. It raises acts the binary abandons and takes nothing from the absolute core, which answers the objection that widening protection dilutes it. The article sets out who belongs in the zone, five elements of the protection standard, the duties those elements impose on providers, and a map of individual AI interactions across the three fora. This classification is not an academic exercise. It decides what can be demanded, kept, filtered, and used against the person who thought it.

title: Measuring Agency-amplifying AI Literacy: The HuskyAI Coaching Platform for Workforce Readiness
abstract: HuskyAI is a web platform on which learners develop AI knowledge by working through authentic challenges in supervised conversations with a generative model, with every message scored in real time on the Prompt Effectiveness Index (PEI). Using a multi-agent architecture, PEI grades the quality of a student's thinking while prompting-across Prompt Structural Quality, Conversation Control, Technical Sophistication, Cognitive Load Management, and Reliance Appropriateness-rather than whether the model produced a correct answer or polished artifact/deliverable. This paper situates the platform within multiple conversations (human agency, the cognitive risks of AI use, AI as an epistemic technology, AI fluency, the science of learning, and evaluative judgement) and shows how the system's architecture is built to meet the theoretical requirements those literatures impose. We argue that PEI provides a metric for detecting whether fluency is exercised in the augmentative mode in which the human remains the author of the collaboration rather than its audience-the conduct recent large-scale evidence (Potts and Sudhof, 2026) identifies as the difference between AI as "a lottery [and] a tool." PEI is a measure, we argue, of human cognitive integrity in an AI context. We describe the agentic evaluator behind PEI, the design choices through which it answers the literature's transparency, calibration, and validity demands, and the limitations of an in-conversation instrument as a learning tool.

title: An Interpretable Non-Invasive Artificial Intelligence Framework for Preoperative Mortality Risk Stratification in Colorectal Cancer With Peritoneal Metastasis: A Multicenter Validation Study
abstract: Background: Preoperative risk assessment in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases (CRC-PM) relies largely on peritoneal disease burden and anticipated completeness of cytoreduction, but these measures do not fully identify patients who remain at high mortality risk. We developed and externally validated the Radiomics–PCI–CRS Mortality Prediction for Peritoneal Metastasis (RPCM-PM), a non-invasive and interpretable artificial intelligence framework for preoperative mortality-risk stratification. Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included 173 patients with CRC-PM from SYSU (n=123), FPH1 (n=35), and FUSCC (n=15), and 34 patients with CRC without PM from FPH0 as an exploratory reference cohort. A logistic-regression model integrated CT radiomics, large language model (LLM)-derived peritoneal cancer index (PCI), and deep-learning (DL)-derived cytoreductive surgery (CRS)-related imaging signatures to predict all-cause mortality status. LLM-derived PCI was used when matched CT reports were available and physician-assessed PCI otherwise. The model was developed using a stratified 7:3 SYSU training and internal-validation split and applied unchanged to FPH1, FUSCC, the pooled external CRC-PM cohort, and FPH0.SHAP analysis and patient-level imaging visualization supported interpretation of RPCM-PM mortality-risk estimates. Findings: RPCM-PM achieved an AUC of 0.867 (95% CI 0.730–0.967) in SYSU internal validation and AUCs of 0.781 (0.500–0.968) in FPH1 and 0.780 (0.462–1.000) in FUSCC, yielding a pooled external AUC of 0.800 (0.628–0.943). The AUC was 0.694 (0.498–0.872) in the exploratory FPH0 reference cohort. At the fixed threshold, PPVs for mortality among patients classified as high risk were 85.7% (18/21) in SYSU internal validation, 86.2% (25/29) in FPH1, and 88.9% (8/9) in FUSCC. Among patients with lower PCI, observed mortality was 82.6% in the RPCM-PM high-risk group and 32.4% in the low-risk group (P<0.001). Among patients with predicted CC0/1, observed mortality was 86.2% in the high-risk group and 34.5% in the low-risk group (P<0.001). Interpretation: RPCM-PM provided additional preoperative mortality-risk stratification among patients with lower peritoneal disease burden or favorable predicted cytoreductive completeness. The framework may support preoperative risk assessment and patient counseling before CRS, but prospective validation is required before clinical use.

title: Beyond Adoption Metrics: Participation Depth and Post-Adoption Mobility in Generative AI Use
abstract: Digital-divide research increasingly recognizes that access does not determine who benefits from digital technologies. For generative AI (GenAI), however, most evidence still measures whether people have used the technology, not whether participation deepens after entry. This study develops a post-adoption mobility framework that distinguishes casual free participation, deep participation, reconfiguration, and exit. Using the 2024–2025 Korean Media Panel Survey—a same-instrument panel capturing ChatGPT-era GenAI diffusion in a digitally advanced early market—we classify GenAI users by two observable participation-depth markers: whether use is located in the work domain and whether it involves paid service access. The work-purpose marker is central to the contribution because it allows us to observe movement into an instrumental application domain rather than only adoption or frequency. Most new or re-entering users enter through casual free use rather than work-oriented or paid forms. Logit models show that education and income predict deep entry among entrants. Among baseline casual-free users, multinomial models show that education and income predict deepening into work-oriented or paid participation, whereas older age predicts exit. Among users who begin in deeper forms, losing a work or paid marker while remaining active is more common than complete exit. These findings show that GenAI inclusion cannot be evaluated by adoption or churn alone; it requires tracking mobility into, out of, and within work-oriented and paid forms of participation.

title: Capped Base-Stock Policies: A 2.33-Approximation
abstract: We study the classical periodic-review lost-sales inventory model with lead times. Since its introduction in Xin (2021), the class of capped base-stock policies has emerged as a state-of-the-art baseline for evaluating both traditional inventory policies and more recent AI-driven approaches. In particular, capped base-stock policies have served as a strong baseline in studies of deep reinforcement learning and, more recently, LLM-based inventory control. Despite extensive numerical evidence suggesting that these policies perform near optimally, their theoretical guarantees remain an open question. In this paper, we prove that the best capped base-stock policy achieves an approximation ratio of 7/3 ≈ 2.33. Our analysis introduces two novel ideas. First, in contrast to the existing literature that predominantly derives lower bounds from single-variable optimization problems, we formulate a two-variable optimization problem that provides a lower bound on the optimal cost. This richer formulation allows a direct policy comparison because each capped base-stock policy is characterized by exactly two parameters. Second, unlike the common approach of bounding the best capped base-stock policy through single-parameter base-stock or constant-order policies, we use each feasible solution pair of the lower-bound problem to construct two policies in the capped base-stock class. We then use a coupling argument to show that the better of the two satisfies the desired approximation guarantee. Although the ratio 2.33 is numerically larger than the long-standing 2-approximation guarantee for the dual-balancing policy established by Levi et al. (2008), the two guarantees concern different policy classes and therefore do not directly reflect their practical performance. Extensive numerical evidence indicates that capped base-stock policies generally outperform the dual-balancing policy, sometimes by a significant margin. Our result therefore closes an important part of the gap between empirical performance and theoretical understanding. It also suggests that the main obstacle to breaking the 2-approximation barrier may lie in current analytical techniques rather than in the capped base-stock policy class itself. The analytical framework developed in this paper provides a foundation for further refinements that may ultimately yield an approximation ratio strictly below 2.

title: SAICP: A Vendor-Neutral Control Plane for Securing AI Interaction Boundaries
abstract: Organizations are adopting generative AI for drafting, analysis, retrieval, and increasingly for actions that affect enterprise systems. The security problem is not limited to whether a model produces a safe answer. Risk also arises at the boundaries where an application chooses a model, retrieves data, accepts instructions from untrusted content, invokes a tool, changes a target after approval, or releases output to a destination. This paper presents the Secure AI Interaction Control Plane (SAICP), a vendor-neutral architecture that places deterministic authorization and evidence controls around those boundaries. SAICP does not treat a model as an authorization authority. Its four core separations are: requested intent from granted authority, classification from source trust, model generation from output release, and individual actions from cumulative session risk. Evaluation used an automated test suite, fourteen prototype scenarios, seven end-to-end conformance cases, and audit-chain verification; all passed at the time of drafting. The results show that the proposed control-plane pattern can keep low-risk assistive use practical while denying unregistered, mismatched, sensitive, high-impact, or un-auditable activity. The prototype remains a reference implementation, enterprise identity, transactional state, production model and tool integrations, stronger scanning, and independent security testing are still required.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Reverse Engineering of a Global SiC PVT Furnace: Selecting Material Properties and Benchmark Validation
abstract: It is an important process in physical-vapor-transport (PVT) growth of bulk Silicon Carbide (SiC) how steeply temperature gradient falls between the growth front and the crystal-crucible lid, and this gradient depends directly on the SiC single-crystal conductivity in a global SiC PVT furnace simulation. This paper shows numerical results of an axisymmetric conduction-radiation Finite Element Method (FEM) code for a global SiC PVT furnace, with the help of a large language model (Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic). To match a given vertical temperature gradient at the benchmark monitoring points, to within 5 K, the SiC crystal conductivity was taken from Joshi's independent phonon-scattering model. Every other material property is traced to a cited source or explicitly flagged where it is an engineering estimate. It is also described the role of the AI assistant in reconstructing, tuning, validating, searching and even discussing in this FEM simulation.

title: Inflation Drivers in Firms' Words: Bridging Micro Narratives and Macro Dynamics *
abstract: This paper develops a framework that links microeconomic narratives to structural macro models of firm pricing. Using the Federal Reserve Bank's Beige Book data, we employ an LLM to extract qualitative measures of firms' price adjustments and factor attributions at the micro level. These measures are then used to estimate a state-space model of aggregate inflation dynamics implied by a menu-cost model featuring lumpy price adjustments and reporting frictions. We demonstrate how micro price narratives provide useful information for correctly decomposing the macro drivers of inflation.

title: Above-ground Biomass Estimation with Geospatial Foundation Models
abstract: Accurate estimation of Above-Ground Biomass (AGB) from satellite imagery is essential for the large-scale monitoring of carbon stocks, yet it remains a challenging regression task at global scale. Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising machine learning paradigm to derive general-purpose representations from Earth observation data, but their utility for quantitative regression tasks like biomass estimation remains largely unexplored, as most benchmarks emphasize classification and segmentation. Here, we present a comprehensive benchmark of GFMs for global-scale AGB estimation using the AGBD dataset, a machine learning-ready benchmark spanning diverse biomes and geographies.
