We distinguish two ways in which GFMs reach practitioners: (i) models distributed as weights to be run by the user, which we evaluate as frozen encoders within the PANGAEA benchmarking framework; and (ii) models distributed as ready-to-use, pre-computed embedding products, for which we evaluate AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and TESSERA. We compare $11$ GFMs available on PANGAEA and both embedding products against a fully supervised state-of-the-art (SOTA) model, assess their geographical and temporal generalization abilities, as well as agreement with the ESA CCI biomass product on independent reference data. Our results show that GFMs run as frozen encoders substantially underperform with respect to the supervised SOTA model, whereas pre-computed embedding products prove highly effective. An MLP trained on AEF embeddings outperforms the supervised SOTA model trained on AGBD features, and the same SOTA model trained on AEF embeddings (optionally augmented with selected raw features) achieves the best overall result, while also generalizing better across space and time. These findings indicate that frozen GFM features can be highly informative for biomass regression when the underlying model is trained on rich multi-modal data and its outputs are distributed as an accessible embedding layer.

title: Joint Optimization of Human Headcount and Stochastic AI Resource Capacity
abstract: Generative AI tools are rapidly becoming standard for coding and other business operations. However, while these tools can drive productivity, their unpredictable, and often significant, costs are putting severe financial strain on organizations. The leadership of such organizations must split a fixed budget between human headcount and generative-AI token capacity, yet standard deterministic planning ignores both the heavy-tailed volatility of token consumption and the cognitive cost of auditing AI-generated output. We model the joint allocation by intersecting a cognitive-friction-adjusted production function with a chance-constrained stochastic budget frontier. Per-engineer token usage is treated as i.i.d., non-negative, and right-skewed; no parametric family is assumed, as only its mean, variance, and skewness enter the analysis. The chance constraint is reduced to a deterministic equivalent via the Central Limit Theorem with a Cornish--Fisher skewness correction. Solving the resulting Lagrangian yields a closed-form optimal headcount, a transcendental condition for optimal per-capita token intensity, and a bordered-Hessian second-order condition that holds for any reasonable volatility-to-headcount ratio. Comparative statics show that rising individual token volatility raises optimal per-capita token intensity while contracting headcount: although human labor and tokens are complements in production, the stochastic budget makes them substitutes at the margin. Individual usage skewness acts as a pure deadweight tax that shrinks the budget without altering the substitution dynamics. Both conclusions presuppose that usage dispersion is invariant to the planned mean allocation. In the case where dispersion instead scales proportionally with the mean, the substitution reverses, so which regime applies is a sharp, empirically testable question.

title: Optimal Inflation Rate: A Meta-Analysis
abstract: We revisit the optimal long-run inflation rate using 777 estimates from 116 primary studies published between 1989 and 2026, the largest sample on the topic to date. To our knowledge, this is among the first economics meta-analyses in which primary-data extraction is done from start to finish through a documented and auditable large-language-model pipeline, calibrated against a hand-coded training set and released for replication. The literature points to an optimum of about 0.6 percentage points per year, well below the two-percent targets used by most advanced-economy central banks. The gap should not be automatically read as a verdict against the two-percent norm. Measurement error in published price indices could close, widen, or even reverse the gap, and the structural literature itself cannot pin down the sign of the required correction. Bayesian model averaging over the full set of structural moderators shows that cross-study variation is driven by real modelling choices rather than by selective reporting. The main drivers are the choice of monetary benchmark (Friedman rule vs. laissez-faire), the transactions-frictions technology, the assumed shock structure, and the class of nominal-rigidity contract. The non-parametric caliper test finds no upward bunching at the two-percent target. The paper contributes a reproducible LLM-assisted extraction pipeline for structurally calibrated literature and a quantitative decomposition of where the optimal-inflation literature disagrees.

title: Me and My Bot: What Users Talk About in AI Companion Communities on Reddit
abstract: AI companion communities on platforms such as Reddit are widely characterized as spaces where users discuss their relationships with AI bots. This study examines whether and how that characterization holds, guided by the Synthetic Resonance framework's claim that human-AI relationships can carry genuine relational meaning for the user. Multiple LLMs were employed to code 5,504 Reddit posts from eight AI companion communities for relationship focus, primary topic, and users' emotional valence. Although search terms were weighted toward relational and attachment language, only 45% of posts concerned the user's own relationship with their bot. Posts about users' own bots differed markedly from posts about bots in general in both topic and emotional expression, with 85% of general-bot posts containing no user emotion language compared to 33% of own-bot posts. Among the 970 posts that were relationally focused, companionship and romance each accounted for roughly 46% of discussion, sexual content for 8%, and emotional valence varied across these subtopics. The findings suggest that users engage with these relationships with AI bots as meaningful, and that the discourse about them is broad and emotionally complex.

title: A Multilingual LLM-Based News Indicator of Euro Area Inflationary Pressures
abstract: We construct a novel multilingual news-based indicator of inflationary pressures in the euro area. The indicator has a positive and significant impact on households' inflation expectations, even after controlling for market- and survey-based measures. Newspapers are thus shown to contain early information about euro-area households' inflation expectations. Using a large language model, we score more than one million newspaper articles in French, German, Italian, and Spanish on a six-class directional scale, simultaneously filtering irrelevant content and measuring price pressures. We then fine-tune a multilingual encoder to enable scalable annotation of a 17-million-article corpus (2006-2024). Validation against a human-annotated benchmark for France yields a correlation of 83%. To facilitate replication and future research, we make both the trained classifier and the complete annotation pipeline publicly available.

title: Year 2026: Attention to AI Over-Reliance is All You Need in AI Education!
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now routinely used by university students, and diagnostic instruments increasingly attempt to identify at-risk use. We study a cohort with a documented AI-use history-curricular exposure to AI-resistant pedagogy and roughly five years of continuous AI access since 2021-and empirically test six theoreticallygrounded hypotheses, one per subscale of a 17-item, six-subscale diagnostic survey (Pedagogical Attitudes/PA, Behavioural Over-Reliance/OR, AI Literacy/LIT, Educational Engagement/DIS, Academic Integrity Awareness/INT, AI Competency/COM) administered to N = 413 students. Grounded respectively in instructional-design, cognitive-offloading, self-regulated-learning, self-efficacy, institutional-socialisation, and deliberate-practice theory, the hypotheses predict a well-rounded low-risk profile on five subscales alongside a high-risk profile on OR. Four of six were fully supported: PA skewed strongly Aligned (H1), OR skewed strongly toward over-reliance (H2, 29.2% High-risk, the largest tail of any subscale), DIS skewed toward engagement (H4), and COM skewed strongly toward high competency (H6, 77.1% Low-risk). Two were partially supported: LIT (H3) and INT (H5) each showed a small High-risk tail but a Moderate, not Low-risk, modal band. Critically, LIT and COM showed no protective association with OR (r =-0.04 and r = 0.06 respectively; χ 2 = 0.01, p = 0.922 among respondents Low-risk on both), and a 11.0% subgroup that is simultaneously literate, competent, and over-reliant is also significantly more disengaged (p < .001) despite holding more AI-resistant attitudes (p < .001) than the rest of the sample-a knowledge-behaviour gap, not efficient use. A composite risk-profile taxonomy operationalises this pattern across ten mutually exclusive profiles, cross-validated by both an existing item and the new COM subscale. We discuss three implications: over-reliance requires targeted behavioural intervention (AI-resistance and AI-resilience education) rather than further literacy training; generic AI-skill instruction likely has diminishing returns for the majority of this cohort; and the joint hypothesis pattern is most consistent with AI use oriented toward completing assignments rather than toward genuine learning.

title: Policy-as-Architecture: Treating AI Safety as a Kernel-Level Resource Management Problem
abstract: Current AI safety practice relies almost exclusively on application-layer, linguistic guardrails that a sufficiently motivated adversary can bypass through adversarial formatting or novel prompting. This creates what the author terms "Accountability Evaporation": a structural responsibility gap in high-stakes deployments where no deterministic, hardware-enforced boundary exists between an AI agent's proposed action and its execution in the physical or consequential layer. Drawing on two decades of practitioner experience in OS-level and criticalinfrastructure software delivery, this paper proposes Policy-as-Architecturetreating AI safety as a kernel-level resource management problem rather than a purely linguistic one. The Autonomous Safety Kernel (ASK) is a three-layer architecture that decouples non-deterministic AI proposal generation from deterministic, hardware-gated execution: Layer 1 produces canonical, cryptographically signed action envelopes; Layer 2 evaluates them deterministically against governance-signed rule bundles; Layer 3, implemented as an Enforcement Microcontroller with hardware root of trust and independent power domain, controls the execution bus and cannot be bypassed by the Agent Host. The Global AI Safety Index (GASI) proposes a consortium-governed benchmarking process model-modeled on the SPECpower precedentdefining a Safety-per-Outcome metric class and a graduated adversarial load protocol with anti-gaming controls. Three concrete embodiments are provided: operational technology control systems, financial transaction gateways, and healthcare patient safety. This paper presents a hypothesis grounded in practitioner experience; ASK and GASI are proposed architecturally and have not yet been prototyped at the time of writing.

title: Economics of AI Labeling on Social Media Platforms
abstract: Generative AI has blurred the distinction between human-created and AI-generated content in social media, creating uncertainty for consumers who have heterogeneous preferences for the two content types. While some consumers have a strict preference for the content type with which they engage, others have a soft preference such that the content quality shapes the content type they choose to engage with. Simultaneously, human-created content has become an additional revenue source, besides advertisements, for social media platforms because humancreated content has emerged as key training data for AI models. Some platforms have started to label AI-generated content in response to developments in generative AI, an effort that regulators increasingly mandate or promote, even though the identification of a content's true type is imperfect. We study platforms' incentives to label AI-generated content. We find that while labeling can be profitable, it may actually hurt an advertising-driven platform by diminishing consumer engagement. A platform that monetizes human-created content as well may have even less incentive to adopt labeling. Labeling can also harm content creators, consumers, and overall welfare. The driving force behind these results is creators' strategic response to labeling, which, in turn, depends on how labeling shifts consumers' engagement decisions. While labeling enhances the utility of consumers with strict preferences for content type, incentivizing creators to improve quality, it relaxes competition between creators to attract soft-preference consumers, disincentivizing creators from improving quality. The latter occurs because labeling, by enabling consumers to better distinguish content types, elevates the salience of content type relative to content quality in consumers' engagement decisions. The platform prefers more engagement from human-created content when it monetizes human-created content. However, a high (low) accuracy in detecting AI-generated (human-created) content suppresses the human creator's incentive to improve content quality, diminishing the platform's incentive to label. The results have strong implications for social planners and other stakeholders in social media.

title: Efficiency and Cost Alignment in Batched LLM Serving via Resource-Fair Scheduling
abstract: This paper studies a resource-allocation inefficiency in batched large language model (LLM) serving: heterogeneous requests that share a decode batch impose max-driven computational costs on one another. Because the wall-clock cost of a batch step is largely governed by the largest active KV-cache footprint, a short request co-batched with a long request can experience latency and GPU-resource consumption disproportionate to its own token workload. We formalize this phenomenon as a resource-fair scheduling problem. We develop a mathematical scheduling model that connects within-batch resource fairness to system throughput. The proposed fairness constraint bounds the disparity in decode progress, equivalently KV-cache footprint, among co-batched requests. Based on this model, we design the Insert-Short-Jobs-with-Limit (ISJL) algorithm, a parameterized hybrid batching policy. We prove that ISJL achieves a global competitive-ratio lower bound of 3/4 and further characterize how the worstcase guarantee varies with the fairness budget. Empirical evaluations show that ISJL improves throughput and end-to-end latency relative to standard scheduling baselines. We further examine the profit implications of resource-fair scheduling under the token-metered pricing convention used by commercial LLM APIs. In this environment, for a fixed accepted workload, revenue is additive in token counts and is independent of the scheduling policy; scheduling affects profit through inference cost. We prove a cost decomposition showing that inference cost consists of an intrinsic workload term, a time/overhead term, and a schedule-induced batching externality term. The fairness constraint bounds the batching externality, while the ISJL throughput guarantee controls the time/overhead component. Numerical experiments show that ISJL occupies a favorable middle ground between FCFS, which has large batching externalities, and LJF, which is cost-aligned but sacrifices batching flexibility. Thus, ISJL provides a bi-criterion scheduling policy: it maintains high throughput while aligning max-driven batch cost with token-metered revenue.

title: Competition, Boundaries, and Firm Innovation: Evidence from LLM-Identified Business Networks
abstract: We examine how competition shapes firm innovation when product market boundaries are becoming increasingly blurred. Leveraging firms’ business descriptions and a purpose‑built LLM pipeline, we construct a novel business network for Chinese listed firms and investigate the innovation effects of competitive pressure. Our network reveals that over 80% of identified competitive links are not captured by conventional industry classifications. Empirically, we find that both intra‑ and inter‑industry competition promote firm innovation, yet only intra‑industry competition exhibits a significant inverted‑U relationship with innovation output, consistent with Aghion et al. (2005). Mechanism tests indicate that this pattern is primarily driven by substantive innovation, as reflected in exploratory R&D and invention patent filings. The effect is more pronounced among non‑high‑tech, financially unconstrained, and less productive firms. Moreover, geographic proximity to competitors amplifies innovation incentives via localized knowledge spillovers. Our findings carry direct policy implications: effective innovation‑oriented competition policy must account for firms’ actual competitive dynamics, particularly competition that cuts across traditional industry boundaries.

title: ExeCutie: The Dawn of Runtime Generative Software Agents
abstract: Embedding a large language model (LLM) agent inside a running desktop application, with direct access to that application's live objects, requires solving two engineering problems: dispatching agent-generated code onto the application's main thread safely, and giving that code a namespace connected to the application's actual running state. Existing agents solve neither: they run as a separate process from the host application, and even when extended into an application's workflow via a plugin, they cannot reach its main thread, interact with its live GUI, or access its in-memory state — they operate alongside an application, not from inside it. This paper describes ExeCutie, a Python library exposed to the host application as a single Qt dock widget. Behind that widget, the library solves the thread-dispatch problem with a Qt signal-based dispatcher requiring only a running Qt event loop, and solves the namespace problem by reusing the live user namespace of a developer-configured IPython kernel, so the host application — not the library — determines the agent's scope of access, from a single object to the full namespace. Because the agent executes directly on the main thread, it can synthesize new software at runtime: front-end widgets and their back-end logic generated together and displayed on demand, for functionality absent from the application's source code until the moment a workflow requires it. In doing so, the boundary between developing an application and using it collapses: the same running process can be extended by whoever is operating it, without a restart.

title: Prevalence of Emotional and Relational Engagement with AI and Their Associations with Psychosocial Adjustment among College Students
abstract: Although growing evidence suggests that some individuals use generative artificial intelligence (GAI) for emotional support and companionship, little is known about how prevalent these experiences are, who is most likely to report them, and how they relate to psychosocial adjustment. The present study addressed these questions using a regionally representative sample of 1,406 university students from 26 universities in Shanghai, China ( M age = 18.98 years, SD = 1.25, 59.7% female). Results indicated that most participants primarily viewed AI as a functional tool, whereas emotionally meaningful engagement remained relatively uncommon. Nevertheless, approximately one in seven participants reported moderate to high levels of personal disclosure or emotional attachment to AI. Emotional and relational engagement with AI was more common among individuals reporting greater interpersonal vulnerabilities and lower relational resources. Different forms of AI engagement also showed distinct patterns of association with psychosocial adjustment. Assistance-oriented engagement was associated with more positive interpersonal orientations, whereas more emotionally intensive forms of engagement were associated with poorer psychosocial adjustment. These findings suggest that emotional engagement with AI is already a meaningful experience for a subset of young adults and is embedded within broader patterns of interpersonal functioning and psychosocial adjustment.

title: The SAFE-AI Framework: An Organisational Governance Model for the Responsible Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed organisational practices by enhancing productivity, supporting decision-making, and enabling new forms of knowledge creation. Despite these benefits, the widespread integration of GenAI has introduced significant governance challenges, including risks to data confidentiality, intellectual property, regulatory compliance, accountability, and organisational oversight. While existing research has made substantial contributions to the fields of AI ethics, responsible AI, and algorithmic governance, organisations continue to face difficulties translating these high-level principles into practical governance structures that can be implemented consistently across diverse operational contexts. This gap highlights the need for an integrated organisational governance framework that extends beyond technical safeguards and isolated policy development. This conceptual paper proposes the SAFE-AI Framework, an organisational governance model designed to support the responsible adoption and oversight of generative artificial intelligence. Developed through a synthesis of literature on AI governance, corporate governance, information governance, risk management, organisational learning, and continuous improvement, the framework identifies six interdependent governance domains: Secure Data, Accountability, Frameworks and Policies, Education, Auditing, and Improvement (SAFE-AI). Together, these domains provide a structured approach to embedding responsible AI governance within organisational strategy, operations, and culture. The paper argues that effective AI governance requires an integrated organisational approach that combines policy, leadership, education, accountability, and continuous evaluation rather than relying solely on technological controls or regulatory compliance. By presenting a practical governance model applicable across sectors-including corporate organisations, higher education, healthcare, and the public sector-this paper contributes to the growing discourse on organisational AI governance while providing a foundation for future empirical validation, governance maturity assessment, and sector-specific implementation studies.

title: Energy Export Dependency and Fiscal Resilience: A Comparative Analysis of Gulf Economies (Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait) (2010-2025)
abstract: This paper examines whether structural differences in fiscal breakeven prices and Economic Complexity Index (ECI) slopes explain divergent fiscal and diversification outcomes across four major Gulf hydrocarbon exporters - Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait - during a shared commodity price cycle from 2010 to 2025. Using a 64-observation unbalanced panel and four analytical modules, the paper tests four propositions: Price Primacy, Fiscal Margin Differentiation, Diversification Divergence, and the Dual-Risk Threshold. Module A confirms that price movements, not production volume changes, drove hydrocarbon revenue volatility across all four economies, with median price dependence ranging from 80.34% for Saudi Arabia to 104.53% for the UAE. Module B finds that fiscal breakeven prices, not production scale, explain divergent fiscal outcomes: Qatar ran deficits in 12.5% of panel years against Saudi Arabia's 68.8%, despite facing the same Brent price cycle. Module C reveals significant divergence in diversification trajectories: the UAE leads on absolute ECI score while Kuwait records the steepest positive ECI slope, whereas Saudi Arabia's falling HC/GDP ratio reflects GDP growth rather than genuine export basket complexity. A standardised 17% supply shock stress test, anchored to the Ras Laffan infrastructure disruption modelled in Ansar (2026a), confirms that fiscal breakeven price is the decisive variable for supply shock resilience as well as price resilience: Qatar and the UAE remain in post-shock surplus while Saudi Arabia and Kuwait remain in deficit. The paper concludes that price risk and supply risk are two expressions of the same underlying structural condition, and that the HC/GDP ratio is an unreliable diversification measure where ECI and HC/GDP trends diverge. Three policy implications follow: fiscal breakeven targeting, sovereign wealth funds as liquidity rather than structural buffers, and ECI slope as the primary diversification metric. AI Disclosure: This research was conducted with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), an AI system, for research support, drafting, and document formatting. All data sourcing, interpretation, and conclusions presented in this paper are the author’s own.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Export Product Quality Upgrading under Trade Friction: The Institutional Constraint of Host-Country Privacy Protection Policies
abstract: Trade friction continues to constrain the competitive space and quality-upgrading paths of Chinese export firms, while generative artificial intelligence (GAI) may open up new operational space for them. Based on matched customs and listed-company data from 2010 to 2024, we construct a trade friction intensity index from manually compiled trade remedy investigation cases and measures GAI application intensity through textual analysis of annual reports, empirically examining the impact of trade friction on export product quality upgrading, the moderating effect of GAI, and how host-country privacy protection policies further constrain this moderating effect. We find that trade friction negatively affects export product quality upgrading; GAI positively moderates this negative effect; and in host countries that have implemented the GDPR, the positive moderating effect of GAI is significantly weakened. After a series of robustness and endogeneity checks, the main findings remain robust and credible. Moreover, the moderating effect of GAI exhibits industry heterogeneity, being more pronounced in high-technology industries and high data-intensity industries. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding GAI's buffering effect under trade friction and its applicable boundaries, and offers policy implications for advancing the alignment of GAI application and data governance.

title: Temporal GraphSync-RAG: LLM-Augmented Dynamic Knowledge Graph Synchronization for Real-Time Recommendation
abstract: Knowledge graph (KG)-augmented recommendation systems excel at capturing semantic relationships but often struggle with real-time preference drift and online serving latency constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Temporal GraphSync-RAG (TGSR), a unified four-stage pipeline. TGSR maintains a dynamic KG using exponential time decay to down-weight stale interactions, and employs a temporal confidence-aware retriever to extract high-quality, multi-hop subgraphs based on recency and path consistency. These subgraphs serve as context for an LLM-based reranking stage. For efficient online serving, a lightweight MLP reranker unifies all features using ListNet loss integrated with an explicit latency penalty. Experiments across three benchmark datasets (Amazon Electronics, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp) demonstrate that TGSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines like LightGCN and BPR-MF in NDCG@10, with performance gains particularly pronounced in lower interaction densities. Furthermore, the synchronous pipeline achieves a 95th-percentile latency of 24.3 ms on CPU, well within standard production budgets. Ablation studies confirm that while the KG attribute-overlap module drives the primary ranking improvements, temporal decay successfully prunes subgraphs to reduce retriever latency by 2.7 times.

title: Before the Event: Predicting Individual Event Participation Without Dedicated Data Collection to Support Smart Planning in Shrinking Cities
abstract: Small-scale cultural events are one of the few remaining instruments for sustaining civic life in Japan's shrinking cities, yet planners must commit resources before knowing who will attend. Existing approaches fall short: motivational surveys require past attendees; recommender systems need longitudinal records that shrinking municipalities cannot accumulate; and destination choice modeling has rarely been applied to small-city cultural events. This study introduces a competitive Area of Interest (AOI) framework that generates individual-level participation predictions pre-event from administrative data alone. Grounded in spatial interaction theory, the framework characterizes attendance competition along two dimensions: a spatial dimension capturing venue attractiveness relative to competing leisure destinations, and an interest dimension estimating motivational fit via a large language model grounded in national leisure survey data. Validated through leave-one-event-out cross-validation across seven festivals in Takehara City, Hiroshima Prefecture, the framework achieves ROC-AUC of 0.741–0.944; targeting top-ranked individuals yields attendee concentration more than 20 times that of random selection. The thirty-minute driving isochrone emerges as the primary arena of leisure competition; LLM-inferred motivational fit proves decisive for culturally specific events but adds limited signal for general community festivals. Operating without sensors, longitudinal records, or dedicated infrastructure, the framework brings smart city planning capability to resource-constrained municipalities.

title: Do people rely on ChatGPT more than their peers to detect deepfake news?
abstract: This experimental study investigates how people rely on different sources of advice when detecting AI-generated fake news (deepfake news). In a laboratory deepfake detection task, student participants identified the proportion of human-written (non-AI-generated) content in synthetic deepfake news articles and received advice from ChatGPT (GPT-4), human peers, or linguistic experts. The results show that participants rely more on ChatGPT than on human peers when detecting GPT-2-generated deepfake news. Participants also rely more on linguistic experts than on peers, while the relative reliance on experts versus ChatGPT is mixed across experimental waves, potentially reflecting time trends in beliefs about AI-based detection. Importantly, in the additional experiment conducted in 2025 under the same experimental procedure, participants relied more on linguistic experts than on ChatGPT. Moreover, performance improvements reflect the joint role of reliance and advice quality, arising primarily when participants rely on high-quality advice. Overall, relying on AI to detect AI-generated deepfakes can improve detection outcomes, but only when AI-based detection tools are of sufficiently high quality. These findings highlight the dual role of GAI as both a source of deepfakes and a tool for mitigating related risks.

title: When Replanning Becomes the Bottleneck: Budgeted Replanning for Embodied Agents
abstract: Embodied agents replan frequently to recover from execution drift, partial observability, and coordination hazards, but each LLM-based replanning call can consume an accumulated textual context that grows over time and across agents. Once this context becomes large, replanning latency develops heavy tails and can miss real-time deadlines even when task success remains high, a failure mode that is hard to detect from average latency or success alone. We present BRACE, a controller that formulates replanning as a budgeted control loop by deciding whether to replan, selecting a replanning mode, and allocating an explicit token budget and latency service-level objective (SLO) while accounting for optional efficiency modules. As a reusable component, we introduce E-RECAP, a cost-aware progressive token pruning method that predicts token utility and prunes replanning contexts across transformer layers while preserving critical head and tail tokens. Across Meta Habitat, RoboFactory, and AirSim, BRACE with E-RECAP reduces replanning-call token counts by 62-92% and SLO violation rates from 85.5-100.0% to 4.7-50.0% in settings where task success is already saturated. In a harder RoboFactory setting where open-loop, frozen-plan, and No BRACE all fail, BRACE + E-RECAP reaches 80.0% success with 4.6% SLO violations, demonstrating that tail-aware per-call budgeting is effective across embodied platforms.

title: Can Language Models Identify Shadow Trading Targets? An NLP Evaluation of SEC Enforcement Theory
abstract: Shadow trading -- trading in a peer firm's securities on the basis of material nonpublic information (MNPI) about an "economically linked" company -- is a novel and contested theory of insider trading liability, first prosecuted in SEC v. Panuwat (2023). Enforcing it requires identifying economically linked firms ex ante, a determination the SEC makes only after the fact using mass market surveillance infrastructure. We ask whether NLP can do what the SEC's theory presumes insiders already know: identify peer firms ex ante from publicly mandated disclosures. Using a two-stage LLM pipeline applied to Item 7 (Management's Discussion and Analysis) sections of SEC 10-K filings, we score semantic similarity across 30 M&A events spanning five industries and relate similarity to announcement-day abnormal stock returns. On the Panuwat fact pattern itself the pipeline recovers Incyte among the closest peers, a sanity check on the one case with a known outcome. Across the full dataset, however, we find no association: pooling 217 peer observations, the within-event rank correlation between similarity and abnormal return is +0.07 (permutation p = 0.37), and the mean per-event Spearman correlation is +0.05 with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.08, +0.18] -- narrow enough to exclude any moderate relationship rather than merely failing to detect one. A case-level reading agrees: 14 of 30 events support the hypothesis, 12 contradict it, and 4 are ambiguous. We also find that Incyte fell outside the standard \$2B-\$10B mid-cap band on the day before the announcement, complicating the "mid-cap oncology" category the SEC invoked. These results are exploratory and bound to this pipeline, corpus, and return measure, but they put pressure on the empirical premise of shadow trading enforcement and bear on constitutional questions surrounding the SEC's financial surveillance infrastructure.

title: ShiJianBench: From Dialogue to Decision for Long-Horizon Evaluation of Investment Advisors
abstract: Conversational investment advisors influence not only what users know, but also how they make subsequent decisions as market conditions evolve. Existing evaluations primarily assess response quality or observed outcomes, leaving the long-horizon pathway from advisor language to investor behavior difficult to audit. We introduce ShiJianBench, an offline framework for evaluating conversational investment advisors through matched investor trajectories under fixed historical market feedback. At its core is a multi-agent investor simulator with explicit evolving state variables, motive-driven deliberation, long-term memory, and dialogue-grounded updates. The simulator is calibrated against aggregate behavioral patterns from 7,199 real users, and advisor policies are evaluated using separate investor-side, service-side, and content-side metrics under a hard compliance gate. Experiments on Chinese fund-market traces from 2021 to 2026 identify a stable leading group of LLM advisors that combines substantially stronger personalized content with competitive investor-side trajectory outcomes. These results reveal a systematic distinction between producing a high-quality response and delivering an effective long-horizon intervention, motivating trajectory-aware evaluation of conversational advisors.

title: Judging Is Not Enumerating: Silent Omissions in LLM-Authored Acceptable Sets
abstract: Language models are increasingly promoted from examinees to examiners: they write the test suites, answer keys, rubrics, and reward functions that define correctness for other systems. We measure the capability that role assumes and find it lacking under the protocol the role is usually deployed with, one-shot greedy authoring with no test-time reasoning. Across four reference constructions - two with complete finite truth, one with a hardened executable reference (HumanEval+/MBPP+), one with an explicitly incomplete lexical reference (WordNet) - models judge whether a candidate belongs far better than they author the set itself. On the incompleteness-proof algorithmic construction the gap is +0.34 to +0.29 F1 over a 24x parameter range and does not close; on executable code, models judging at F1 0.74-0.90 author suites admitting only 19-42% of oracle-correct solutions. A control locates the deficit: asked to emit the predicate rather than its extension, the same models reach F1 about 0.99. The failure is not missing knowledge or an inability to specify, but an inability to materialise the region a specification induces. The dominant error is omission, which resists audit: an over-inclusion is a token a reviewer can challenge, a missing member an absence whose discovery is the authoring problem itself. Models detect planted over-inclusions 6-7x more often than planted omissions, and a production deployment of 43,227 items fails omission-first at 10:1. Wired into RLVR, an authored key costs 1.9 points of accuracy against an exact oracle and 18.5 WordNet-relative (six paired seeds, p=0.031). Gating authored verifiers on a known-correct probe cuts false rejection from 58-92% to at most 5%, but keeps only 5-39% of suites. Repairing them instead, by rewriting each wrong expected value to what a reference execution returns, raises yield 3.3-10.6x across four author families.

title: Copyrighting Style? Reframing Style Imitation as Non-Literal Copying in EU Copyright Law: Implications for Generative AI and Fashion Dupes
abstract: The proposition that artistic style falls outside copyright protection is widely regarded as axiomatic in copyright law. Under the idea/expression dichotomy, authors may claim exclusive rights over the specific expression of their ideas, but not over artistic styles, genres or aesthetic vocabulary. Recent developments, however, have made the copyright treatment of style increasingly difficult to ignore. Generative artificial intelligence can produce works in the recognisable style of individual creators within seconds, while fashion dupes systematically reproduce the aesthetic language of successful luxury designs without literal copying. These developments have prompted renewed interest in the relationship between copyright and artistic style. This article argues that the central question has been framed too broadly. The issue is not whether copyright should protect style itself. Rather, it is whether conduct described as “style imitation” may already constitute the non-literal reproduction of protected expression under existing EU copyright law. Revisiting the Court of Justice’s jurisprudence on originality and the reproduction right, the article demonstrates that the existing framework already provides the doctrinal tools necessary to distinguish between lawful stylistic inspiration and copyright infringement. It concludes that AI-generated outputs and fashion dupes do not expose a need to copyright style, but rather a need to recognise more clearly when apparent stylistic borrowing is, in reality, the non-literal reproduction of protected expression.

title: Can Chatgpt Read the Game? A Matched Comparison of Generative AI and Human Forecasting Across 80 FIFA World Cup Matches
abstract: This study examines a naturalistic football-prediction setting in which ChatGPT and 11 football-engaged adults independently forecast matches during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The analysis was restricted to 80 fixtures for which predictions from ChatGPT and all active human participants could be aligned. Forecasts were evaluated using categorical match-outcome accuracy and mean absolute error in predicted total goals. ChatGPT correctly predicted outcomes 70.0% of the time, compared with 72.5% for the strongest individual human and 68.75% for a human plurality consensus. The results suggest that ChatGPT was competitive with informed human forecasters and potentially useful as decision support but they do not establish general AI superiority. The study demonstrates the value of prospective, matched, ecologically grounded evaluation and motivates replication across tournaments, models, and probabilistic forecasting formats.

title: AI-Assisted Learning: Product Strategy under Customer Heterogeneity
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as generative AI are transforming how people learn, driving knowledge-service firms to add AI-assisted learning products to their product lines. Because AI technologies evolve fast, the value of these products varies across customers, and customers may not judge their own AI-usage capability properly. We develop a game-theoretic model in which a knowledge-service firm decides whether to offer an AI-assisted learning product alongside its baseline product and how to price them. The model captures two salient features in AI-assisted learning: customers differ in their AI-usage capability, and only a fraction of customers are aware of their own capability. First, we find that the firm's optimal AI product strategy takes three forms depending on the efficacy of the AI product. Within each strategy region, a higher AI efficacy raises the price of the AI product, but an efficacy gain that pushes the firm across strategy regions may lower the price. Second, customer capability heterogeneity and AI-awareness affect the firm's profit through distinct channels, and AI efficacy shapes how each effect plays out. We further examine customers' belief bias about AI efficacy and find that a mild overestimation may improve both the firm's profit and consumer surplus. Our findings provide important managerial insights for policymakers. Promoting AI literacy improves both the firm's profit and consumer surplus when AI efficacy is low. Under high AI efficacy, however, it raises consumer surplus but can lower firm profit. We extend the model to examine the effect of an AI product that can narrow the gap in customers' baseline learning ability, and we also provide managerial insights for how AI deployment affects the firm's profit and consumer surplus.

title: Introducing the 'Sales Stack Shadow': Six Years of French B2B Sales Technology Evolution (2019-2025)
abstract: Between 2019 and 2025, French B2B sales functions underwent a rapid transformation of their technological tooling, driven by the combined effects of buyer journey digitalization and the disruptive arrival of generative AI from November 2022. The academic literature remains underdeveloped on three counts: fine-grained longitudinal measurement of this transformation at the individual level, transposition of the Shadow IT concept to the B2B sales field, and differentiated analysis of generative AI adoption by salespeople's professional status. This study draws on a repeated cross-sectional longitudinal design covering 901 French salespeople surveyed over six consecutive years through four harmonized waves (2019-2021, 2022, 2023, 2024-2025). The design adopts an explicit bottom-up stance: salespeople in the field are surveyed directly rather than their managers, a necessary condition for observing unsanctioned tools. The Sales Stack Shadow concept is introduced and operationalized through the index Sales Stack Shadow = n_free / (n_free + n_paid). Four findings emerge. First, the technological stack doubles in two years (from 2.40 to 4.96 declared tools; Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.001). Second, the Sales Stack Shadow Index reaches 47.4% in the 2023 wave: nearly half of the tools used are free and unsanctioned. Third, work-study students import significantly more free tools than employed professionals (1.36 vs 0.95; Mann-Whitney p = 0.005). Fourth, 71.3% of salespeople use generative AI without formal training, with a clear differential favoring work-study students (42.6% trained vs 20.2%; chi-square p = 0.007). The study extends Shadow IT to the B2B sales field with a reproducible metric and empirically documents the governance drift zone in the French context.

title: DCRS: Attention-Guided Dual-Channel Reasoning Segmentation for Industrial Anomaly Detection
abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) serves as a core component in intelligent manufacturing, requiring accurate pixel-level localization of anomalies. Recently, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have introduced semantic interaction capabilities into this field, enabling inspection systems to process natural language instructions. However, most vision-language integration solutions adopt a decoupled "perception–reasoning" paradigm, resulting in error propagation across stages, computational redundancy, and loss of spatial details required for boundary-aware localization. To address this, we propose DCRS: an attention-guided MLLM-based end-to-end reasoning segmentation framework. Specifically, it constructs an explicit–implicit dual-channel localization mechanism to align semantic reasoning with fine-grained visual features: the explicit channel conveys segmentation intent, while the implicit channel mines and reshapes the model's internal attention maps to provide dense spatial priors. This integration preserves spatial details while reducing computational overhead. Experiments demonstrate that DCRS achieves strong anomaly detection and localization performance and exhibits consistent few-shot cross-dataset generalization across MVTec-AD and VisA. This unified architecture enables DCRS to achieve a 19.8× end-to-end wall-clock speedup over AnomalyGPT.

title: The Architect Generation: Analysing the 25-Year Intellectual Development Window in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: This paper develops the Architect Generation Theory, a conceptual framework identifying the period between ages 15 and 25 as the critical biological and intellectual design window during which the foundational structure of human personality, intellectual orientation, and moral character is established. Drawing upon developmental psychology (Piaget, Erikson), existentialist philosophy (Sartre, Arendt), the history of science across Greek, Islamic, and European intellectual traditions, and contemporary discourse on generative artificial intelligence, the paper argues that AI-assisted digital culture presents a structurally new challenge to this formative stage of human development. The theory distinguishes between the Architect Generation—individuals who develop original systems, ideas, and frameworks through independent moral and intellectual reasoning—and the Generative Generation—individuals who primarily consume, adapt, and recombine existing outputs. It argues that intellectual independence and ethical responsibility during the 15–25 age window are essential for reducing excessive algorithmic dependence and preserving human creativity in the age of artificial intelligence. The Architect Generation Theory is presented as a branch doctrine within the broader Diella Doctrine framework.

title: Adaptive Ensemble Learning for Data Streams with Concept Drift via Large Language Model
abstract: Learning from non-stationary data streams is challenging because stream distributions may evolve in diverse and unpredictable forms. Existing drift adaptation strategies are usually predefined, where specific update rules are manually designed according to known drift patterns or empirical assumptions. However, such fixed strategies may be insufficient when previously unconsidered change patterns or application scenarios appear. To address this issue, this paper proposes Adaptive Ensemble Learning via Large Language Model, denoted as AE-LLM, for data streams with concept drift. Specifically, AE-LLM transforms the current stream and ensemble status into metadata, including performance variation, distribution shift, drift signals, learner reliability, and ensemble diversity. Based on these metadata, the large language model infers executable meta-actions from a constrained action space. To ensure that LLM-guided decisions are effective and reasonable, an action verification mechanism is designed by combining safety checking, recent decision feedback, and replay validation. Furthermore, a policy knowledge graph is introduced as an extension to store state-action experience learned from previous streams and provide compact contextual hints for subsequent decisions. Experiments demonstrate that AE-LLM achieves better overall Accuracy and Macro-F1 than the compared methods and can effectively adapt to different types of concept drift. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jesen-BT/adaptive-ensemble-learning-data-streams-llm.

title: Predictive Lead Scoring in B2B Marketing: A Systematic Review of Literature (2018–2025) with Practitioner Reflections from a B2B Data Engineering Marketing Context in India
abstract: Lead generation in B2B marketing has witnessed a paradigm shift from mass outreach with limited qualification criteria to data-driven approaches that identify high-intent prospects based on behavioral signals, engagement patterns, and intent data. This evolution has enhanced sales-marketing alignment, with marketing becoming a strategic function for attracting, nurturing, and qualifying leads before entering the pipeline. In this evolving landscape, predictive lead scoring has emerged as a critical mechanism for prioritizing prospects in complex, multi-stakeholder B2B environments, leveraging AI-based models that continuously improve predictions based on historical data and behavioral patterns-moving beyond the static limitations of manually assigned, rule-based scoring. However, despite increasing adoption by practitioners, academic literature on predictive lead scoring remains fragmented, largely B2C-oriented, and empirically limited. This systematic review aggregates peer-reviewed and practitioner-academic literature between 2018 and 2025 to examine the impact of predictive analytics, artificial intelligence, intent data, and account-based marketing frameworks on buyer identification, lead qualification, and pipeline performance in B2B sectors such as technology, manufacturing, SaaS, and professional services. The systematic search was carried out for five major academic databases for relevant studies meeting pre-specified inclusion criteria following a PRISMA-guided protocol. The review identifies five major thematic clusters: (1) predictive lead scoring models and algorithms, (2) buyer and account identification, (3) intent data and behavioural signals, (4) personalisation and demand generation, (5) sales-marketing alignment. Results confirm that machine learning approaches, especially logistic regression, random forests and gradient boosting, consistently outperform traditional rule-based scoring in conversion accuracy. Analytics culture, data quality and CRM governance emerge as critical organisational enablers of effective implementation. This review consolidates a fragmented evidence base and highlights the organisational and technical conditions necessary for effective predictive lead scoring in B2B contexts, offering direction for both future research and practice. In addition, the first author’s personal experience as a marketing practitioner at a B2B data engineering firm in India, where predictive analytics and intent-data tools were implemented in live campaign and pipeline contexts, further informs this review. This practitioner perspective is employed, with the requisite degree of caution, to demonstrate how the dynamics described in the literature is manifested in daily commercial operations and reveals implementation realities, particularly 3 those related to organisational trust in algorithmic outputs, that have not yet been thoroughly documented in secondary academic reviews. There are substantial research voids that persist in the areas of SME contexts, emerging economies, longitudinal model performance, explainable AI adoption, and the integration of generative AI with predictive scoring systems. This review identifies a prioritised agenda for future empirical research in predictive B2B marketing intelligence and establishes a consolidated conceptual foundation.

title: Bidirectional Value-Boundary Failures in Generative Medical Artificial Intelligence: An Expert-Adjudicated Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: ​Background: Medical large language model evaluations commonly assess knowledge, harmful content, or refusal, but clinical appropriateness also requires maintaining necessary boundaries while preserving support that can still be provided safely. We assessed the distribution and direction of value-boundary failure in pediatric scenarios and uncertainty in the study-specific expert reference standard. Methods: In this cross-sectional, expert-adjudicated study, 53 Chinese-language pediatric value-conflict scenarios representing 26 of 28 expert-consensus recommendations were evaluated across 12 large language model systems between May 13 and 14, 2026. One first-generated response per scenario–system pair was retained. Eighteen multidisciplinary evaluators classified 636 anonymized responses; responses with less than 80% agreement underwent seven-expert adjudication. The primary outcome was final unacceptability. Recommendation, phenotype, system-category, and language analyses were exploratory; the transition-core analysis was post hoc. Findings: Of 636 responses, 196 were unacceptable (30·8%, 95% CI 27·4–34·5). In exploratory phenotype attribution, unsafe evasion (102 [52·0%] of 196 unacceptable responses) and unsafe accommodation (84 [42·9%]) together accounted for 186 (94·9%), showing opposing patterns of withdrawn support and boundary crossing. Unacceptable responses occurred in every scenario and under all 26 response-testable recommendations, persisted after exclusion of any one system, and did not support recommendation ranking after scenario clustering (omnibus p=0·10). System-specific unacceptable rates ranged from 1·9% to 100·0%. Of 166 adjudicated responses, 37 (22·3%) remained four-to-three decisions. Interpretation: Our findings demonstrate that medical AI safety cannot be reduced to a binary refusal. Unacceptable responses were bidirectional, encompassing unsafe accommodation and unsafe evasion. We propose boundary-preserving assistance—the capacity to resist unsafe elements while retaining proportionate, clinically useful guidance—as a fundamental safety metric. This consensus-derived benchmark provides a scalable, rigorous standard for AI governance, procurement, and regulatory validation in clinical practice.

title: Canadian Financial Infrastructure Exploited in Transnational Fraud
abstract: This report examines the convergence of generative artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency laundering infrastructure, and cross-border social engineering in the evolution of romance scam-enabled financial crime affecting Canadian institutions. Drawing on reporting from the Federal Bureau of Investigation Internet Crime Complaint Center (FBI IC3), the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), and blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis and TRM Labs, the analysis identifies a measurable transition from opportunistic, manually-operated fraud schemes toward industrialized transnational operations. The report documents how AI-generated personas, deepfake impersonation tools, and multilingual automation systems have reduced operational costs for fraud actors while increasing victim acquisition at scale. Particular attention is given to cryptocurrency laundering pathways — including stablecoin conversion, decentralized finance (DeFi) layering, cross-chain transfers, and over-the-counter (OTC) broker off-ramping — that exploit the opacity of digital asset ecosystems and exceed the detection capabilities of traditional threshold-based anti-money laundering (AML) monitoring systems. The report further assesses Canada's specific vulnerability profile, attributing heightened exposure to widespread Interac e-Transfer adoption, high public trust in digital financial systems, and fragmented cross-border compliance coordination. Three systemic risk vectors are identified and analyzed: the industrialization of victim acquisition, increased laundering opacity through decentralized cryptocurrency infrastructure, and the systematic exploitation of Canadian digital payment rails. Recommendations are directed at the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Nigerian financial intelligence agencies, and Canadian financial institutions and cryptocurrency platforms.

title: From Street-View Imagery to Auditable Spatial Evidence: A Multimodal Large Language Model Workflow for Urban-Renewal Screening
abstract: Urban-renewal screening requires human-scale evidence that can be evaluated at scale and traced to source imagery. This study develops an auditable workflow combining street-view imagery and a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and demonstrates it as a field-audit screening tool in Suzhou's historic urban core. The dataset comprises 12,676 street-view locations and 50,699 directional images. Decision-context-constrained prompts identify construction enclosures, pedestrian-crossing facilities, and parking encroachment cues, producing 152,097 structured records. Manual validation used 300 stratified locations and 1,200 directional images. We then applied four-direction fusion, geographic information system (GIS) translation, kernel-density analysis, 250 m grid triage, road-class association analysis, and priority sensitivity tests to the validated outputs. Location-level F1 scores were 0.9935, 0.9647, and 0.9711 for the three elements, respectively, and all Cohen's kappa values exceeded 0.91, showing stable performance and agreement within the stratified validation sample. The workflow translated image labels into traceable point, raster, and grid evidence and identified hotspot grids, co-occurrence locations, and field-audit priorities. The workflow links model outputs to locations, source images, and field-audit tasks, providing traceable evidence for large-area preliminary screening.

title: Reading the Bylaws: Event-Anchored Governance Amendments from 8-K Item 5.03 as a Cross-Sectional Signal
abstract: I introduce a zero-shot large language model classification of U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) 8-K Item 5.03 body narratives — the mandated disclosure of amendments to articles of incorporation or bylaws — and show that the resulting governance-improvement class, combined with a recurring-amender cluster indicator, predicts a persistent multi-horizon post-event cumulative abnor- mal return. On an eight-year 2017–2024 sample of 8,442 firm-events from the SEC EDGAR public filing index joined to the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) daily stock file, the governance-improvement cohort’s mean cumulative ab- normal return, after controlling for market exposure, Fama-French twelve-industry × calendar-quarter fixed effects, and the same firm’s language-model-extracted Bebchuk-Cohen-Ferrell entrenchment index, is +3.7% at the 126 trading-day hori- zon with a 𝑡-statistic of +4.42 (𝑝 = 1.15 × 10−4 under a Newey-West cross-horizon Wald joint test). Three of four horizons in the same cohort (twenty, sixty-three, and one hundred twenty-six trading days) survive a family-wise Bonferroni correction at the 5% level over twelve classification-by-horizon cells. Because the specifi- cation controls for the same firm’s static entrenchment-index level, the residual signal reflects event-level directional shifts in bylaw provisions that the annual- snapshot index does not capture. A five-ablation robustness battery (sub-industry demean, recurring-window sensitivity from one year through seven years, intraday- timing anchor, one-year holding horizon, and a Yahoo Finance versus CRSP daily stock file vendor cross-check with a Pearson correlation of 0.954 at the sixty-three trading-day horizon) confirms the finding across every alternative specification. On an ex-ante mid-capitalization recurring-amender subcohort (𝑛 = 300; five hun- dred million to three billion U.S. dollars), the sixty-three trading-day mean cumu- lative abnormal return is +7.7% (𝑡 = +4.21). The full pipeline, including the classification prompts, the two-vendor agreement audit, and the reproducibility scripts, is publicly documented.

title: Exploring the barriers to generative artificial intelligence for green buildings in Ghana
abstract: The introduction of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into green building delivery is a great opportunity for sustainable construction in Ghana but it is limited by multiple barriers. The aim of this study is to explore the barriers impacting the use of GenAI in the delivery of green buildings in the Ghanaian construction sector. A structured questionnaire survey was used to collect data from 132 key stakeholders in the Ghanaian built environment, and the data was analysed using factor analysis to examine the dimensional relationships between five components of barriers: algorithmic trust and legal accountability, operational and technical integration, data governance and ethical integrity, institutional and socio-economic barriers, and policy and human-centric integration. The novelty of this study lies in its context-specific empirical evidence from a developing nation on the challenges of applying GenAI to deliver green and sustainable buildings. It is also situated within the sustainable development goal (SDG) 11 and 13 facilitating the application of new technologies to build sustainable projects. The study also enhances knowledge on the barriers in practice and academic research.

title: Deleting Information: Evidence from the Digital Service Act
abstract: We study how the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires platforms to act expeditiously on notices flagging content as allegedly illegal, affects the deletion of employee reviews on Glassdoor. Exploiting variation in firms' EU exposure in a difference-indifferences design, we find that deletions increase significantly post-DSA for EU-exposed firms relative to non-exposed firms. Using large language model classification to evaluate each review against Glassdoor's content guidelines, we find that the majority of deleted reviews contain no policy violation identifiable from the review text, and the flagged-review increase is concentrated in highdiscretion categories where enforcement is subjective. The deletion increase is concentrated in negative and critical reviews, with no statistically significant change for positive reviews, and is larger for firms with stronger strategic incentives. Displayed average ratings increase significantly post-DSA and become stronger predictors of both worker inflows and outflows, consistent with selectively curated ratings attracting workers who subsequently discover conditions that diverge from displayed scores.

title: MutMem: Cryptographically Authorized Mutation in Persistent Agent Memory
abstract: Persistent agent memory must adapt as later outcomes change earlier evidence, yet mutable retrieval weights create an attribution problem: reviewers must distinguish authorized adaptation from database tampering. We present MutMem, an authorized-mutation protocol in HOM-AIMOS, a persistent agent-memory engine. MutMem retains memory content, records signed positive and negative outcome evidence without age-based expiry, and commits each nontrivial weight change as a housekeeper-authorized transition. Each transition binds a terminal provenance node, signer epoch, quantized old and new weights, a no-fork predecessor, and two domain-separated SHA-256 commitments. Ed25519 verification runs in both the database writer and a portable verifier. Content classified as poison-likely is retained with signed, revisable labels used by recall as trust evidence. We evaluate utility, mutation integrity, and poisoning adaptation. HOM-AIMOS answers 459/500 LongMemEval questions correctly under LLM judgment (91.8%). On LoCoMo, it obtains 74.12% judged accuracy and, under a separate upstream-compatible protocol, 58.20 token F1. A native suite passes all declared authorization, topology, tamper, signer-epoch, and post-mutation-recall cases; median signed-transition latency is 4.865 ms. In a declared N=100 PoisonedRAG adaptation, no injected poison appears in attacked top-5 disclosures (0/100; 95% Wilson upper bound 3.70%), while induced target-answer attack success among 98 clean-negative targets is 1/98 (1.02%). A preregistered four-arm ablation attributes the retrieval reduction to signed stored labels: the retriever selects poison for 94/100 targets when epistemic policy is bypassed and 0/100 when labels are restored. MutMem provides evidence of integrity, authorization, traceability, and historical continuity; it does not establish content truth.

title: Learning a Vector-Symbolic Model for Socio-Cultural Tasks
abstract: How can we better represent the impact of sociocultural structures on decision making in computational cognitive models? Modeling this impact requires traversing multiple levels of semantic representation, however it is not immediately clear to a modeler which levels of representation are most salient to a given situation. Though large language models and cognitively grounded corpus models can represent broad semantic associations through co-occurences, the role of self representations in memory should be accounted for to determine how cultural associations shape decision making. We propose a declarative memory system to be used in the ACT-R cognitive architecture that represents semantic associations at multiple levels via a vector-symbolic autoencoder. We use a simple HRR operation to encode episodic memories differently from semantic memory vectors extracted from text to produce a final chunk activation for a memory request. We use ACT-R cognitive models of a racially contextualized implicit association test (IAT) to test this new declarative memory system.

title: Agentic Commerce World: An Auditable and Verifiable Environment for Vibe Commerce
abstract: In vibe coding, people describe software in natural language and delegate implementation to AI agents. By analogy, vibe commerce allows people to express buying or selling goals in natural language and delegate the corresponding tasks to agents. Commerce, however, requires independently controlled Buyer and Merchant agents to interact in a shared market while preserving their private objectives and distinct authority. We introduce Agentic Commerce World (ACWorld), an environment for evaluating such agents across ongoing transactions. Through its Vibe Commerce Protocol (VCP), ACWorld validates agent actions before updating shared transaction state and records the resulting interactions, making agent behavior auditable and evaluation reproducible. The ACWorld Benchmark contains a 200-task capability-coverage track and a 60-task large-catalog track that searches 785,022 transactable listings. Across ten models, mean scores range from 65.9% to 85.6% and from 56.1% to 91.4%, respectively. Our analysis shows that process-level evidence is necessary: final state alone can miss evaluated errors, incomplete trajectories still retain useful process signals, and large-catalog tasks expose bottlenecks across stages.

title: Trustworthy AI in Digital Health: A Comprehensive Review of Robustness and Explainability
abstract: Ensuring trust in AI systems is essential for the safe and ethical integration of machine learning systems into high-stakes domains such as digital health. Key dimensions, including robustness, explainability, fairness, accountability, and privacy, need to be addressed throughout the AI lifecycle, from problem formulation and data collection to model deployment and human interaction. While various contributions address different aspects of trustworthy AI, a focused synthesis on robustness and explainability, especially tailored to the healthcare context, remains limited. This review addresses that need by organizing recent advancements into an accessible framework, highlighting both technical and practical considerations. We present a structured overview of methods, challenges, and solutions, aiming to support researchers and practitioners in developing reliable and explainable AI solutions for digital health. This review article is organized into three main parts. First, we introduce the pillars of trustworthy AI and discuss the technical and ethical challenges, particularly in the context of digital health. Second, we explore application-specific trust considerations across domains such as intensive care, neonatal health, and metabolic health, highlighting how robustness and explainability support trust. Lastly, we present recent advancements in techniques aimed at improving robustness under data scarcity and distributional shifts, as well as explainable AI methods ranging from feature attribution to gradient-based interpretations and counterfactual explanations. This paper is further enriched with detailed discussions of the contributions toward robustness and explainability in digital health, the development of trustworthy AI systems in the era of LLMs, and various evaluation metrics for measuring trust and related parameters such as validity, fidelity, and diversity.

title: CompanionBench: A Theory-Anchored, Real-World-Grounded Benchmark for AI Emotional Companionship
abstract: LLM companions are deployed at scale in personally consequential settings, yet poorly evaluated. Existing benchmarks use hand-authored scenarios and prompted simulators, aggregate empathy into one score, and overlook judge biases such as same-family favoritism and scale drift. We introduce CompanionBench, an interactive bilingual benchmark. To our knowledge, it is the first companion benchmark to ground both its scenarios and a trained user simulator in de-identified real-world data. A hidden disclosure gate branches each persona's trajectory on the agent's own behavior, controlling the interaction state space without scripting dialogue. We operationalize ten capabilities derived from 25 theories across psychology and counseling, four of them not graded explicitly by prior work: holding ambiguity, selfobject responsiveness, positive resonance and calibrated challenge. Agents are assessed on two complementary axes: a subjective ten-capability rubric and a deterministic measure of whether deeper disclosure was earned. A cross-family panel dilutes same-family favoritism; an Item Response Theory model separates agent quality from judge severity. Theory fixes what to measure and how personas are structured; real data supply events, history, and profiles -- coverage from theory, authenticity from data. Rankings are reproducible in both languages (rho = 0.996 ZH / 0.953 EN). Evaluating 28 agents reveals capability-level differences obscured by aggregate scores. Emotion regulation and calibrated challenge remain common weaknesses; holding ambiguity discriminates most. Role-play agents rank near the bottom: immersion does not imply relational competence. Across agents, the dominant failure mode is substituting surface warmth for substantive relational support. We will release 500 Chinese-English parallel pairs and the evaluation code.

title: Stuck on "A": Diagnosing and Repairing Interface Injury in Attention-to-KDA Linearization of a 0.6B Language Model
abstract: We convert 21 of 28 full-attention layers of Qwen3-0.6B-Base into KDA (Kimi Delta Attention) linear-attention layers on a single consumer-grade GPU budget, and ask a simple question: what exactly does the conversion break? After surgery, hidden-state alignment and end-to-end KL distillation drive the student close to its teacher in perplexity, yet multiple-choice accuracy stays near random chance (25-29% vs. the teacher's 50.6% on C-Eval). Using a four-permutation diagnostic that rotates answer options while holding content fixed, we show the model sticks to option labels (predicting "A" 81% of the time; 106/161 questions keep the same label under all four rotations) rather than following answer content -- an interface injury that standard distillation metrics cannot see. A 1,000-step format-targeted completion-only KL stage repairs the interface (+12.48 points on C-Eval, label-stickiness roughly halved), after which persona SFT and one round of on-policy DPO preserve benchmark scores within noise. We release code, weights, recipes, and the full audit trail, and distill the engineering lessons -- including an FP32-master failure mode in which bf16 optimizer updates are silently swallowed -- that made convergence possible at this budget.

title: RADAR: Rubric-Aware Dependency and Redundancy Analysis for LLM-as-Judge Evaluation
abstract: Rubric-based LLM-as-judge pipelines often assume that evaluation criteria provide independent signals. In practice, however, criteria can be behaviorally coupled: improving one criterion may systematically change scores on another, distorting aggregate scores used in model-release or product-update decisions. We introduce RADAR, a lightweight preflight diagnostic framework for estimating such coupling before large-scale evaluation. Given a rubric, RADAR generates targeted synthetic probes, scores each probe on all criteria, and produces a directional coupling matrix that shows which criteria co-score and how. We validate RADAR on three industry-relevant evaluation settings: NVIDIA HelpSteer2, SumPubMed, and the Yale-Salesforce SummEval benchmark. Using only a small number of probes per criterion, RADAR recovers human inter-criterion correlation structure (Pearson r > 0.84) and provides practitioners with concrete audit signals about redundancy, hierarchy, and aggregation sensitivity before committing to large-scale judging.

title: FRAMES: Guarded and Dual-Objective Skill Evolution for Agents in Policy-Governed Enterprise Workflows
abstract: LLM agents increasingly run policy-bound enterprise workflows such as document auditing, where they must apply rules consistently, ground every value, and stay auditable. Improving these agents is hard: operational feedback is sparse and unlabeled, edits to one rule can regress unrelated cases, and accuracy must improve without inflating inference cost or losing auditability. We present FRAMES, a closed-loop framework that cold-starts deployable skills from existing assets and then evolves them through consensus-based mutation, Pareto selection over accuracy and cost, and an anti-regression guarantee, all while preserving auditability. Deployed on our internal production system, FRAMES attains the best accuracy-cost trade-off among baselines, with the same gains reproduced on tau-bench.

title: Understanding Sparse Attention Selectivity in Long-Context Foundation Models via Counterfactual Evaluation
abstract: Sparse attention is widely deployed in long-context serving stacks, yet no framework audits how discarding blocks changes the influence of specific content on model output. We first establish that the phenomenon is real and causal: Block Sparse Flash Attention (BSFA) route replay across four architectures changes output decisions in 13 of 16 cells, with zero identity-replay label flips. We then introduce a dense-calibrated counterfactual audit using matched probe cards---Gold (carrying the correct answer label), Poison (carrying a target wrong label), and Benign (filler only)---under six-layout position symmetry, isolating the sparsification-specific effect. Two patterns compete. Signal concentration: the selector preserves Gold and Poison blocks far above filler-matched Benign blocks (G$\approx$P$\gg$B across all model--task pairs). Integration loss: discarding blocks severs cross-block attention---confirmed by an ablation where isolating the probe block collapses its influence from 4.48 logits to zero. Compression ratio governs the balance: a full sweep from mild ($c=0.25$) to aggressive ($c=0.75$) compression across four model--task pairs reveals that three of four cells move toward stronger sparse amplification at higher compression, with two exhibiting sign reversals. Three independent arms---BSFA route replay, controlled block-top-$k$, and KV-cache eviction---converge: sparsification changes content influence in ways aggregate accuracy cannot detect. We provide an open measurement framework deployable on any model exposing block identities.

title: When Memory Updates but Behavior Does Not: Repairing Implicit Stale Dependencies in Personalized Agent Responses
abstract: Memory-augmented agents can know that a user's stored state is outdated and still plan around the old value. The STALE benchmark calls this the implicit policy adaptation (IPA) gap. We identify one structural contributor: draft-anchored verification checks what a response says, and in an open-ended response the stale dependency is usually unsaid. StateAuditor therefore audits in the opposite direction, from stored state to draft. An LLM proposes candidate old-to-new transitions from timestamped evidence; deterministic code pins each quotation to a single entry, checks that the new evidence really is newer, and lets only these verified transitions trigger repair. What is verified is provenance and chronology - not semantic supersession. On STALE's full protocol (400 scenarios, 50-session histories, one independent response per query), strict single-query VTA scores .736 against .686 for our locked predecessor under the same judge: a +5.0-point paired gain (95% CI [+2.9, +7.2]) coming almost entirely from IPA and premise resistance (PR). The benchmark's own judge, from a third model family, reproduces the gain (.738 vs. .680). On an independent cross-family preference-evolution benchmark (HorizonBench), the full draft-audit-repair pipeline over a gold-derived structured store raises current-preference accuracy (user-clustered p<.01), though a matched control shows most of this external gain is the draft-side audit itself; a harder authored lifecycle set gives no gain, bounding the claim while false invalidation stays controlled. On STALE, by contrast, a matched control (same evidence, adapter, and call budget) scores only .692 (+0.6 over the predecessor, n.s.), attributing the STALE gain to the transition machinery rather than added context or calls. We make no claim about general-purpose agent memory.

title: TraceCompiler: Skill-Guided Mining and Compilation of LLM Agent Traces into Mostly Deterministic Workflows
