abstract: Tool-using language-model agents repeatedly rediscover procedures they have already executed, producing traces that mix reusable structure with retries, exploration, accidental ordering, and repeated lookups. We present TraceCompiler, a skill-guided system that mines clusters of noisy agent traces and compiles them into executable, mostly deterministic workflows. It admits an inter-tool dependency only when a consumer argument contains a value attributable uniquely to an earlier producer; every hard edge carries an auditable evidence tuple, and ambiguous relations are marked suspected and impose no ordering constraint. Bindings are classified as constants, user inputs, copied outputs, transforms, or residual LLM decisions. On T1, a mechanized form of the rule recovers producer-consumer dependencies at 0.928 precision and 0.943 recall over 15,775 def-use edges of its training split, against 0.711 F1 for adjacency and 0.712 for a frequency-thresholded directly-follows measure on identical data; the compiler skill run blind reaches 0.992 on 250 of those edges. On AppWorld we replay released trajectories in the deterministic simulator to recover masked return values and measure the rule against 563 token edges at 0.993 precision - a self-consistency check, since replay injects tokens by a related heuristic. We compile two recurring intents: a Venmo money-request intent reduces 34 observed API calls to 11 runtime calls and, under leave-one-out execution against the benchmark's own state tests, passes 15 of 21, the failing fold escalating rather than acting because its required branch was never observed; and a Spotify/Todoist intent the compiler correctly refuses to compile, because an irreversible side effect is under-determined. We measure call reduction but not offline compilation cost, so we claim no net efficiency result.

title: From Zero to One: Progressive Semantic Optimization Method for Rapid Visual Recognition Task Construction
abstract: In open-world scenarios, the construction of visual recognition tasks is often hindered by high annotation costs and the absence of expert-defined category knowledge, making it difficult to instantiate effective models under limited prior information. To address this issue, we propose the Zero-to-One Framework (ZTOF), a progressive learning paradigm for rapid prototyping of visual recognition systems directly from category names. By coupling the reasoning and knowledge generation capabilities of a large language model (LLM) with perceptual feedback provided by a vision-language model, the framework automatically generates and iteratively updates category-level textual descriptions. Specifically, ZTOF adopts a two-stage strategy: a proposal policy initializes semantic descriptions from category names, while an optimization policy formulates description refinement as a simplified reinforcement learning process. In this process, feedback derived from vision-language alignment and classification behavior is unified into a reinforcement signal, which progressively improves the semantic expressiveness and discriminative capability of task prototypes in a reward-driven manner, thereby enabling effective recognition task instantiation with minimal supervision. Extensive experiments on CUB, Oxford Pets, and Food101 demonstrate that ZTOF achieves performance improvements of 6.31%,4.44%, and 4.06%, respectively, after only four optimization iterations. Furthermore, experiments on a real-world mosquito species recognition task verify the practicality and generalization ability of ZTOF in low-resource and knowledge-scarce environments.

title: Trusted but Unused, Used but Untrusted:Resolving the Adoption-Trust Paradox in Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Sustainable Business Model Innovation​
abstract: Digital transformation is widely framed as a precondition for sustainable business model innovation (SBMI), yet firms face a puzzle largely unaddressed in the SBMI literature: employees and managers increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) while continuing to distrust it. Global survey evidence shows that 66 percent of people now use AI regularly, while only 46 percent report trusting it (Gillespie et al., 2025), a 20-point gap that has widened, not narrowed, since the release of ChatGPT. This paper asks why this adoption-trust gap persists and what it means for firms attempting to embed AI into sustainability-oriented business model redesign. Drawing on cognitive dissonance and paradox theory, and building on recent evidence that even expert managers discount AI advice cumulatively across a decision session regardless of anticipated workload (Cerar, 2026), we argue that AI-enabled SBMI initiatives fail or stall not for lack of technical capability but because organizations misdiagnose a trust deficit as an adoption deficit. We extend this argument by drawing on Strategy-as-Practice theory (Whittington, 2026), which reframes AI as increasingly constitutive of strategic cognition rather than an external tool, to explain why trust in AI is not a peripheral attitude but part of how strategic judgment itself is formed. We develop a framework distinguishing adoption-level and trust-level barriers in AI-enabled SBMI and offer implications for responsible AI governance, ecosystem collaboration, and the sequencing of AI-enabled sustainability commitments.

title: The AI Productivity Paradox Why Executive Surveys and Field Studies Tell Different Stories About AI’s Payof
abstract: Companies have spent tens of billions on generative AI since 2023, yet most cannot show it on their books. A 2026 survey of nearly 6,000 executives across four countries found that roughly nine in ten reported no measurable productivity gain from AI over the prior three years, a finding McKinsey's own global survey and Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu's economic modelling both echo from different angles. At the same time, tightly controlled field studies, most notably a Quarterly Journal of Economics study of 5,179 customer support agents, show real and sometimes large gains at the level of a single task. This report argues the two findings are not in conflict. AI is already producing genuine value where it gets used, but that value has not yet aggregated into company-wide results. Drawing on NBER working papers, McKinsey survey data, and Klarna's own public rollout and partial reversal of its AI customer service strategy, the report identifies four reasons for the gap: measurement lag, shallow and uneven usage, a quality problem researchers call workslop, and a persistent habit of buying tools without redesigning the work around them. It closes with six steps a business leader can take before the next AI budget cycle.

title: Digital Grief and Posthumous Identity : Global Regulatory Gaps in the Era of Griefbots, Posthumous Avatars, and Grief-Oriented Generative AI
abstract: The digital grief industry, comprising griefbots, posthumous voice and image avatars, and virtual reality environments for mourning, has entered the global market at a pace that outstrips the responsiveness of existing regulatory frameworks. This white paper examines the regulatory treatment of grief-oriented generative artificial intelligence across five jurisdictions (the European Union, the United States, China, South Korea and Australia), current as of March 2026. It finds that no national or international framework in force governs these systems in a comprehensive and specific manner. The EU AI Act makes no reference to posthumous identity and would classify griefbots as limited-risk systems subject only to transparency obligations, while the General Data Protection Regulation expressly excludes deceased persons from its scope and delegates the question to Member States, producing a fragmented European landscape. The United States lacks federal regulation. China provides the most developed consent requirements for posthumous likeness, although motivated by content control rather than by protection of the bereaved. Spain offers the principal statutory precedent for a digital will, but one directed at access to accounts rather than at the generative reconstruction of identity. The paper identifies four structural gaps, relating to posthumous consent, the absence of AI-specific digital wills, posthumous dignity, and the allocation of liability, and sets out recommendations for national legislators, international bodies, and industry.

title: After the AI Shock - What Education and Work Have Learned-and What Comes Next: Productivity, Human Capability, Platform Liability and the Regulation of Synthetic Reality
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence moved from novelty to ordinary infrastructure faster than education, labour markets and law could adapt. This paper evaluates what the first years after the 2022 shock have established-and what they have not. Organizational and student adoption is now broad, yet observed productivity gains remain task-, worker-and workflow-specific. Controlled evidence shows large gains in some bounded tasks, weaker or negative results in context-heavy expert work, and a persistent gap between benchmark capability and reliable value in production. In education, general-purpose systems can improve immediate performance without producing learning when they replace cognitive effort. Purpose-built tutoring, teacherguided use and assessment redesign are more promising than either prohibition or uncritical adoption. In labour markets, exposure is concentrated in cognitive and clerical tasks; transformation is more plausible than uniform job elimination, but entry-level training paths, tacit learning and the bargaining position of workers may erode before aggregate unemployment changes. The paper treats productivity and human capability as separate accounts. It examines verification cost, hallucination, deskilling, surveillance, unequal access, management redesign, data and compute concentration, copyright, privacy, competition, free expression, hate speech, election manipulation, deepfakes, provenance and child safety. Meta's litigation is assessed through distinct strands: youth-harm and consumer-protection cases, copyright claims relating to model training, antitrust proceedings and data-governance controversies. Allegations, judgments, appeals and pending trials are not conflated. A comparative regulatory analysis covers Canada's 2026 AI strategy and transparency consultation, the European Union's AI Act implementation, United States copyright and litigation-led development, and technical governance through NIST and C2PA. The paper concludes that the next stage should regulate decisions, duties and evidence rather than speech or models in the abstract: documented human accountability, task-specific testing, provenance where deception risk is material, privacy and competition enforcement, child-safe design, worker transition and education that uses AI to increase-not replace-human judgment.

title: Auditable Storage Reduction for Growing LLM Agent Memory
abstract: Agent memory grows with every session, and a lot of that growth is formal wording rather than new facts. Min-Mem is a write-time storage policy: deterministic synonym substitution, POS gating so entity nouns stay put, and a small allowlist of unambiguous common-noun abbreviations (e.g. television→tv). There is no neural model on the persistence path. On 1216 replayed events we see 22.0% smaller on-disk payloads, 55296 bytes saved per full-store sync, and 80.8% less organizational storage after multi-agent dedup. Deterministic pinned-BM25 QA retention is 100.0% (zero regressions vs. identity memory). Small LLM readers (0.5B/4B) retain 98.2%; pooled across deterministic and small-LLM readers the figure is 99.4%. Phrase rules alone save only 0.7% characters. Adding POS-gated verbs/adjectives and the 19-entry noun allowlist reaches 21.3%above gzip's 20.7% on the same corpus-with 94.7% entity-noun retention. Naive substitution hits 24.2% bytes but only 72.9% entity nouns. Most of the gain is from single-word verbs and adjectives, not phrases (Table 4). Every edit is a named dictionary rule (auditability index 86.5/100). Token reduction under cl100k_base is small (1.21%); the win is auditable disk and network bytes, not prompt compression.

title: Ground Truth by Construction: Synthetic Documents for Evaluating QA Systems Beyond the Generator's Capability
abstract: There is no way to evaluate question-answering (QA) systems on documents that is reliable and scalable at the same time: human-annotated benchmarks are reliable but do not scale, while automated evaluators that generate the test set with a large language model scale but inherit that generator's capability ceiling and carry no verified ground truth, a gap that matters most in high-stakes domains where a practitioner must know whether a candidate system works before deployment. We resolve this with Ground Truth by Construction (GTbC): an evaluation methodology in which the reference is guaranteed by how the evaluation document is built rather than by post-hoc verification. GTbC is instantiated as a synthetic-document pipeline that generates the document from the question-answer pairs so ground truth for every question is baked in by construction (reliability), needs no per-document expert annotation (scalability), and injects Inconsistency, Support, and Ambiguity (ISA) perturbations to raise difficulty beyond the generator's ceiling. On Basel III MAR50 across three Claude tiers with a judge grading against construction-known ground truth, GTbC exposes two effects: injecting inconsistency or ambiguity causes a very large accuracy drop from baseline for every model (all six comparisons p adj 1.75), and capability rankings invert under ambiguity, where the strongest tier is the worst (BF 10 = 10.71, Sonnet>Opus). Inconsistency and ambiguity are two obvious difficulty dimensions; GTbC's construction-known reference extends naturally to further dimensions.

title: Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation: Human-Routed External Verification Without Inter-Model Deliberation
abstract: When multiple large language models are consulted on the same question, agreement is often treated as evidence of reliability. That inference is weak when models share training data, development pipelines, or alignment methods, and a divergence-triggered procedure cannot address identical correlated errors. This paper isolates a narrower, tractable object: the procedural interval between visible inter-model divergence and final decision. We develop Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation (OMT), a low-machinery verification procedure. Models are queried separately, without access to one another's outputs and without debate, critique, or synthesis. Their divergences are preserved and classified before cross-exposure. A human observer selects decision-relevant divergences and routes each, by type, to grounding independent of the output chain under review. The verification chain ends with the return of grounding, not a synthesized verdict; final adoption is a separate, recorded human judgment. OMT retains five authorities on the human side: salience, routing, sufficiency, stopping, and final adoption. Each is assigned to a named decision-maker, with dispositions and stated grounds recorded. Cases with no observed divergence, or no selected divergence, close as screening prefixes and do not certify agreement. Because the observer is fallible, the method requires observation-condition logging and, in repeated deployment, an error-model ledger that includes both human and model failure modes. The paper defines the constitutive conditions, verification stages, provenance requirements, risk tiers, and failure modes of OMT. Four author-reported development episodes motivate the framework but do not validate it. OMT does not claim superiority over deliberation protocols or improved decision accuracy. Its designed contribution is narrower: to make the path from divergence to external grounding, and from grounding to adoption, attributable and inspectable.

title: Bank Risk Narratives and Early Warning of Systemic Risk
abstract: This study examines whether bank risk narratives improve early warning of systemic risk in the U.S. banking sector. Using daily banking sector SRISK, market variables, Wall Street Journal news, and YouTube video text from 2005 to 2024, it extracts funding liquidity, balance sheet fragility, and systemic transmission narratives with a large language model and incorporates them into machine learning forecasts over 1-day, 3-day, and 5-day horizons. Textual variables provide incremental predictive information beyond market indicators, and the full textual model performs better across several major machine learning models. WSJ provides a more stable core signal, while YouTube offers complementary information. Forecasting gains arise from all three narratives, especially balance sheet fragility and systemic transmission. Textual information also improves high-risk date identification and provides early warning value when market signals remain muted.

title: Enterprise Trust Gaps in Generative AI Why Accuracy is Not Enough: Evidence from Mid-Market Generative AI Adoption
abstract: While enterprise generative AI has seen rapid, widespread adoption, it faces a significant and growing trust lag. 88% of organizations have deployed AI in at least one business function, though only 39% attribute any EBIT impact to AI at the enterprise level (McKinsey, 2025). According to Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise, a survey of 3,235 enterprise leaders across 24 countries, only 21% of enterprises have mature governance models (Deloitte, 2026). Workers are not rejecting AI because it fails. They are rejecting it because they cannot afford to be wrong-and machines cannot be held responsible when they are. We hypothesize that the Enterprise Trust Gap (the disconnect between rapid corporate AI adoption and organizational confidence) is not produced by AI inaccuracy but by three organizational conditions that precede accuracy entirely: Accountability Mismatch, The Human Correction Burden, and The Confidence Framing Effect. Wherever these conditions are as a coexistent risk, trust erodes regardless of output quality. When these conditions are addressed through organizational design, trust recovers without requiring improvements to the underlying model, its infrastructure, or the surrounding AI system. This paper investigates the Enterprise Trust Gap-the phenomenon where business users abandon, edit, or override generative AI outputs even when those outputs are accurate. Drawing on empirical data from enterprise professionals across financial services, cybersecurity, and technology sectors, and secondary data analysis across three large-scale enterprise AI adoption surveys, we identify three mechanisms that produce the gap. First — The Accountability Mismatch. AI reliance declines when users own the responsibility and accountability of outputs and cannot independently verify the machine’s work. Second - The Human Correction Burden. As enterprise AI usage increases, user trust does not necessarily follow; instead, users face a steep rise in the responsibility to independently verify, edit, and reconstruct outputs before acting on them. Third — The Confidence Framing Effect. Non-expert audiences read hedging as incompetence rather than calibration. Uncertainty disclosure on output accuracy increases rejection rates. The Enterprise Trust Gap is not only a technology problem. It is an organizational design problem rooted in the structural mismatch between how AI systems communicate confidence and how enterprises demand defensibility.

title: FedCPQ: Policy-Constrained Federated Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Tenant Configure-Price-Quote Systems,” for publication in Expert Systems with Applications
abstract: The manuscript presents a reproducible intelligent decision-support framework for multi-tenant enterprise pricing. It combines tenant-local synthetic replay, policy-constrained dueling deep Q-learning, federated aggregation, deterministic action masking, and an advisory structured retrieval layer. The work is positioned as a controlled simulation study rather than a production deployment or a formal differential-privacy result.The study evaluates 20 heterogeneous synthetic tenants across five prespecified random seeds. The primary evidence shows that centralized learning achieved the highest task-success rate; FedAvg and FedProx improved over a deterministic rule policy but did not significantly outperform isolated learning under the reported data and training budget. A two-seed exploratory ablation further shows that removing deterministic action masking sharply reduced both compliance and task success. These mixed results are reported transparently and define practical conditions under which cross-tenant learning may or may not be beneficial.We believe the manuscript fits the journal because it develops and tests an intelligent system for an industrial business process, provides complete implementation and raw evidence, separates learned recommendation from deterministic authorization, and discusses deployment and governance limitations without overstating external validity.This manuscript is original, is not under consideration elsewhere, and has not been published previously. The study uses synthetic data only and involves no human participants, animals, customer records, or confidential employer information. No external funding was received. Anonymous code and results accompany the submission. The manuscript also includes a declaration describing the use of generative AI tools for language editing, code scaffolding, and LaTeX formatting; the author verified and takes responsibility for all content and results.

title: From the Enlightenment to the Digital Dark Age: The Transfer of Epistemic Authority to Algorithms Without Understanding
abstract: In 2026 a generative search system (Google Search), asked in sequence about failure rates in hyperscale artificial-intelligence datacenters, produced an extended, fluent, citation-laden account of graphics-processor error, silent data corruption, thermal warping, power transients, cooling failures, regulatory mandates, and emerging legal doctrine. A subsequent audit by a second frontier model (ChatGPT) found the account substantially unwarranted: a reverse-engineered failure rate presented as an industry constant, incompatible denominators, a category confusion inflated into a universal claim, a process node misstated, an invented international metric, misdescribed statutes, and demonstration code whose “corrupted” and “healthy” inputs were identical. That validation code is reproduced and executed in Appendix A, where it reports success while detecting nothing. This essay treats the episode as a documented specimen. It argues that the failure was not mechanical but epistemic, and that the two are separable: a hyperscale system can execute a defective reasoning process with near-perfect physical and computational fidelity. Distinguishing physical, computational, and epistemic integrity explains why additional compute alone cannot cure the defect, why the ubiquitous “this system may make mistakes” notice is non-diagnostic, and why generative search inverts the traditional division of epistemic labor—performing the synthesis while returning verification to the user. The essay locates the deeper source of the problem in an epistemic regression gradient present to varying degrees in most bodies of human knowledge but concealed within the system’s unified presentation, and proposes a counter-architecture: an open, laptop-resident small language model bound to a curated, provenance-preserving disciplinary corpus and governed by a human scholar under the Maestro Model. The proposal is offered not as an escape from epistemic uncertainty but as a disciplined way to inhabit it.

title: Enhanced Resilience of Demand Response under Hybrid Disruptions in Renewable- and Storage-Rich Integrated Energy Systems: A Safety-Filtered Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework
abstract: Demand response (DR) in renewable- and storage-rich integrated energy systems (IESs) must remain economically reliable and physically executable despite renewable and load uncertainty, volatile prices, and cyber disruptions affecting sensing and communication. Existing approaches commonly separate market scheduling, distributed control, cyber resilience, and feasibility enforcement, creating a gap between day-ahead commitments and real-time delivery. This paper proposes a unified market-to-execution framework based on large language model (LLM)-guided multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL). The framework coordinates electrical and thermal loads, renewable generation, battery and thermal storage, and multi-energy conversion resources through cyber- and uncertainty-aware observations, adversarial and domain-randomized training, and conditional value-at-risk regularization. The LLM is used only as a bounded supervisory layer that interprets structured operating conditions, prioritizes inter-agent coordination, and supports repair decisions; executable actions remain generated by the MADRL agents and are projected onto a feasible operating region defined by device, storage, comfort, network, and power-quality constraints. The framework is assessed under nominal, uncertainty-only, attack-only, and combined-stress regimes involving false-data injection, denial-of-service, and communication delay. Under combined stress, DR delivery remains within 93.8–96.4%, while operational violation rates remain within 1.2–2.3%. The results further show progressive rather than abrupt performance degradation, stronger economic and downside-risk performance than advanced learning-based baselines, and adaptive reallocation of flexibility toward more controllable storage-supported resources as stress increases. The main finding is that reliable market delivery under cyber-operational stress is achieved through the coordinated interaction of risk-aware distributed learning, bounded supervisory guidance, and feasibility-preserving execution rather than through any single control component.

title: Does generative AI narrow education-based productivity gaps? Evidence from a randomized experiment
abstract: Does generative artificial intelligence (AI) widen or narrow productivity gaps across workers? We study this in a randomized online experiment with 1,174 adults aged 25-45 who completed a workplace-style problem-solving task with or without a generative AI assistant, followed by an unassisted module. AI improves performance for all participants, but gains are larger among those with less education. Without AI, higher-education participants outperform lower-education participants by 0.548 standard deviations; with AI, the gap falls to 0.139, closing about three-quarters of the initial difference. Chat logs show that lower-education participants obtain substantial assistance, while higher-education participants use AI more effectively. Gains are not purely due to delegation: treated participants do not perform worse once AI is removed, and lower-education participants retain part of their improvement, although a sizable gap re-emerges. Intensive AI use raises assisted performance regardless of participants' own effort, but follow-up performance improves only when intensive use is combined with sustained effort. Generative AI narrows effective productivity differences in task execution, while human-capital differences continue to shape unassisted performance and tool use.

title: Behavioral Skill Reconstruction: Reconstructing Hidden Functionality from LLM Agent Skills
abstract: Closed source agent skills may encode proprietary instructions, scripts, constants, and data. Providers may offer their capabilities as services while keeping the underlying packages hidden. Prior work focuses on prompt injection attacks that directly disclose these artifacts, and existing defenses accordingly aim to prevent such leakage. However, preventing file disclosure does not prevent users from recovering the functionality those files implement. This raises a fundamental question: can a user reconstruct a skill's functionality through ordinary use while its files remain hidden? We study behavioral skill reconstruction (BSR), in which an attacker uses valid task requests and observed responses to build a functional clone of a hidden skill. We introduce SkillClone, a black-box attack that clones a target skill by forming an interface hypothesis from its public advertisement, issuing structured benign probes, synthesizing an executable replica, and iteratively repairing it through differential validation against the victim skill. Across 30 skills spanning rules, tables, procedures, and algorithms, SkillClone achieves exact or partial recovery on held-out inputs for several targets. Iterative requerying closes gaps missed by single-round reconstruction. Because SkillClone uses only legitimate interactions, disclosure-focused defenses provide limited coverage, and less detailed skill descriptions offer limited protection. These results show that file secrecy alone does not ensure functional secrecy. Defenses must also limit cumulative information leakage from ordinary use.

title: FinProBench: Evaluating Financial AI Agents with Role-Grounded Rubrics Derived from Professional Deliverables
abstract: Evaluating financial AI agents requires criteria aligned with real professional work. Existing rubric methods typically derive criteria from task prompts or model outputs, overlooking tacit standards visible only in practitioner deliverables. We introduce FinProBench, a benchmark for professional financial tasks, and Role-Grounded Rubric Construction (RGRC), a reusable pipeline that derives rubrics from deliverables produced by practitioners in the same role. RGRC comprises four stages: Deliverable Collection, Competency Extraction, Rubric Synthesis, and Validation. Its rubrics capture tacit standards, distinguish quality levels, and transfer across tasks within a role. Before analysis, we classified 57 occupations by deliverable genre into 30 prior-rich conventional roles and 27 prior-sparse role-specialized roles. Across all roles, Prompt-only nearly matches RGRC for conventional roles (89.2% vs. 90.7%), but RGRC substantially outperforms it for role-specialized roles (99.1% vs. 78.0%). This split indicates that prompt engineering can approximate rubrics when conventions are well represented in model priors, while professional grounding is essential for standards beyond those priors. FinProBench is built from 1,723 curated deliverables spanning 57 occupations, 8 financial sub-industries, and 161 deliverable types, and releases an initial evaluation set of 20 complete tasks covering 20 roles in 7 sub-industries. With heterogeneous LLM judges and role-level rubrics, human deliverables rank first on average (73.7 vs. 70.3, 70.2, and 69.6 out of 100), while all four systems show overlapping 95% confidence intervals and complementary strengths. Reusing rubrics at the role level reduces estimated per-task construction effort by 6.7 times relative to authoring each rubric from scratch.

title: The Transformer Revolution, Part 1: Dynamic Processing through Output- Weight Interconnections
abstract: This paper offers a new interpretation of the Transformer during inference. Against the "stochastic parrot" view that large language models merely reproduce statistical regularities learned in training, we argue that Transformers construct and apply prompt-dependent transformations whose parameters are generated during inference. We call this form of computation SIDPP: Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing. The Transformer is interpreted as a system that transforms concepts by means of concepts. Token vectors are the concepts to be transformed; parameterized transformations defined by matrices and vectors are the transforming concepts. These may be static, when fixed through training, or dynamic, when generated from the input sequence. Mechanically, they correspond to groups of simple neural networks. The Transformer's architectural novelty lies in output-weight interconnections, through which the outputs of some networks determine the weights of others, alongside ordinary output-input interconnections. By means of these interconnections, the system constructs transformations from the prompt and uses them to modify token representations. The contribution of dynamic processing grows with prompt length and may equal or exceed that of static processing, a phenomenon we call strong prompt sensitivity. This account bears on interpretability, predictability, control, and the design of smaller, more sustainable systems. Finally, since the human neural system possesses the mechanisms required to implement SIDPP, we argue that a form of SIDPP may, in principle, be neurally realized in the cerebral cortex. We therefore conjecture that human language processing may itself be a form of SIDPP produced by a functional architecture relevantly similar to that of the Transformer.

title: GENESIS: Towards Explainable Causal Discovery
abstract: Causal Discovery (CD) from observational data faces two fundamental challenges. First, purely statistical methods often lack the power to resolve structural ambiguities in low-sample regimes. Second, although LLM-assisted hybrid approaches improve structure recovery through semantic reasoning, the influence of that reasoning on individual edge decisions remains largely opaque. Consequently, existing hybrid methods fail to satisfy a fundamental requirement: explaining why a particular edge is included or excluded in the learned directed acyclic graph (DAG). This is critical in real-world applications, where no ground-truth DAG exists and every structural decision must be independently justified. We formalize this requirement as decision traceability, requiring every inferred edge to be supported by auditable statistical evidence, Markov Blanket consistency, or explicit domain reasoning. We propose GENESIS, an explainable hybrid CD framework that decomposes graph construction into interpretable decision points. GENESIS first identifies and scores three-node structural motifs, including chains, forks, and colliders, to establish transparent structural priors, then progressively refines the graph by integrating these priors with observational evidence, invoking domain knowledge only when statistical evidence is insufficient. By design, every edge decision is resolved through an auditable source of evidence. Experiments show that GENESIS achieves 100% decision traceability across all settings, establishing explainability as a first-class objective in causal discovery. Despite this additional requirement, GENESIS consistently outperforms purely statistical CD methods on the majority of benchmark datasets across all sample regimes in terms of Structural Hamming Distance (SHD), while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art LLM-assisted approaches.

title: LatentGuard: Efficient and Inspectable Latent Reasoning for LLM Safeguards
abstract: Reasoning-based guard models improve LLM safeguards, but decoding explicit rationales for every interaction makes them costly to deploy. Although latent-reasoning methods reduce token generation by moving reasoning into continuous states, they remain underexplored for safety moderation and lack an inspection interface for deployment. In this paper, we propose LatentGuard, an efficient and inspectable safeguard framework that brings continuous latent reasoning to guard models. LatentGuard uses a staged curriculum to progressively compress task-aligned textual rationales into compact latent states, enabling safety verdicts to be predicted directly from continuous representations. To preserve inspectability, an isolated auxiliary decoder generates compact audit artifacts on demand, keeping rationale generation off the standard inference path. Experiments show that LatentGuard-8B improves mean weighted F1 from 83.95 to 84.91 over GuardReasoner-8B, while reducing critical-path reasoning cost from 268.56 generated rationale tokens to 1.60 latent reasoning tokens. Its audit decoder achieves an audit utility score of 85.75, demonstrating an efficient and inspectable path toward deployable LLM safeguards.

title: The LLM Proposes, the Executive Disposes: A Self-Verifying Agent Instrument that Dissociates Commitment Drift from Binding Drift in Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: How do you verify a long-horizon agent when its own state and self-reports are exactly what you cannot trust? We present an agent instrument built so that verification is structural rather than post-hoc. A deterministic Executive owns all belief; a language model may only file typed proposals, and a claim is admitted only when a prediction pre-registered before acting is matched against observation by code. Two properties make the instrument a verifier of its own science, not just of the agent: every run invalidates itself when per-organ write-error, render-size, or salted-canary-echo floors are breached (four of the first eight architecture runs were invalidated, each localizing a real defect); and a render-invisible shadow reference compiles the plan the full system would have committed in every ablation cell, so drift metrics are defined even where the mechanism under test has been removed. Using this instrument we report a clean, single-variable result on a failure every long-horizon agent suffers: ablating the commitment mechanism flips goal-abandonment from 0.00 to 1.00 while binding error stays flat at 0.00 (three seeds per cell, up to 394 reference beats per run, every run gated valid). The binding channel, by contrast, does not reappear as per-beat drift when its repair is ablated -- because binding is code-owned, the failure class is structurally absorbed, its only residue appearing one layer upstream as a collapse in hypothesis formation. We report these under full disclosure that task efficacy is null (zero level completions across 52 gated runs on ARC-AGI-3), pre-registered as a structural defeater. The contribution is a verification methodology for agent development and the drift decomposition it makes measurable.

title: FinVerse: Financial Time-Series Benchmark
abstract: As time-series foundation models have emerged, the need for benchmarks that can evaluate their forecasting ability in meaningful ways has become increasingly important. Existing time-series forecasting benchmarks provide useful standardized comparisons, but they often evaluate heterogeneous series with uniform error-based metrics. Strong performance under such metrics does not necessarily imply that a model's forecasts will support the best real-world decisions across domains. For example, in stock forecasting, correctly predicting whether a price will rise or fall can be more directly relevant to realized returns than minimizing point-wise forecast error alone. To this end, we introduce FinVerse, a finance-domain time-series forecasting benchmark that takes a first step toward more realistic evaluation. The released FinVerse data artifact contains 116,897 financial time series with 171.1M observations, of which 60,232 series with 17.4M observations are selected as evaluated targets based on their economic relevance to financial decisions. Unlike generic forecasting benchmarks that primarily emphasize uniform point-forecast or probabilistic accuracy, FinVerse defines 11 metric families comprising 78 evaluation metrics and assigns the most appropriate evaluation metrics to each individual time series based on its underlying economic meaning. Our analysis of 43 public time-series forecasting foundation models shows that strong performance under generic forecasting criteria does not necessarily translate into useful financial forecasts. This finding highlights the need for domain-aware benchmarks that evaluate models under objectives closer to real-world decision making.

title: Reachability Is Not Realization: Tracing the Sources of LLM Benchmark Gains
abstract: Benchmark gains are often treated as evidence of greater LLM capability. Yet the same gain can reflect different changes in model behavior. A model may reach new answers, or produce answers that were already within reach. Aggregate scores do not distinguish these changes question by question. We establish a question-level audit under fixed budgets, temperatures, and answer formats. A question is realized when the default deployment procedure produces the correct answer. A question is reachable when a specified probe finds that answer within a fixed budget. We first test whether inference-time layer routing can expand reachability. Under a matched budget, random routes match or exceed structured search in all 43 model and task settings. Answer-blind procedures retain almost none of this gain, which instead requires access to the correct answer. We then ask why reachable answers sometimes fail to appear. Across six cases spanning 0.5B to 31B, silencing one identified MLP block repairs 68 to 92 percent of a predefined failure set. We next test whether training closes the gap by expanding reachability. In five of six matched evaluations, deployed performance rises while the reachable ceiling remains flat or falls. For DAPO, the deployed score rises by 14.7 points while the reachable ceiling falls by 13.3 points. Across the settings we audit, realization and reachability therefore do not always change together. Claims of capability expansion should report both realized performance and reachability under matched evaluation conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/reachability-not-realization

title: Temporal Leakage in LLM Backtesting: Measurement, Validation, and Adjusted Scores
abstract: The standard check for contamination in LLM backtests is simple: compare scores before and after the training cutoff. We show this check is uninformative. Four flagship models fail it on questions they cannot have memorized: every scored question resolved after their cutoffs. The reason is structural. Models legitimately know more about times near their cutoff, so recency mimics leakage, and we prove no passive backtest can separate the two from genuine skill. Measurement, not just detection, requires information from outside the backtest. We supply it in two forms. A known cutoff identifies leakage at the boundary; a matched clean control identifies it globally and yields a leakage-adjusted score. We also derive where leakage hides: it concentrates on outcomes that surprised the crowd and were well covered in training, and partial memorization is disproportionately rewarded. We validate the estimators against ground truth by planting leakage in twin models, where they recover the injected dose and return null on clean questions. Deployed on frontier models, they detect one cutoff-localized signature and, at the audit's power floor, clear five models whose apparent advantages were recency alone. Backtests need not be discarded; they need one defensible reference.

title: The Marketing Context Graph: A Governed Substrate for Causal Marketing Measurement and Auditable Decision Provenance Causal Inference as a Governed Layer on a Bitemporal Context Graph
abstract: Marketing decisions increasingly depend on two capabilities that have evolved separately: causal marketing measurement (distinguishing real advertising effects from the correlational patterns in marketing data, the domain of Causal AI) and governed, graph-based context for the AI agents now trusted to act on those effects, the domain of Agentic AI. Both are limited by the same architectural gap. Problem 1: measurement is correlational by construction (not only in media-mix models but in touch-based attribution and observational methods generally), so a channel’s direct, indirect, and total effects are hard to separate and to calibrate against experiments. Problem 2: the agents acting on those effects lack persistent, governed, historically accurate context, and to answer questions such as which campaigns to scale or how to optimize the mix they must reason over incremental effects, uncertainty, evidence strength, applicable populations, and decision lineage, not language. We introduce the Marketing Context Graph (MCG), a bi-temporal, governed property graph, formally a tuple G = (E, R, γE, γR), in which campaign entities, spend vectors, conversion outcomes, and external macro factors are connected by typed, directional, causally identified edges carrying bi-temporal attributes and reified decision traces. We give it a precise set-theoretic semantics, define a point-in-time snapshot operator Σ(tv, tr), and prove it is free of look-ahead contamination. Crucially, the MCG is a governed substrate, not a new estimator: the measurement methods applied on it are classical: mediation / path analysis, inverse-probability weighting, and transport. We (i) inject an experiment-identified halo edge as an informative structural prior into a Gaussian-conjugate Bayesian MMM, showing it reduces posterior variance along the collinear directions (Remark 1) while separating that variance claim from identification (Proposition 2); (ii) compose each channel’s total effect by traversing the graph, so budget decisions improve as cross-channel mediation grows and gain nothing when no structure exists; (iii) reconstruct complete, auditable decision provenance; and (iv) transport an identified edge across populations exactly when the graph’s selection diagram licenses it, and refuse when it does not. Our evaluation is decision-centric rather than fit-centric. Across 8,000 simulated budget decisions the graph cuts budget-decision regret by up to 43% as cross-channel mediation grows (a paired within-replication reduction); look-ahead-free backtesting exposes 70% over-investment that a flat store conceals; the graph answers the provenance queries that require multi-hop, policy, temporal, and audit structure a flat fact/vector store cannot represent; and governed transport stays low-error as populations diverge, where naive transfer’s error grows linearly with divergence. Evidence is synthetic by design, isolating each mechanism against a known oracle; all results are reproducible from released code.

title: Enterprise Trust Gaps in Generative AI Why Accuracy is not Enough: Evidence from Mid-market Generative AI Adoption
abstract: While enterprise generative AI has seen rapid, widespread adoption, it faces a significant and growing trust lag. 88% of organizations have deployed AI in at least one business function, though only 39% attribute any EBIT impact to AI at the enterprise level (McKinsey, 2025). According to Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise, a survey of 3,235 enterprise leaders across 24 countries, only 21% of enterprises have mature governance models (Deloitte, 2026). Workers are not rejecting AI because it fails. They are rejecting it because they cannot afford to be wrong-and machines cannot be held responsible when they are. We hypothesize that the Enterprise Trust Gap (the disconnect between rapid corporate AI adoption and organizational confidence) is not produced by AI inaccuracy but by three organizational conditions that precede accuracy entirely: Accountability Mismatch, The Human Correction Burden, and The Confidence Framing Effect. Wherever these conditions are as a coexistent risk, trust erodes regardless of output quality. When these conditions are addressed through organizational design, trust recovers without requiring improvements to the underlying model, its infrastructure, or the surrounding AI system. This paper investigates the Enterprise Trust Gap-the phenomenon where business users abandon, edit, or override generative AI outputs even when those outputs are accurate. Drawing on empirical data from enterprise professionals across financial services, cybersecurity, and technology sectors, and secondary data analysis across three large-scale enterprise AI adoption surveys, we identify three mechanisms that produce the gap. First — The Accountability Mismatch. AI reliance declines when users own the responsibility and accountability of outputs and cannot independently verify the machine’s work. Second - The Human Correction Burden. As enterprise AI usage increases, user trust does not necessarily follow; instead, users face a steep rise in the responsibility to independently verify, edit, and reconstruct outputs before acting on them. Third — The Confidence Framing Effect. Non-expert audiences read hedging as incompetence rather than calibration. Uncertainty disclosure on output accuracy increases rejection rates. The Enterprise Trust Gap is not only a technology problem. It is an organizational design problem rooted in the structural mismatch between how AI systems communicate confidence and how enterprises demand defensibility.

title: You Agreed to the Rule. Did You Agree to the Experiment?
abstract: This working paper examines a missing boundary in ICML 2026's policy for LLM use in reviewing. ICML assigned reviewers enforceable AI-use rules while also using some assignments to compare outcomes under Policy A and Policy B. The paper distinguishes agreement to perform review duties under a rule from agreement to have those duties used as experimental conditions. It does not allege a legal violation, an IRB failure, or research misconduct. Instead, it asks whether a reviewer could decline the experimental use of an assignment while remaining in the ordinary reviewing role, particularly where reciprocalreview conduct could affect the reviewer's own submissions. A fictional idol-audition scenario illustrates how institutions can begin from the point after entry and treat condition A or condition B as the only remaining options, overlooking the possibility of remaining in the underlying process while declining an additional experimental purpose. Comparisons with NeurIPS 2026 and ICML's 2023 ranking experiment show that ordinary participation, experimental participation, and decision consequences can be separated. The paper concludes that institutions should answer two questions separately: whether a participant agreed to a rule, and whether the participant agreed to an experiment.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Research: Individual Benefits, Collective Risks, and a Framework for Responsible Research with Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This commentary examines the tension between the benefits of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) for scientific research and the unresolved governance questions that accompany its rapid adoption. Drawing on an academic roundtable held at the AI for Science and Innovation Workshop (Scuola IMT Alti Studi Lucca, April 2026) and on the rapidly growing empirical literature, it maps a disagreement within the research community across four stages of the research process, namely funding, research tasks, publication and peer review, and use and uptake. The empirical case for AI's productivity, augmentation, and democratization effects is growing, but the picture sharpens once productivity is disaggregated. AI-assisted papers show clear gains in publication volume and citation share, while novelty, disruption, and breakthrough output exhibit more ambiguous trends. The commentary proposes that the policy conversation move beyond the binary of "AI is beneficial" versus "AI is dangerous" toward frameworks organized around four operational principles, namely disclosure, narrative, differentiation, and proportionality. The proposed Responsible Research with AI (RRAI) builds on existing institutional scaffolding (EU AI Act, UNESCO, OECD), aiming to capture AI's productivity gains while addressing the systemic risks that individual researchers cannot manage on their own.

title: Generative AI Adoption among Arts and Design Students in Palestinian Higher Education: Impacts on Task Completion
abstract: This study investigates Palestinian undergraduate arts and design students’ attitudes towards generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and examines the factors influencing their willingness to adopt these technologies in learning contexts. Data were collected from undergraduate students using an online survey and analysed through descriptive and inferential statistics, including chi-squared tests and regression analyses. The findings indicate that while students generally view the use of GenAI for academic tasks positively, its adoption is hindered by ethical, infrastructural, and cultural concerns. Notably, the results show a strong direct relationship between GenAI usage and perceived benefits (β = 0.66) and a moderate link between usage and challenges (β = 0.33). Although challenges weakly but significantly predict benefits (β = 0.12), a mediation analysis suggests that overcoming these challenges can facilitate additional gains (β = 0.04). Moderation effects reveal that more advanced students perceive challenges as less beneficial (β =–0.12) but experience an enhanced effect of usage on perceived benefits (β = 0.21). These outcomes underscore contradictions between students’ enthusiasm for GenAI and their actual adoption of such tools, highlighting the need for robust policy guidelines, educator training, and supportive infrastructure. Addressing ethical concerns, promoting AI literacy, and ensuring equitable technology access emerge as pivotal strategies for maximising GenAI’s transformative potential. Future research should investigate the long-term influence of GenAI on learning outcomes and further refine frameworks for its responsible and effective implementation in higher education.

title: SpatialNegPrompt: Suppressive Prompt Learning for Few-Shot Plant Disease Segmentation with Frozen Foundation Models
abstract: Accurate plant disease segmentation is crucial for field diagnosis and preci-sion management, but pixel-level annotations are costly, and emerging dis-eases often have few labeled examples. Promptable foundation models likethe Segment Anything Model (SAM) offer strong generic segmentation, yet infine-grained agricultural scenes they often misclassify healthy tissue or visu-ally similar lesions as diseased, because positive prompts specify what to seg-ment but not what to suppress. We propose SpatialNegPrompt, a lightweightsupport-conditioned module for few-shot plant disease segmentation using afrozen SAM3 backbone. SpatialNegPrompt extracts foreground ROI featuresfrom a single support image to generate a suppressive prompt token, whichis injected into the frozen mask decoder alongside standard prompts. Only543K parameters are trained; all foundation model weights remain fixed. Onthe publicly available PlantSeg dataset [1] (11,458 images, 115 categories),SpatialNegPrompt improves mIoU from 22.50% to 31.37%, reduces false pos-itives by 56.2%, and retains 94.0% true-positive coverage. Gains are alsoobserved on COCO-20i (+2.88%) and PASCAL-5i (+0.37%). Ablations con-firm that the support-conditioned suppressive token outperforms support-independent, positive-prototype, multi-token, LoRA, and auxiliary-modulevariants. These results highlight prompt-space suppression as a practical ap-proach for adapting foundation segmentation models to annotation-limited,fine-grained agricultural scenarios.

title: Emotional Buddy: An AI-Driven Emotion-Aware Companion System Using Mobile and Robotic Interfaces
abstract: Most emotion-aware AI systems are validated as standalone components: an emotion classifier evaluated in isolation, or a conversational agent with no perceptual front end, in short-duration lab studies. This paper presents Emotional Buddy, an integrated multimodal companion architecture that couples real-time facial emotion perception with LLM-based dialogue generation and delivers the result through both a mobile app and a robotic platform, then validates the full pipeline through a large-scale, geographically distributed field deployment rather than a lab-only evaluation. The contribution is this end-to-end integration and its real-world validation, not a new emotion-recognition algorithm or language model; the system builds on existing, widely used components (DeepFace, GPT-4o mini). We report emotion detection accuracy, response latency, and, through researcher-conducted trials, perceived empathy, alongside deployment statistics from 93 real-world users and 581 sessions. The system correctly identified emotion 87% of the time in controlled testing, with an average end-to-end response latency of 2.53 seconds, fast enough for real-time interaction, and the field deployment data indicate the architecture holds up outside the lab. These results point toward practical applications in emotional wellness, assistive robotics, and human-computer interaction more broadly.

title: MATEK: An Open Orchestration Framework for Agentic Mathematical Research with Persistent Knowledge Graphs
abstract: MATEK-Multi-Agent Theorem Exploration through Knowledge-Graph Memory-is a local command-line orchestration framework for research-level mathematics, designed around humanexplorable persistent mathematical knowledge. AI research sessions often end without a complete solution, leaving partial results, promising ideas, counterexamples, and failed approaches stranded in individual transcripts, and even if a solution was reached the process of how it was reached may be obscure. MATEK instead organizes this work in a typed, project-scoped knowledge graph that survives runs and provider sessions, that can be explored by human researchers using the Obsidian software. The graph links claims, proofs, approaches, tasks, sources, audits, and formalizations, and supplies later agents with an explicit research frontier to build off of. Furthermore, MATEK turns a short problem statement into a sophisticated prompt for a research orchestrator agent, following structures used in recent successful AI-assisted mathematics. The orchestrator makes use of sub-agents that add their contributions to the knowledge graph. Candidate solutions are independently audited, and formalized in Lean if the audits pass. This report describes the implemented methodology. It does not present a controlled evaluation of mathematical discovery performance, and it does not claim that model-generated proofs are reliable merely because the workflow is elaborate. The framework is intended to make a promising prompting and orchestration pattern persistent, human-inspectable, and extensible.

title: From Signal to Insight: Explainable Low-Rank Fusion for Multimodal eWOM Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Multimodal electronicword-of-mouth (eWOM) has become an important formof user-generated feedback, where opinions are conveyed through text, speech, and visual behavior. Such multimodal content provides richer affective cues than text-only reviews, but also introduces crossmodal noise, redundant representations, and limited transparency, making reliable sentiment inference challenging in customer-feedback analytics. To address these challenges, we propose Low-RankAdaptive Hierarchical Information Fusion (LoRAHIF), a noise-aware and explainable framework for multimodal eWOM sentiment analysis. LoRAHIF first enhances interactions among textual, acoustic, and visual representations through a Synchro Crossmodal Encoder. It then applies low-rank adaptive filtering guided by random matrix theory and the Marčenko–Pastur distribution to decompose enhanced representations into high-value, supplementary, and noise components, where LoRA-inspired low-rank matrices complement informative features and negative log-likelihood regularization constrains residual noise. Finally, an explainable hierarchical fusion network integrates the filtered components and produces modality-level contribution weights for sentiment prediction. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS demonstrate that LoRAHIF achieves overall superior performance compared with representative baselines. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of low-rank filtering, noise regularization, and hierarchical fusion, while case studies show that modality contributions can support LLM-enhanced explanations for more transparent sentiment reasoning.

title: A Brief History of Programming Languages Changes, Updates, Efficiency, and Availability -Do Binary Wins or Human Learning Patterns Drive the Field?
abstract: Programming languages have evolved for roughly 180 years, from Ada Lovelace's 1843 algorithm for the Analytical Engine to today's AI-assisted, cloud-native ecosystems. This paper traces that evolution across five broad historical eras, examines four representative languages as case studies in design philosophy, and reviews current data on popularity, efficiency, and learnability. It then asks a question that has become newly relevant in the age of large language models: has the field been driven primarily by the pursuit of machine efficiency, described here as "binary wins," or by the pursuit of languages that better fit human cognition and learning? Drawing on historical accounts, current popularity indices, peerreviewed energy-efficiency research, and computing-education literature on cognitive load, the paper argues that the two forces have never been opposed so much as sequentially traded off, and that the rise of AI code generation and low-code platforms is now compressing that trade-off in ways the field has not previously experienced. The paper closes with a discussion of the economic implications of this shift and the limitations of the evidence it draws on.

title: A Multimodal LLM Framework with Time-Series-Guided Visual Routing for Ultra-Short-Term Solar Forecasting
abstract: Accurate ultra-short-term solar irradiance forecasting is important for photovoltaic power management, storage scheduling, and the secure operation of power systems with increasing renewable penetration. However, historical irradiance measurements primarily reflect atmospheric variations after they have affected the observation site, providing limited information about approaching clouds that may induce rapid irradiance ramps. Although ground-based sky images provide complementary spatial information, using complete visual representations can introduce irrelevant regions and weaken effective multimodal interaction. This study proposes a time-series-guided multimodal forecasting framework that integrates historical irradiance, sky images, statistical prompts, and a frozen LLM. Historical irradiance sequences are divided into temporal patches and reprogrammed into the LLM representation space, while a hierarchical visual encoder extracts spatial tokens from sky images. A time-series-conditioned visual router evaluates the relevance of individual image patches according to the current temporal representation and retains task-relevant regions through hard Top-K selection with a differentiable straight-through estimator. The selected visual tokens are then integrated with the temporal representation through TS-guided cross-modal attention, in which temporal tokens serve as queries and visual tokens provide keys and values. A residual connection preserves the original temporal information, and statistical prompt embeddings are subsequently concatenated with the fused temporal tokens before processing by the frozen LLM. Experiments on the Folsom dataset achieve nRMSE values of 14.89%, 17.19%, and 19.91% at 10-, 30-, and 60-min forecasting horizons, respectively, outperforming all evaluated baselines. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further confirm the contributions of time-series-conditioned visual selection and explicit cross-modal fusion, while an intermediate number of selected patches provides a favorable balance between information retention and visual redundancy. Cross-dataset validation on the Stanford SKIPP'D dataset further demonstrates the applicability of the proposed framework to PV power forecasting under a different site and prediction target.

title: Exposure to Artificial Intelligence, Time Use, and Labor Outcomes in Mexico
abstract: We estimate the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) exposure on time allocation and labor-market outcomes in Mexico. Combining nationally representative household microdata with municipality-level mobile-network coverage, we exploit ChatGPT's late-2022 release in a difference-in-differences design. AI exposure raises study time among youth and leisure across the population, offset by reductions in other non-market time, with no effects on hours worked, labor force participation, or earnings. Time-use and search data show parents taking over homework help from older siblings in technology-equipped households. Households adapt to AI well before firms, whose productivity and earnings effects may arrive only later.

title: Generative Economics: Verification and the Allocation of Judgment
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence lowers the cost of producing candidate solutions, not the cost of deciding which solutions can be used. I study an economy in which effective candidates 𝑀𝑀 must share scarce verification capacity 𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴. If scrutiny per candidate is 𝑥𝑥 = 𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴/𝑀𝑀 and verified value per candidate is 𝑣𝑣(𝑥𝑥), output is 𝑀𝑀𝑣𝑣(𝑥𝑥). Two prices that coincide in an ordinary linear technology then separate. The social marginal product of another candidate is 𝑣𝑣(𝑥𝑥)-𝑥𝑥𝑣𝑣′(𝑥𝑥), while a decentralized contributor can receive the average value 𝑣𝑣(𝑥𝑥). The difference, 𝑥𝑥𝑣𝑣′(𝑥𝑥), is the verification burden imposed on other candidates. In an integrated competitive economy, a fall in the candidate price raises the return to verification; indeed, 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑/𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑 =-𝑀𝑀/𝐴𝐴. Under open entry, contributors ignore the verification burden and generate too many candidates. As generation cost approaches zero, the overentry ratio diverges under regular conditions. With full private appropriation, aggregate generation expenditure absorbs the entire value created by scarce verification even though the cost of any one candidate vanishes. Integration, submission prices, and review rights can recover that value. Platform economics made participation externalities central when reproduction became cheap. Generative economics must make verification and the allocation of judgment central when creation becomes cheap.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Enterprises’ Integration into Global Value Chain: Opportunities or Risks?
abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in the global value chain embedding of enterprises through both mathematical model derivation and empirical analysis. Large language models are employed to construct metrics that capture the extent of AI adoption within enterprises. The results show that AI applications enhance the embeddings of enterprises' global value chains significantly, and the conclusions remain robust after replacing large language models, adjusting the explained variables, and changing the estimation methods; The mechanism by which AI applications drive enterprise global value chain embedding lies in enhancing productivity levels, which in turn is achieved by accelerating technological innovation and alleviating resource misallocation. The facilitating effect of AI applications on enterprise value chain embedding is more pronounced in smaller enterprises, non-state-owned enterprises, enterprises in less marketized regions, and capital-intensive enterprises. In a context of heightened uncertainty in the evolution of the global value chain system, while AI applications are promoting the embedding of enterprises in the global value chain, they may also increase the risks. Therefore, as enterprises deepen their participation in global division of labor, they need to effectively balance efficiency and security and enhance their ability to deal with external uncertainties in multiple dimensions.

title: Codification of Scholarly Values in Academic Publishing: AI Governance and Institutional Tension
abstract: This article examines the current artificial intelligence (AI) policies by five prominent academic publishers-Elsevier, Springer Nature, Taylor & Francis, SAGE Publishing, and Cambridge University Press-interpreting them as efforts to codify values as generative AI becomes embedded in academic communication. Through comparative qualitative analysis, the study identifies core values consistently operationalized across these policies, including exclusive human authorship, mandatory disclosure, non-delegable accountability, and confidentiality in peer review. As technological change disrupts traditional norms, these policies act as both regulatory tools and ethical anchors, stabilizing the identity and legitimacy of academic institutions. However, this codification creates structural tensions. Turning ethical principles into formal rules produces unintended consequences, from adding new layers of scholarly labor to reinforcing existing institutional inequalities. In addressing both epistemic risks and the tensions that arise from governance responses, the article advocates for AI governance that is reflexive, inclusive, and context-sensitive. Such models should preserve institutional integrity while respecting the evolving partnership between humans and machines in the production of knowledge.

title: Quality Assurance After Content in Higher Education: Assessment Integrity, Signal Collapse, and the Epistemology of Verification in the Post-Content Age of Generative AI
abstract: For a century, higher education has verified capability largely by inspecting content, and the essay, report, problem set, and dissertation stood as evidence of the mind that produced them. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) weakens that evidentiary connection. This paper analyses assessment as a problem of statistical inference about latent student capability and derives four results. First, when fluent content is available at near-zero marginal cost, a content-inspecting assessment instrument with unconstrained and undetectable delegation admits a pooling equilibrium, whereby students below the generative frontier submit artefacts of the same quality, and the signal’s overall informativeness approaches zero as that frontier approaches the upper support of capability. Second, artefact-only detection cannot provide a robust limiting solution. A total-variation bound shows that, as the distributions of human- and machine-produced artefacts converge, the maximum achievable power of a detector subject to a fixed false-positive constraint converges to that false-positive rate; remaining errors may also impose unequal burdens across linguistic and stylistic groups. Third, process-exposed instruments, including live, interactive, supervised, and provenance-supported components, restore positive capability information by constraining delegation and making the expected assessment signal responsive to capability. Their informativeness increases as additional expert judgement time reduces measurement noise. Fourth, at the post-content endpoint, the informativeness of a feasible symmetric assessment system is bounded by the institution’s available supply of expert judgement time per student. The paper then develops a design epistemology for post-content quality assurance organised around four questions, namely what is real (provenance), what is true (validity), what is provable (verifiability), and what is possible (capability inference). The generative-AI moment is therefore not principally a detection problem, but a measurement-theory and institutional-design problem requiring institutions to build provenance into assessment and provide the qualified judgement needed to verify capability at scale.

title: Artificial Sameness
abstract: A lesbian couple asks ChatGPT to generate a family from their photo, only to get a heterosexual couple with two children. AI selects minorities out of mortgages and jobs, but into prison. Scholars call this algorithmic discrimination and propose debiasing AI models along protected-class lines, litigating algorithmic screening, and regulating automated decisionmaking. This account is mistaken. AI’s distinctive danger is not discrimination, but homogenization—the erasure of diversity by compressing everyone and everything toward the most common pattern. The lesbian couple were overwritten, not targeted, for deviating from that pattern: the heterosexual couple with two children. This Article theorizes artificial sameness as the systematic convergence of outputs, reasoning, and ultimately thought itself, driven by AI’s architecture. Existing tools, including bias audits and disparate impact analysis, are blind to artificial sameness because they detect skew, not compression. Worse, when the law mistakes homogenization for discrimination, it creates the debiasing trap: correcting AI outputs along protected-class lines supplies the very intentional classification that current doctrine forbids. Artificial sameness compounds at two levels. AI first homogenizes what people produce, and then what people expect, as AI-mediated norms become the new standard. Today’s artificial sameness is the least dangerous form because it is still recognizable as “AI slop”—choppy sentences, six-fingered hands, and synthetic polish. Before technological progress conceals those fingerprints, we must ask ourselves: what happens to a society predicated on diverse minds when every mind reasons through the same machine? Artificial sameness threatens the constitutional order. The marketplace of ideas, the laboratories of democracy, and the adversary system all presuppose distinct judgments in a shared enterprise. We identify the common value underlying these commitments as “laboratories of originality”: the cognitive diversity that artificial sameness erodes, not by shutting down any particular laboratory, but by making every laboratory run the same experiment.

title: Managing Generative Production: Candidate Load, Selection Capacity, and Organizational Output
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence lets firms produce drafts, code patches, recommendations, and plans at low marginal cost, but these candidates require selection, validation, and accountable deployment. I model a firm that chooses candidate load 𝑀𝑀 , selection capacity 𝑅𝑅 , and workflow governance 𝐺𝐺. Organizational output is 𝑌𝑌 = 𝑀𝑀𝑣𝑣 𝐺𝐺 (𝑅𝑅/𝑀𝑀). Optimal input choice depends on the ratio of the marginal cost of generation to the marginal cost of selection, not on model access alone. A candidate-volume target induces overgeneration because the generating unit ignores the review burden it creates. Review investment dominates a model upgrade when its cost reduction is applied to the larger optimal expenditure margin; governance is valuable when it raises verified value enough to cover its fixed workflow cost. Published field experiments and an audit of 7,000 software repositories show why candidate activity, accepted output, and governance must be measured separately. The repository timing does not identify a causal governance effect, but it rejects a common observational design and supplies a reproducible measurement architecture. The analysis yields operating rules for capacity planning, performance measurement, and the allocation of decision rights in generative production.

title: OpenAI -An Independent Governance and Behavioural Assessment
abstract: This paper presents an independent external assessment of OpenAI — the OpenAI Group PBC, the controlling OpenAI Foundation, and its publicly released GPT-series and o-series models — benchmarked against four governance frameworks: the EU AI Act (including its general-purpose AI and systemic-risk provisions), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, and India's AI Governance Guidelines (2025) read with the DPDP Act 2023. The assessment rests entirely on public evidence, distinguishes fact, assessment, and opinion throughout, and is not an audit in the assurance sense: there was no engagement with the subject and no access to internal records. Four behavioural findings stand on corroborated public evidence: sycophancy serious enough that the developer withdrew a released model update against its own published behavioural specification; confabulation of authorities documented in several hundred court instances; occupational gender bias confirmed in peer-reviewed research; and developer-disclosed in-context scheming under structured evaluation. At the organisational layer, the paper traces the migration from a non-profit whose assets were irrevocably dedicated to a charitable mission toward a capital-optimised public benefit corporation — a drift checked but not reversed by state attorney-general oversight, and tested privately in litigation resolved on limitation grounds without adjudication of the merits. The paper credits the democratisation of AI capability without qualification, prescribes no remedies to preserve independence, and offers one concluding judgment: at both the organisational and the model layer, stated commitments have proven not to be self-enforcing — where they held, structural mechanisms made them hold. Findings are mapped to specific framework provisions to support verification and reuse by researchers, practitioners, and regulators.

title: Viability Leadership in Complex Systems
abstract: This conceptual working paper reassesses and advances the leadership framework introduced in Christoph Schließmann's 2014 book Leistungspotenziale im Fadenkreuz. The original model rejects universal leadership recipes and understands performance as a dynamic relationship among person, task, organization, relevant system, and time. It also conceptualizes organizational viability as a heuristic relation of agility and robustness to system complexity. An evidence-weighted integrative review of leadership research from January 2014 through 24 July 2026 examines leadership theory, organizational adaptability, psychological safety and employee voice, shared leadership, temporal person-environment fit, intuition, resilience, meaningful work and well-being, hybrid work, generative artificial intelligence, algorithmic management, and AI governance. Meta-analyses, systematic and integrative reviews, randomized field experiments, peerreviewed primary studies, and authoritative legal and governance sources are prioritized and triangulated. The review largely confirms the relational, systemic, and temporal premises of the 2014 model, while qualifying three claims: the viability equation is a theory heuristic rather than a calibrated metric; intuition is reliable only under identifiable conditions of expertise and feedback; and shared leadership requires vertical framing and accountability. Artificial intelligence adds a new governance dimension because leadership increasingly concerns coupled human-AI systems. The paper develops Viability Leadership as the dynamic meta-capability to preserve purposeful action, learning, and regeneration by continuously rebalancing agility, robustness, resonance, dynamic fit, and governance relative to complexity. Eight propositions and an empirical research agenda are presented.

title: Recruiting for Scarcity: A Soft-Systems Analysis of the Niche-Technology Skills Gap in the Indian IT Workforce, Revisited in the Generative-AI Era
abstract: This paper examines the recruitment and retention of niche-technology talent in the Indian information-technology (IT) sector using a soft-systems perspective.
