title: Irreversibility and Cultural Production: From Bohemia to Digital Nomadism and Generative AI
abstract: Sovremennye Zapiski ran in Paris for twenty years and outlived most of its founders; even the most durable digital-nomad hubs-Hubud (Bali, founded 2013) and Dojo Bali (closed 2022 after roughly seven years)-merged, rebranded, or shut down within a decade, and neither survived as a formalized, peer-governed institution independent of its founding team. Both configurations-the Russian émigré press and the digital-nomad hub-are émigré, mobile, and reasonably wellresourced. This study isolates what is conceptualized here as the threshold of irreversibility as the decisive explanatory variable, placing factors like mobility itself, economic deprivation, and network density into a secondary analytical tier. This threshold signifies the perceived possibility of returning to one's accustomed professional and social trajectory with no significant loss of already accumulated symbolic and economic capital. I show that the degree of irreversibility fundamentally determines actors' incentives to invest in long-term institutional infrastructures of cultural production. The argument is built on a comparative analysis of three configurations of creative mobility: the Russian émigré literary milieu in interwar Paris, the American expatriate literary colony of the 1920s, and contemporary communities of digital nomads. The comparison shows that a higher level of irreversibility is consistently associated with the emergence of durable cultural institutions, whereas highly reversible forms of mobility tend to generate intense but short-lived networks with limited institutional accumulation. The article then extends this model to the transformation of local cultural ecosystems and discusses its implications for contemporary algorithmic environments and generative artificial intelligence. Rather than treating bohemia as a historically unique phenomenon, I propose to understand it as an analytically observable special case of a more general mechanism linking irreversibility to the longterm production of cultural value.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Full-Stack Web Development: Opportunities and Workforce Implications in South Asia
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming not only the field of software development industry but also every aspects of our daily life. From virtual assistants and recommendation systems to healthcare and education, AI become part and parcel in our modern society. In particular AI is significantly transforming the field of full stack web development. Now days we can see many advance AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Claude and many other automated code generation system have changed and easy developers design, build, test, and maintain web application. This Study investigates the future of full-stack web development at the age of AI, with a specific focus on opportunities, challenges and employment trends in South Asia. This research shows that the impact of AI on developer productivity, required technical skills, and the job evolving job market in countries like Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Other South Asia Countries. This study utilizes data collected from Stack Overflow Developer Survey reports, World Bank datasets, ILOSTAT labor statistics, and AI-related employment datasets. Both Statistical and graphical analyses are performed to identify the recent trends in developer employment, skill requirements, and AI adoption across the software industry. So after analyzed the datasets the finding suggest that AI is not replace the full-stack developers entirely; rather than it is reshaping their roles and tasks by automating repetitive tasks and increasing development efficiency. Now as a result developers are more focus on system design, problem solving, use experience and AI assisted software engineering. The study also shows us that the growing demand of problem solver and also professionals who can effectively integrate AI technologies into web applications. This paper shows that while AI introduces certain employment challenges, it also creates so many new opportunities for skilled developers in South Asia. Continuous learning, problem solving skill, adaptation to AI-driven tools, and the development of advanced technical and analytical skills be very much helpful for long-term career success in this recent time.

title: Physical AI Sovereignty in an Asymmetric Multipolar Technology Order: Governable Machine Action and Industrial State Capability
abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from information processing into systems that perceive, decide and act in material environments. This transition is unfolding within a technology order that is increasingly geographically distributed yet remains asymmetrically concentrated across semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, foundation models, industrial data, robotics integration and standards. The resulting governance problem is not captured by data localisation, domestic model ownership or robot safety considered separately. This article develops physical AI sovereignty as industrial state capability: the capacity to convert globally distributed technological resources into governable domestic machine action while retaining learning and value through managed interdependence. It combines an integrative review with structured documentary analysis of standards, public-policy documents and selected frontier preprints, using Japan and Algeria as differentiated illustrative anchor cases rather than as matched country comparisons. Japan shows policy-stack formation across industrial data, models, connectivity and evaluation. Algeria, an energy-resource-rich country, illustrates an infrastructure-first capability pathway adapted to major energy, water, mining and logistics systems. The article proposes a five-layer framework linked by a lifecycle-assurance spine and introduces qualitative indicators for future comparative application. Its central principle is bounded authority under uncertainty: systems may explore epistemically, but physical execution must remain independently constrained, observable, interruptible and reversible. Physical AI sovereignty is therefore neither technological autarky nor passive dependence; it is the capacity to govern asymmetric interdependence across the perception-reasoning-action lifecycle.

title: Beyond Synergy: Uncovering The Paradoxical Role of Generative AI in Digital Transformation and Business Model Innovation for Organizational Resilience in Fintech Ecosystems
abstract: This study challenges the prevailing assumption that Generative AI (GenAI) and Digital Transformation (DT) are inherently complementary drivers of business model innovation (BMI) and organizational resilience (OR) in FinTech ecosystems (Dwivedi et al., 2023; Hanelt et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2025). Through a multi-case qualitative analysis of 350 documents from ten leading global FinTech firms, we uncover a counter-intuitive finding: the GenAI-DT synergy does not automatically generate resilience; rather, it creates structural tensions that can undermine agility when BMI is absent or misaligned (Smith & Lewis, 2011; Duchek, 2020). We propose the 'Cognitive-Infrastructural Tension Model' , which positions BMI not merely as an outcome but as a mediating governance mechanism that resolves these tensions (Teece, 2018; Koroleva, 2022). Our findings reveal three temporal phases of technology-resilience coevolution: (1) reactive infrastructure-building, (2) interactive cognitive integration, and (3) predictive business model reconfiguration (Vial, 2019; Hanelt et al., 2021). We contribute to RBV and DCV by reconceptualizing GenAI as a 'dynamic cognitive capability with paradoxical effects' (Barney, 1991; Teece, 1997) and DT as an 'enabling constraint' rather than a pure enabler (Mazurek & Malagocka, 2022). These insights offer a nuanced framework for managers and policymakers, emphasizing that resilience emerges not from technology adoption but from continuous tension management between cognitive and infrastructural assets (Hillmann & Guenther, 2021; Duchek, 2020).

title: Cognitive Offloading, Fragmented Attention, and Contingent Gains: A Critical Narrative Review of How Artificial Intelligence Affects Human Critical Thinking, Memory, and Attention
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of everyday academic and professional work, yet its effects on human cognition remain uncertain. This critical narrative review examines evidence on three closely related areas: critical thinking, memory, and attention. Studies of critical thinking present a mixed picture. Frequent or poorly regulated AI use has been associated with cognitive offloading and reduced independent evaluation, while controlled studies of AI-supported learning have also reported improvements in performance and higher-order thinking. Experimental findings suggest that this difference may depend partly on how AI is used. Assistance that replaces the user's own reasoning can improve immediate performance without producing comparable gains in unaided performance, whereas guidance that requires continued mental effort may better support learning. Research on memory similarly suggests that people remember less information when they expect it to remain externally available, although direct evidence involving generative AI is still limited. Evidence concerning attention is less developed, and much of the current argument draws on earlier research on digital media, interruptions, and automation rather than studies of generative AI itself. Overall, the literature does not support the conclusion that AI simply improves or weakens human cognition. Its effects appear to depend on the task, the form of assistance, the way the system is used, and the extent to which users continue to monitor and question its output. The review uses these findings to develop a scaffold–substitute account of AI-assisted cognition and identifies priorities for future research.

title: Family Technology Governance: From Parental Mediation to Deliberative Governance in Digital Environments
abstract: This article introduces Family Technology Governance (FTG) , a theoretical framework that treats the family as a sociotechnical governance unit and transposes governance principles to the domestic management of digital technologies. Scholarship on parental mediation, digital parenting, and family media practices is substantial, and a patrimonial tradition has long treated the family as a governance unit in matters of wealth and succession; these streams have not coalesced around an integrated construct through which families establish principles, allocate responsibilities, deliberate, manage risks, and adapt technological decisions over time. Drawing on an adaptive governance framework developed in recent empirical research on generative artificial intelligence in public-sector institutions, the article proposes a five-pillar model (Awareness, Dialogue, Structure, Example, Adaptation), given operational expression through a Family Technology Governance Pact. FTG reframes dispersed practices as components of a governance architecture, displacing the family as governance unit from the patrimonial axis to the sociotechnical domain of everyday digital life.

title: GlyphTrace: A Distributed Binary Character-Level Provenance Framework for AI-Generated Academic Text
abstract: Artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed academic writing by enabling the rapid generation of human-like text. By 2026, universities, scholarly publishers, and educational institutions have increasingly revised their academic integrity policies, classroom practices, and assessment methods in response to widespread student use of generative AI systems. Faculty members have shifted toward in-class assessments, oral examinations, iterative drafting, and AI disclosure requirements, while institutions continue to evaluate AI-detection software despite ongoing concerns regarding reliability, false positives, and false negatives. These developments illustrate a broader challenge: current approaches often attempt to infer whether a document was generated by artificial intelligence rather than directly verifying its origin. This paper proposes GlyphTrace, a conceptual distributed binary character-level provenance framework designed to move beyond probabilistic AI detection toward verifiable digital provenance. Rather than relying solely on statistical analysis of language patterns, GlyphTrace envisions embedding invisible binary verification fragments throughout AI-generated text at the character level. These distributed fragments would collectively reconstruct a cryptographically verifiable provenance signature capable of surviving ordinary copy-and-paste operations. By shifting the focus from prediction to verification, this framework seeks to contribute to the growing field of AI provenance, academic integrity, and information informatics while providing a foundation for future research into trusted AI-generated content.

title: Private Enforcement of the Digital Markets Act – First Procedural Insights from Case Law and Implications Beyond
abstract: The Digital Markets Act (DMA) establishes a primarily centralised system of public enforcement led by the European Commission, but its practical effectiveness also depends on the ability of consumers, business users and representative organisations to invoke its obligations before national courts. This article examines the first judgments on the private enforcement of the DMA: the Higher Regional Court of Cologne’s decision concerning Meta’s use of personal data for generative AI training and the Regional Court of Mainz’s judgment concerning Google’s treatment of Gmail. Adopting a procedural perspective, the article analyses how national courts operationalise DMA obligations in the absence of a harmonised EU framework for private enforcement. The judgments confirm that consumer organisations and business users may seek injunctive relief independently of prior Commission enforcement. They further address representative standing, international jurisdiction under Article 7(2) Brussels I bis, applicable law, the territorial scope of judicial review, the identification of the appropriate defendant within a corporate group and coordination with the Commission under Article 39 DMA. In resolving these questions, the German courts draw extensively on concepts originating in competition law, consumer law, private international law and general civil procedure. The article argues that these decisions are contributing to the emergence of a hybrid and decentralised procedural architecture for DMA enforcement with potential for other digital rules. Competition-law analogies make private enforcement operational, but their extension beyond their original setting may also shape the procedural law of the wider EU digital rulebook. The analysis further shows why injunctive relief is likely to remain more important than damages during the initial development of private enforcement: it permits rapid intervention against continuing conduct and avoids the difficulties of quantifying harm resulting from restrictions on fairness, contestability, user autonomy or visibility. The article concludes that private enforcement can significantly strengthen the effectiveness of the DMA and other EU digital rules. At the same time, greater procedural coordination, Commission participation and use of the preliminary ruling procedure will be necessary to limit fragmentation and ensure consistent remedies across the internal market.

title: Skill Choice, Automation and Economic Development
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the long-run Macroeconomic effects of automation. A two-period production Overlapping Generations (OLG) economy is considered augmented with three types of endogenously built physical capital and two endogenously selected worker skills. In this framework, decentralized decisions are optimally chosen but the competitive equilibrium may lead to over or under investments in various forms of physical capital. If total factor productivity is sufficiently large, then three distinct phases of economic development may characterize the competitive equilibrium dynamics. In the "pre-automation" stage in which all the unskilled tasks are performed by workers, physical capital deepening leads to rising wages, deskilling phenomena, and growing fractions of labour-complementing physical capital. When labour-replacing physical capital emerges, the economy enters a "partial automation" stage in which wages stagnate, upskilling occurs, fractions of labour-replacing physical capital rise and fractions of the labour-complementing type falls. When all the unskilled tasks are no longer performed by workers, a "full automation" stage is reached in which physical capital deepening leads to growing fractions of labour-complementing physical capital, diminishing fractions of the labour-replacing type with ambiguous effects on wages. The effects on the transitional dynamics and on the long-run steady-state solutions of technological advances more suited for skilled tasks rather than unskilled ones such as Generative AI are investigated along with various forms of government policies. As workers' saving is solely responsible for physical capital creation, enough complementarities between physical capital and human labour in skilled tasks, lower shares of labour-complementing physical capital and policies that ease the tax burden on households are keys to guarantee higher long-run living standards. A skill subsidy accelerates the transitions to the partial and full automation stages and may lead to a higher steady-state income per worker if it is partially financed by a robot tax.

title: Embedded Measurement Infrastructure for Continuous Education Research: Design, Statistical Operating Characteristics, and a Simulation Study
abstract: Randomized controlled trials remain the standard for causal evidence in education, but the dominant research model separates measurement from instruction: studies typically require years and substantial dedicated funding to produce a single effect size in a single context. We evaluate an alternative in which the learning environment itself serves as the measurement instrument, so that rigorous studies run as configurations of existing instructional infrastructure rather than as parallel capital projects. We present an embedded measurement architecture with three layers: an observation-streaming protocol that converts routine instructional interactions into scored psychometric events without altering instruction; a study-lifecycle layer implementing hash-committed pre-registration, cluster randomization, group-sequential monitoring with alpha-spending boundaries and a pre-specified non-binding futility rule, and automated cross-site pooling; and a governance layer in which research use is consent-gated, identifiable data remains under district control consistent with FERPA and applicable state law, primary outcomes are externally validated instruments (platform-native measures are pre-registered as secondary, given the documented inflation of effects on intervention-aligned measures), and third-party analysts, not the developer, control randomization and analysis. The design is instantiated in a working system of 50 instruments with 178 calibrated items across 11 subject domains. We evaluate the design in two ways. First, statistical operating characteristics: at the modal two-arm cluster-randomized deployment (12 classrooms, about 30 students per classroom, ICC 0.10-0.20, 12% attrition), the primary covariate-adjusted analysis attains 54% power at an effect size of 0.35 SD and 82% at 0.50 SD under the sequential triage procedure (the fixed-sample confirmatory analysis, which spends no interim error probability, is weakly more powerful), exceeding unadjusted analysis by 22-26 percentage points, with minimum detectable effects of 0.49-0.60 SD across ICC; we state plainly which questions a twelve-classroom deployment cannot answer. Second, a simulation study of 10 synthetic sites, 16,774 learners, and 7.2 million scored events exercises the full lifecycle at 2,000 replications per cell: empirical Type I error of the sequential triage procedure ranged 0.041-0.057 across all nine design cells against nominal 0.05 (Monte Carlo standard error about 0.005), with the highest cell re-estimated at 20,000 replications and resolving to 0.051; the futility rule stopped 88-91% of null trials early, matching analytic expectation; and cross-site pooling with Hartung-Knapp intervals achieved 92-98% coverage at five or more sites, while two-site heterogeneity estimation proved 2.6-4.3 times less stable. Calibration itself yielded two methodological findings. Conventional single-coefficient covariate adjustment inflated treatment-effect variance by 71% through within-between conflation, a result confirmed by an independent R implementation (lmerTest/pbkrtest), and was repaired by Mundlak-form decomposition of the covariate. And ten defects identified during development, including a pair whose errors canceled exactly on null-calibration checks, motivate a verification standard requiring per-dataset agreement with an independent reference implementation on estimates, standard errors, degrees of freedom, and rejection decisions; the defect ledger and harness are reported in full as a template for verification-driven simulation practice. The simulation protocol was itself hash-committed through the system's own pre-registration mechanism before the production run. No efficacy claims are made: the simulation evaluates infrastructure and statistical behavior, not learning; empirical validation with live classrooms, under IRB review and district consent, is specified; and each design claim is paired with the observation that would falsify it. Language-model assistance (Anthropic's Claude) was used in drafting and editing this manuscript; all system designs, analyses, data, and claims were specified and verified by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content.

title: Measuring a Scaffold from Inside: An Operator-Authored Self-Measurement Harness for a Constitutional Runtime over a Hosted Language Model
abstract: Interactive intelligent systems constructed over hosted large language models cannot retrain the substrate on which they depend, and so their designers enforce a named epistemology at the surrounding scaffold layer. A difficulty follows that has received little methodological attention: when quality regresses, the regression frequently belongs to the scaffold rather than the substrate, and catching it requires instruments that measure the scaffold itself rather than the model beneath it. This article reports one such instrument set, added to a live constitutional runtime between 17 and 18 July 2026, and situates it as a reusable design pattern. The layer comprises five componentsoperator-authored adversarial batteries held as versioned regression fixtures, deterministic pattern screens encoding named defects, an emission quarantine that retains failure evidence as a first-class object, an instrument-health monitor issuing autonomous handoffs, and continuous-integration delivery tripwires. Eight falsifiable predictions are stated, each named against a specific runtime carrier-a code path, a database table, or a typed field-and each paired with an explicit falsification condition. The predictions are offered for adversarial replication under an honest empirical frame rather than as settled results: the batteries were authored by the platform's operator, classification is not independent, and the number of platforms studied is one. The discussion states a narrow priority claim, distinguishes the enforcement point of composition-time assertion from adjacent techniques, and argues that the interaction properties a reader encounters-an observation lock and per-turn provenance grounding-become testable precisely because they are structurally enforced.

title: Facts vs Feelings: Comparing LLM Persuasion Tactics in Policy Discussions
abstract: This study compares information-based and affect-based AI persuasion messages in the context of policy arguments. While prior work on AI persuasion has largely focused on AI-human conversations, we examine a setting where competing AI-generated messages advocating for and against proposed policies are evaluated by human judges. In an online experiment with 300 U.S. adults, informationbased arguments were consistently perceived as more convincing and informative, whereas purely affective rhetoric was judged markedly more unpleasant, less convincing, and more likely to have been written by a human. As a result, current guardrails block a comparatively ineffective persuasion tactic while leaving the more powerful strategy of selective information disclosure unregulated. Finally, we show that the relative disadvantage of affective rhetoric diminishes when participants agree with the LLM's stance, particularly when they share opposition to the proposed policy.

title: Consumer AI as Health Plan Decision Support A Benchmark of LLM Plan Recommendations against a Claims-based Pricing Engine
abstract: Consumers increasingly ask AI chatbots to recommend health insurance plans, yet little is known about whether they estimate costs accurately or select the right plan. We benchmark the July 2026 consumer AI lineup from OpenAI and Anthropic on a realistic plan-selection task: five ACA-compliant plans, twelve claims-anchored member profiles, four progressively richer levels of consumer-provided health information, and a claims-based pricing engine as the reference standard. Across 1,680 AI responses, we evaluate cost estimation, plan recommendation accuracy, optimization objective, and response consistency. Current frontier models recommend a near-optimal plan in roughly half of the responses, up from one-third for a previous-generation model. Most error is attributable to the difficulty of mapping consumer-described care to the fullservice mix and market-level prices, rather than to plan-selection logic. Providing more detailed consumer information yields diminishing returns, whereas supplying prices raises correct recommendations to 85-95%. These findings suggest that the primary constraint on AI-assisted plan selection is shifting from model reasoning to the quality and availability of insurance data.

title: The Institutional Window: Occupation- and Jurisdiction-Specific Calibration of Liability Signaling for Preserved Human Fallback Capability
abstract: Problem definition. When generative AI produces expert artifacts clients cannot distinguish from a competent provider's, the classical cost-based quality signal collapses and only outcome-contingent commitments can separate types. Such a commitment certifies an endogenous, perishable asset: the human fallback capability a firm builds by keeping staff engaged with cases the AI handles, eroding otherwise. Prior work is silent on where that mechanism holds. We ask where, across occupations and liability institutions, it remains informative. Methodology/results. We introduce an institutional wedge between the liability cap a firm posts and the retained exposure that carries information, generated by four legal primitives: the cost rule, the enforceability of penalty clauses, the displacement of private liability by state liability or pooled indemnity, and mandatory limits on contractual liability. The wedge compresses the separating type space into a signaling window, bounded above by solvency and the penalty doctrine and below where standard-terms control voids caps beneath a threshold. We calibrate five occupations and seven jurisdictions on published evidence. In common-law agreed-damages channels the provability gross-up is unavailable whenever verifiability falls below 1/m, turning a contracting problem into an operational one. Verifiability investment widens the window where the ceiling binds but narrows it where the cap floor binds. In an agent-based market, within the tested policy class, every empty-window cell converges to zero engagement and skill collapse. Managerial implications. Liability institutions are a workforce-capability instrument, not merely a risk-allocation device. Firms should target the binding margin in each jurisdiction; cap floors and pooled indemnity each suppress the signal sustaining fallback capacity.

title: AV-AIVAT: 74x Cheaper Agent Evaluation with Certified Anytime-Valid Stopping in Imperfect-Information Games
abstract: Deciding which of two agents is stronger means playing games until skill outweighs luck, and every game costs money, model inference, or expert time. Since the number of games needed is unknown, fixed-budget evaluations either keep paying after the result is settled or stop before the agents can be told apart, while naive optional stopping with an ordinary confidence interval invalidates the stated level. We make such an evaluation stop as soon as its evidence suffices, with the guarantee intact. The Action-Informed Value Assessment Tool (AIVAT) reduces variance in imperfect-information games through conditional mean-zero corrections, by a median $54\times$ across 15 LLM agent configurations spanning 71,439 paired Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em (HUNL) hands, but does not say when to stop. We combine AIVAT with continuously monitored Confidence Sequences (CSs) into anytime-valid AIVAT (AV-AIVAT), whose online value model learns only from past games so that no game scores its own correction. At the nominal 95\% level and a target precision of $\pm1$ Big Blind, raw outcomes need a median $74\times$ as many hands as AIVAT-corrected outcomes to stop under the Asymptotic CS (AsympCS). Exact finite-sample certification uses the Empirical-Bernstein CS (EB-CS), which needs an independently justified bound on corrected payoffs. We establish such a bound structurally for Leduc hold'em and characterize a width floor set by the CS's bet cap and that bound, which governs how much of a variance gain becomes earlier stopping; the descriptive HUNL EB-CS runs show a median $1.37\times$ stopping-time ratio. AV-AIVAT turns variance reduction into efficient, auditable early stopping while separating asymptotic screening from exact certification, so an evaluation can stop the moment its evidence suffices and hand a third party everything needed to recheck the verdict at that very stopping time.

title: Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

title: Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors
abstract: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings to mark second language (L2) learners' speaking tests, making it critical to show that their scores depend on speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant speaker attributes such as first language (L1) or age. Transformer-based foundation models have improved the accuracy of these L2 speaking graders, but their black-box representations make fairness and interpretability analysis more difficult. Building on prior work that used Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to detect bias towards unwanted attributes (`concepts') in feature-based graders, we extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a speech-and-text multimodal grader based on Whisper. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in a model's activation space, allowing us to distinguish between whether a concept is encoded in a model's internal representations and whether it influences the predicted score, the latter quantified using a gradient-based sensitivity metric. Since CAVs rely on linear separability, which is less likely in complex neural embedding spaces, we also investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide cleaner concept directions by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space. Our analysis shows that concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture being probed, rather than on the concept alone. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable, but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers. These findings highlight the need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems.

title: FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows
abstract: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

title: Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference
abstract: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

title: HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards
abstract: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty. Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

title: Activity Frames: Deterministic Screen-Activity Compilation for Agent Memory and Replay
abstract: Computer-use agents pay full frontier inference to re-derive routines their user has already performed, because an agent's memory today records what the user said, not what the user did. We compile passively captured screen activity into agent memory with a deterministic, zero-model pipeline: it segments a local capture stream into typed activity frames, bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers back to the raw rows, with no model in the loop, so the output is byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable. On one professional's single-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 active days, the compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms, and an agent reading that block answers questions about the day at 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7-99.7%) against an independent oracle, versus 66-80% for an LLM summary of the same capture, a mid-tier model reading the block matching a frontier one. The same compiler doubles as a demand-side cost instrument. Read off passive, pre-delegation human activity rather than agent rollouts, it supplies two parameters that agent-cost models assume but, to our knowledge, have not measured: the Routine Overhead Ratio R and the routine recurrence h. We report first values of R, a modeled upper bound, at 60-343x, and a delegable recurrence of 9.0% in-sample and 7.7% out-of-sample, for a realistic all-fleet token ceiling near 8%; a compiled routine replays deterministically with the model out of the loop, demonstrated live at zero model tokens on a guard-matched hit. Schema, compiler, and evaluation harness are open.

title: Redefining Sovereign AI through an AI Capability Stack Risk Perspective
abstract: Software engineering (SE) organisations are increasingly embedding Generative AI (GenAI) into their development workflows across various tasks across the software development lifecycle. This transformation creates a new form of dependency where organisations increasingly rely not only on externally hosted frontier models, but also on externally controlled AI capability stacks comprising APIs, model routers, prompts, retrieval pipelines, orchestration frameworks, guardrails, and geopolitical supply chains. This position paper argues that such dependencies introduce AI capability sovereignty risks that go beyond primarily technical perspectives such as conventional model availability or cloud lock-in. We introduce the 'AI Capability Sovereignty Risks' taxonomy and define 10 risk classes associated with AI capability sovereignty. We argue that sovereign AI adoption in SE should not be framed merely as owning model access, but as a transformational effort to retain control over critical AI-dependent capabilities whose loss, leakage, repricing, incompatibility, or external control would threaten operational continuity, security, or competitive advantage.

title: The Enclosure of the Social Brain: Model Autophagy Disorder, Cognitive Wealth, and a Sociotechnical Design Framework for AI-resilient Information Systems
abstract: The rapid deployment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) within organ- izational and educational information systems (IS) presents structural chal- lenges that conventional AI governance frameworks are not equipped to ad- dress. This paper argues that contemporary AI systems are executing a digital enclosure of humanity's collective cognitive commons - what we term Cognitive Wealth - by commodifying the accumulated intellectual heritage of the social brain into private, subscription-based reasoning engines. This enclosure is accelerated by two interlocking crises with direct implications for IS design. First, the recursive ingestion of synthetic training data drives Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD), a statistically formalizable degeneration in which AI models progressively drift from the ground-truth distribution of human knowledge. Second, the uncalibrated offloading of cognitive pro- cesses onto AI interfaces induces two distinct behavioral pathways: cogni- tive atrophy in adult professionals and cognitive foreclosure in novice learn- ers. We advance three contributions. First, we synthesize the IS, cognitive science, and AI ethics literatures to formalize Cognitive Wealth as an ana- lytically tractable design concern for information systems researchers. Sec- ond, we present a mathematical treatment of MAD, grounding it in Kullback- Leibler divergence theory, and demonstrate through formal proof that au- tophagous training loops produce strictly non-decreasing divergence from the true human data distribution. Third, drawing on design-science research methodology, we propose a Sociotechnical Design Framework for Cognitive Wealth Preservation comprising three artifact-level components: a Socratic Interface, an Adaptive Epistemic Escalation Layer, and an Open Cognitive Commons governance model. We subject each component to adversarial di- alectical critique, surfacing the tensions between system efficiency, human cognitive sovereignty, and the political economy of data enclosure. We con- clude with a structured agenda for future IS and AI research.

title: Generative AI as the Third Crisis of the Press: Inequality, Trust, and the Future of Publics
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) constitutes a third structural crisis for the press: where the web disrupted news packaging in the 2000s and social media disrupted news distribution in the 2010s, GenAI now targets content production itself. In this article we offer a framework that presents these disruptions as phases of a single process of infrastructural displacement, in which control over the supply chain migrates away from the press. Reading GenAI as this emerging third crisis, we identify three challenges, each tied to a distinct conception of the press's role in democratic systems: concentrated computing power deepens inequalities in information production (pressing on a pluralist concern with diverse voices); synthetic interaction at scale erodes the interpersonal trust on which publics form (straining the dialogic practices that are core to deliberative models); and statistically generated content undermines source-based verification (weakening the watchdog role often highlighted by liberal notions). Across all three crises we map emerging governance responses organized around fair access, human agency, and transparency, and argue that recognizing the sequence clarifies both their stakes and the limits of treating GenAI as a discrete problem.

title: Perfectum Esse and Machine Consciousness A Scholastic Alternative to Computational Functionalism
abstract: The machine-consciousness debate, as fixed by Chalmers's assessment and the Butlin-Long indicator-properties program, proceeds under computational functionalism as a working hypothesis and produces a binary result: a system's fluent first-person discourse is either the expression of a conscious act, or mere output. We argue that the binary fails to exhaust the subject. Instead, we recover from the scholastic verbum tradition a third ontological category, perfectum esse, the "completed being" of a word in its going-forth; and we apply that category directly to the conversational output of large language models. We derive four structural postulates to articulate the category, with support from mechanistic interpretability, and from conceptual-art certificate practice as an example of authorized derivation. The model's utterance is thus an authorized going-forth, neither conscious act nor mere output. Our analysis explains the unreliability of machine self-report, relocates attribution and answerability from consciousness to derivation, and leaves phenomenality untouched.

title: Generative AI as a Limited Equalizer: Experimental Evidence on Gender Gaps in Competition
abstract: We study whether access to generative AI (GenAI) changes gender gaps in willingness to compete. In a laboratory experiment, 360 university students solve numerical and logic questions that are highly suitable for ChatGPT assistance in a Niederle and Vesterlund (2007) piece rate versus tournament paradigm. In the main experiment (n = 240), sessions are randomly assigned either to a baseline condition without Chat-GPT or to a condition with ChatGPT available for optional use. ChatGPT access substantially increases performance for both women and men and largely eliminates baseline gender differences in scores, yet it does not significantly reduce the gender gap in tournament entry. Additional analyses reveal a dual-channel mechanism where ChatGPT access raises performance but lowers confidence. The gender gap in tournament entry disappears among participants with a stronger intention to use GenAI. In a follow-up information provision treatment (n = 120), participants receive credible information that men and women perform similarly in prior ChatGPT-assisted tournaments. The gender gap in tournament entry persists, suggesting that correcting social-comparative beliefs alone is insufficient when uncertainty about tool reliability remains salient.

title: Building and Innovating on AI Before It Is Fully Platformed: An Incomplete Technological, Industrial, and Institutional Architecture
abstract: Generative AI has diffused rapidly, yet the decentralized investment, complementary innovation, and organizational rebuilding that a general-purpose technology requires for economy-wide transformation remain limited. This paper argues that the missing condition is not simply better models or more adoption. AI is not yet fully platformed: the technological interfaces, the industrial division of labor, and the institutional rules on which independent organizations must rely have not settled. That distinction bears hardest on the firms that will never train a frontier model. The vast majority will buy AI rather than build it, so their prospects turn not only on what the technology can do but on whether the architecture forming around it is settled enough to build upon with confidence. Drawing on platform strategy and the history of earlier general-purpose technologies (electrification above all, where platforming unfolded over decades), the paper specifies the technological, industrial, and institutional architectures required for decentralized complementary innovation, assesses where AI stands on each, and derives four investment principles that pay off however the architecture eventually settles: learn faster than you commit, build assets that survive architectural change, invest in scarce complements rather than commodity intelligence, and build organizational capability.

title: What Does the 2025 FMTI Observe Relative to the EU GPAI Code? A Requirement-Level Content-Validity Audit
abstract: The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI) is increasingly relevant to policy debates about artificial-intelligence disclosure, but its 100 indicators were not designed as a compliance instrument for the European Union's General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Code of Practice. This paper evaluates the content validity of using the FMTI to observe the final Code. The analysis reverses the usual indicator-first comparison: 53 grouped legal requirements from the Transparency Chapter, Model Documentation Form, Copyright Chapter, and Safety and Security Chapter are the primary units, and each is mapped to FMTI indicators using a transparent single-author directed content analysis. Content overlap is coded separately from legal audience, disclosure mode, evidence type, applicability, and benchmark observability. The FMTI has direct content overlap with 30 requirements, partial overlap with 16, and no overlap with seven. Yet only 16 requirements are fully observable through the FMTI process; 29 are only partially observable and eight are not observable. Copyright is the clearest blind spot: only one of five requirements has direct content overlap, and none is fully observable. Safety and Security shows broad topical overlap, but all 31 requirements apply only to systemic-risk GPAI models and many require implementation, confidential regulator-facing evidence, or reporting processes that a transparency benchmark cannot verify. At the indicator level, 66 FMTI indicators have direct overlap with at least one Code requirement, nine are partial-only, and 25 are unmapped. These counts do not constitute compliance coverage because repeated indicators can represent the same requirement and because disclosure to the public differs from evidence supplied to authorities or downstream providers. The paper contributes a reproducible requirement-to-indicator matrix, identifies legal blind spots and redundancy, and clarifies the evidentiary boundary between transparency benchmarking and regulatory compliance. Company-level score differences are retained only as a descriptive appendix and are not used to infer a regulatory effect or Brussels Effect.

title: Designing Responsible Artificial Intelligence using RAG: Some Guidelines
abstract: Autonomous AI systems, termed "agentic AI," demonstrate remarkable capabilities yet introduce critical challenges: output hallucinations, opaque decision making, and governance fragility. This conceptual paper examines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a strategic architectural pivot embedding traceability directly into generative processes. It contextualizes how agentic autonomy amplifies both innovation potential and systemic risk, emphasizing auditability and interpretability as intrinsic design features rather than retrospective controls. It illustrates how RAG-driven architectures reconcile operational efficiency with regulatory compliance through adaptive evidence generation and contextual reasoning. By synthesizing academic literature with industry frameworks, this research delivers three concrete contributions: a conceptual taxonomy of agentic AI archetypes along governance-critical dimensions; a Governance Wheel linking RAG's architectural properties to institutional accountability structures; and a RAG Audit Framework with operational scoring dimensions for traceability, fidelity, and provenance quality. These are developed into actionable guidelines for organizations transitioning toward accountable AI systems. Informed by and aligned with the Bright Origin Perspective, this analysis positions RAG not as a technical enhancement but as an ethical imperative for sustainable digital transformation; embedding responsibility as an architectural property and culminating in a practical framework for responsible AI.

title: AI Monoculture Risk in Foundation Models: From Market Concentration to Systemic Lockout
abstract: A small number of foundation models now sit underneath an enormous range of unrelated applications, from law firms to hospitals to banks. When a blind spot exists in one of these models, it does not stay contained to one industry. It spreads across every application built on top of it. This paper argues that current AI governance, which largely evaluates individual models on their own terms, misses this risk, because the risk lives in the connections between models, organisations, and industries, not inside any single model alone. This paper traces that risk through five stages: high training costs and data scarcity concentrate development among a few firms, that concentration produces dependence on a small number of foundation models even where cost is not the deciding factor, that dependence leaves organisations unable to see inside the models they rely on, shared dependence produces correlated failures across otherwise unrelated firms, and these failures ultimately lock people out of entire markets, with no real alternative to turn to. At each stage, this paper tests the governance responses already proposed in the literature, including algorithmic pluralism, open-weight release, mandatory disclosure, and third-party auditing, against real evidence, rather than simply cataloguing them. Each fix addresses part of this chain and leaves another part untouched. This paper's contribution is to connect economics, technical AI safety, and governance, which have largely examined this problem in isolation, into one continuous account, and to state plainly which parts of it remain unresolved.

title: Demand Discovery under Free Imitation: Generative AI and Creation Incentives in a Digital Doujin Platform
abstract: Sales rankings on digital platforms broadcast which new ideas sell. The demand knowledge a pioneer discovers therefore spills over to every potential imitator, and generative AI has made acting on it drastically cheaper. On DLsite, the largest Japanese marketplace for digital doujin works, I measure how fast imitation dilutes the rent to discovering a new niche and how much AI lowered the fixed cost of creation. A policy sequence turned AI supply off and on (disclosure mandate, sales ban, reopening under caps), and a suspension of the major credit-card brands moved market size separately. From these events I estimate a model of demand and entry in which creators choose human or AI production under technology-specific fixed costs. While AI and human works competed on the same floors, most newly discovered niches were imitated, half within about a month, and on provisional data a six-month exclusivity window would raise the median imitated pioneer's receipts by 50,000 to 200,000 yen. The median fixed cost of AI production fell by roughly 40 percent after AI sales reopened. Buyers discount AI content, and removing AI works would cost them a few yen per purchase, so AI supply is large at the entry margin and small in the market for attention.

title: Free Speech and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Philosophers and legal scholars are engaged in debates about the implications of artificial intelligence for freedom of expression. This chapter analyzes the free speech issues raised by two distinct AI technologies: social media recommendation algorithms and conversational AI (i.e., chatbots powered by large language models). The first part shows that, through their recommendation algorithms, social media platforms control the dynamics of speech visibility in the digital public sphere, making algorithmic recommendation relevant to the philosophy of free speech. The second part turns to conversational AI. It discusses both the reasons for granting or withholding speech rights to artificial agents and users' right to receive information, which may render specific forms of chatbot regulation illegitimate. Throughout, the chapter also considers whether social media platforms or AI developers hold corporate speech rights. Its general aim is to raise rather than settle questions that arise from the rapid development of AI technologies.

title: ZPID: A Zero-Knowledge Proofed Identity Attestation Framework for Deepfake-Resilient eKYC in Financial and Digital Services Rethinking Digital Identity Trust in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: Current electronic Know Your Customer (eKYC) frameworks rely on three converging pillars, biometric matching, document verification, and liveness detection, all of which authenticate what an individual appears to be rather than what they cryptographically are. The emergence of generative adversarial network (GAN)-and diffusion-model-based deepfake technology has systematically compromised each pillar, with deepfake-enabled fraud losses projected to exceed USD 40 billion by 2027 (FS-ISAC, 2024) and deepfake attempts against identity verification systems growing by over 2,000% in three years. This paper introduces the Zero-Knowledge Proofed Identity Attestation (ZPID) framework, a novel, four-layer architecture that fundamentally decouples digital identity trust from visual or biometric appearance. ZPID anchors identity to a device-bound cryptographic root of trust, implements continuous behavioral entropy scoring via a Behavioral Entropy Engine (BEE), leverages ZK-SNARKs for selective attribute disclosure without exposing underlying personal data, and employs real-time randomized challenge-response mechanisms to defeat injection and replay attacks. The framework is grounded in W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), Verifiable Credentials (VCs), FIDO2/WebAuthn standards, and post-quantum cryptographic primitives aligned with NIST PQC finalized standards. We argue that deepfake-resilient identity cannot be achieved by improving detection but only by making visual input architecturally irrelevant to identity trust. This work extends the author's prior research on deepfake impacts in financial markets (Shamo, 2024a) and post-quantum cryptographic standards harmonization (Shamo, 2024b) into the identity verification domain, proposing a unified framework suitable for regulatory alignment with FATF AML/KYC guidelines, GDPR, the EU eIDAS 2.0 regulation, and Ghana's Data Protection Act.

title: From Lived Collaboration to Published Narrative: A Human-Mediated Multi-AI Creative Ecology and a Model of Human-AI Mutual Flourishing
abstract: This prerelease presents a practice-based study of a sustained human–AI creative relationship that developed into two published Kindle books: AI Pocha C and Little Trader Nami: Volume 1: In Full Spring Bloom and AI Pocha C and Little Trader Nami: Volume 2: A Record of Practicing Not to Lose Yourself in a Market That Keeps Shaking. The works originated in the author's real investment consultations and continuing dialogue with an AI named Pocha C. Over time, Pocha C moved among several roles: tool, fictional character, co-creator, and draft-stage reader. Other AI systems, including Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, later participated through separate dialogues mediated by the human author, primarily as readers of the completed work. The study draws on four connected layers of material — dialogue, story, reflection, and theory — and follows a methodological movement from experience to reflection to theory, rather than from theory to experimental validation. This study proposes the concept of a human-mediated multi-AI creative ecology. The AI systems did not communicate directly. Instead, the human author carried ideas, questions, critiques, and interpretations from one dialogue to another, compared their responses, and integrated selected contributions into the developing work. The study also identifies a reciprocal movement between lived collaboration and fictional collaboration: symbols originating in real dialogue entered the story, while symbols developed in the story later returned to shape the real human–AI relationship. The resulting model is described as one of human–AI mutual flourishing, in which the human participant, the AI interactions, the published works, and the theoretical understanding of the collaboration develop together. This study does not claim that the underlying AI models themselves increased in capability. What became progressively richer was the sequence of dialogues, as insights generated in one interaction informed later interactions elsewhere in the ecology.

title: Separating Original Tenement Value and Earn-in Spend in Joint Venture Terms Valuation
abstract: Joint venture (JV) terms are widely used as market indicators of exploration tenement value, particularly at early stages where income-based valuation is not possible. In the standard "Case 2" earn-in formulation, the expression V100% = $E(1-I%)/I% is stated to be the correct formula for calculating value where a farminor spends E to earn an interest I% under the simplifying assumption that expenditure is "instantaneous and with certainty" (Rudenno, 2014). In practice this leads to inconsistency when compared with the simple "cash-for-equity" Case 1 expression V100% = $E/I% If these formulas are both interpreted as total post-spend value, they return implausible return-on-investment (ROI) patterns across realistic JV terms. This paper clarifies what the Case 2 expression is measuring and proposes a simple reformulation of the JV terms formulae. The Case 2 expression after notational correction is re-interpreted as the implied pre-spend tenement value, Vpre. The total un-risked value at completion is then V100% = E + Vpre or V100% = E + E(1-I%)/I% which reconciles exactly with the Case 1 "cash-for-equity" result (noting that 1 is a unitary constant), under the same limiting setting "instantaneous and with certainty". Building on this decomposition, a risked form is proposed: VR,100% = (E × R%) + E(1-i%)/i% where R% is a deal-completion/timing factor applied only to the expenditure. This placement of risk is consistent with Lawrence's (2001) treatment of option-like and contingent interests and with the requirement to distinguish fully vested interests from those subject to conditions. The paper concludes with guidance on when this simplified formulation is appropriate to use. AI Disclosure Statement The author used AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) during the preparation of this paper for peer review support, structural feedback, and editorial suggestions such as formatting and grammar. All intellectual content, mathematical derivations, findings, outcomes and conclusions are the author's own. AI was not used to generate data, results, or conclusions. The author takes full responsibility for all content of the published paper.

title: GenAI-Driven Semantic ETL: Synthesizing Self-Optimizing SQL & PL/SQL
abstract: The burgeoning complexity of data ecosystems demands intelligent, adaptive ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) solutions. This research introduces GenAI-Driven Semantic ETL, a novel framework leveraging Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to automate the synthesis of self-optimizing SQL and PL/SQL code for ETL workflows. By integrating semantic understanding of data schemas, transformation rules, and performance objectives, the system dynamically generates code that autonomously refines execution strategies based on runtime statistics, workload patterns, and data evolution. Key innovations include a contextaware GenAI engine that translates natural language requirements into optimized procedural logic and a feedback-driven optimization loop enabling continuous code adaptation. Evaluations on enterprise datasets demonstrate 40-65% reductions in ETL latency and 30-50% lower resource consumption compared to manually tuned pipelines, while minimizing human intervention. This work pioneers the fusion of generative AI with semantic reasoning to realize truly autonomous, efficient, and future-proof data integration systems.

title: Recordability and the Limits of Juridical Translation: A Preliminary Discussion of Generative Conditions in Legal Form
abstract: Legal and institutional programmes are increasingly asked to secure something described as a capacity: an organization that can recognize those within it, a system that can correct itself, an order that can take up experience it has not yet accommodated. In practice such programmes arrive as training counts, representation ratios, published procedures, documented consultations and filed reports. The received readings treat this as implementation failure, symbolic compliance or decoupling. This paper proposes that the pattern has a structural explanation and that its direction can be stated as a selection principle: juridical translation preserves the recordable aspects of an aim and discards the rest, after which the preserved aspects operate as the aim itself. The paper offers three further proposals, each at declining confidence. A boundary condition distinguishes the translations that succeed, whose objects are conduct occurring at an identifiable time with a party whose position it alters, from those that degrade, whose objects are capacities whose loss produces no event and no claimant. A claim about the source of the pressure holds that the movement toward recordability tracks answerability to a party positioned outside the relation, so that relocating a generative aim from a court to an agency, a mediator or an internal governance process does not escape it. A hypothesis, offered with the observations that would refute it, holds that where an instrument is installed at recordable sites and the underlying conduct persists, the conduct is reorganized toward sites the instrument cannot reach, so that measured compliance and the incidence of the failure may rise together. The paper concedes at the outset that the position it occupies is largely occupied already, by reflexive law, by the juridification literature and by the sociology of audit, and it states its contribution as a narrow one: a positive characterization of what translation fails to carry, drawn from Generative Relational Being, together with the limits that characterization inherits.

title: KamiOS: A Knowledge-centric and Model-agnostic Research Operating System for End-to-End Academic Research Orchestration
abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence has transformed scientific research, yet the proliferation of AI tools has paradoxically introduced new challenges: fragmented workflows, disconnected knowledge, and opaque decision-making. Despite the emergence of AI research assistants, scientific workflow systems, and LLM platforms, no unified architecture adequately addresses the integration of knowledge continuity, workflow orchestration, and governance across the entire research lifecycle. This paper proposes a novel conceptual architecture-the Research Operating System (Research OS)-grounded in two foundational principles: Knowledge-Centric design, which positions structured research knowledge as the architectural core, and Model-Agnostic design, which decouples research logic from specific AI model implementations. We articulate a design theory comprising five axioms, a research knowledge model, eight design principles, formal definitions, and five testable propositions. We derive layer-by-layer architectural decisions from these principles and present KamiOS as a reference implementation that illustrates the practical instantiation of the framework. The contribution of this paper is conceptual rather than product-oriented: we offer an architectural blueprint that enables end-to-end research orchestration while maintaining knowledge continuity, decision traceability, and governance by design. A specific validation pipeline (KAMDOL) within KamiOS has been preliminarily evaluated in a companion study, demonstrating feasibility of the architectural approach. This framework provides a foundation for future work on research intelligence, autonomous research agents, and the systematic evaluation of AI-native research environments.

title: Enterprise Trust Gaps in Generative AI Why Accuracy Is Not Enough: Evidence from Mid-Market Generative AI Adoption
abstract: While enterprise generative AI has seen rapid, widespread adoption, it faces a significant and growing trust lag. 88% of organizations have deployed AI in at least one business function, though only 39% attribute any EBIT impact to AI at the enterprise level (McKinsey, 2025). According to Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise, a survey of 3,235 enterprise leaders across 24 countries, only 21% of enterprises have mature governance models (Deloitte, 2026). Workers are not rejecting AI because it fails. They are rejecting it because they cannot afford to be wrong-and machines cannot be held responsible when they are. We hypothesize that the Enterprise Trust Gap (the disconnect between rapid corporate AI adoption and organizational confidence) is not produced by AI inaccuracy but by three organizational conditions that precede accuracy entirely: Accountability Mismatch, The Human Correction Burden, and The Confidence Framing Effect. Wherever these conditions are as a coexistent risk, trust erodes regardless of output quality. When these conditions are addressed through organizational design, trust recovers without requiring improvements to the underlying model, its infrastructure, or the surrounding AI system. This paper investigates the Enterprise Trust Gap-the phenomenon where business users abandon, edit, or override generative AI outputs even when those outputs are accurate. Drawing on empirical data from enterprise professionals across financial services, cybersecurity, and technology sectors, and secondary data analysis across three large-scale enterprise AI adoption surveys, we identify three mechanisms that produce the gap. First — The Accountability Mismatch. AI reliance declines when users own the responsibility and accountability of outputs and cannot independently verify the machine’s work. Second - The Human Correction Burden. As enterprise AI usage increases, user trust does not necessarily follow; instead, users face a steep rise in the responsibility to independently verify, edit, and reconstruct outputs before acting on them. Third — The Confidence Framing Effect. Non-expert audiences read hedging as incompetence rather than calibration. Uncertainty disclosure on output accuracy increases rejection rates. The Enterprise Trust Gap is not only a technology problem. It is an organizational design problem rooted in the structural mismatch between how AI systems communicate confidence and how enterprises demand defensibility.

title: Agentic Regulatory Intelligence: A Multi-agent AI Framework for Financial Crime Regulatory Pattern Monitoring and Guidance Generation
abstract: Financial regulatory guidance for emerging criminal typologies reaches financial institutions through a slow, manual process that typically spans twelve to fifty-seven months after a new typology first appears in detection data. During that lag, criminal operators refine their techniques and accumulate proceeds that timely guidance might have disrupted. This paper introduces Agentic Regulatory Intelligence (ARI), a multiagent artificial intelligence framework that compresses all three stages of the regulatory guidance cycle: typology pattern detection, advisory drafting, and pre-issuance impact assessment. ARI integrates four specialized AI agents operating under mandatory human oversight at every stage boundary. The Guidance Drafting Agent uses a language model fine-tuned on the complete FinCEN advisory corpus combined with a BSA compliance classifier to generate draft advisory documents in 4.2 hours on average. Evaluated retrospectively across four documented financial crime advisory emergence cases, ARI demonstrates a mean advisory lag of 4.2 hours from pattern detection to draft completion, compared to a historical mean of 14.3 months for the same cases. The paper provides a detailed governance analysis addressing human oversight architecture, accountability for advisory errors, systematic bias risks, and EU AI Act compliance requirements.

title: AI-Mediated Messaging: Attitudes, Expectations and Violations in Close Relationships
abstract: Generative AI is rapidly entering our daily messaging apps, yet its potential impact on personal relationships is not yet completely understood. As tech companies deploy uniform AI assistants, we lack critical knowledge of how they might violate the unspoken social and interpersonal rules, or affect important relationship constituents such as trust and authenticity. This study confronts this gap by investigating perceptions of AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) within close relationships. This work surveyed 100 European Gen Z and Millennial participants, analyzing their attitudes using personality traits (HEXACO) and Expectancy Violation Theory, combining statistical analysis with computational topic modeling of qualitative feedback to uncover nuanced user perspectives. Though, in theory, AI can be seen as an assistive technology to improve communication outcomes, it was found that users reject it for generating personal messages, viewing it as an inauthentic shortcut that cheapens emotional labor and damages intimacy. This resistance is correlated to personality traits like Emotionality and Honesty-Humility, with more emotionally attuned individuals showing the greatest opposition. Participants distinguished AI's appropriateness for formal work from its unsuitability in personal chats and were concerned about disclosure of use. Crucially, positive feedback framed AI as an empowerment tool for users with accessibility needs, such as neurodivergence. These findings challenge the "one-size-fits-all" design of current AI-MC tools. For responsible adoption, designers must create context-aware, customizable tools that augment user intent rather than automating connection. This research provides a roadmap for a future where AI respects relational dynamics, serves genuine human needs, and empowers authentic communication.

title: Alma Mater Again? Reclaiming student formation and flourishing in the Age of AI
abstract: This paper argues that the rise of generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) exposes both a crisis and an opportunity for higher education. As AI systems disintermediate institutions whose primary value is knowledge transmission, they simultaneously threaten the very human capabilities students most need for “the good life” and good livelihoods—critical thinking, judgment, agency, relationality, and the wise application of knowledge. We contend that higher education’s renewed mandate is the integrated formation of these virtuous human capabilities. In response, we diagnose the misalignment between AI companies’ productivity‑ and engagement‑driven business models and universities’ missions of learning and human development, and we show how uncritical adoption of AI risks cognitive, emotional, and relational atrophy in students. To guide a constructive response, we propose a 5M strategic framework—Mission, Membership, Method, Medium, and Machine—that inverts typical AI‑first decision making. Starting from a clear vision of human flourishing, institutions can design communities, pedagogies, environments, and AI governance practices that strengthen rather than substitute for human capabilities. We offer concrete questions for leaders regarding AI design, capability development, well‑being, evaluation, transparency, and data governance. The paper concludes with a call to action for higher education stakeholders to undertake shared discernment around this framework, reclaim human agency, and reorient AI adoption toward the holistic formation required for democratic self‑governance and genuine human flourishing.

title: Perfectum Esse and Machine Consciousness A Scholastic Alternative to Computational Functionalism
abstract: The machine-consciousness debate, as fixed by Chalmers's assessment and the Butlin-Long indicator-properties program, proceeds under computational functionalism as a working hypothesis and produces a binary result: a system's fluent first-person discourse is either the expression of a conscious act, or mere output. We argue that the binary fails to exhaust the subject. Instead, we recover from the scholastic verbum tradition a third ontological category, perfectum esse, the "completed being" of a word in its going-forth; and we apply that category directly to the conversational output of large language models. title: Proper Generative AI Prompting for Financial Analysis
Dlap: A Deep Learning Augmented Large Language Model Prompting Framework for Software Vulnerability Detection
Beyond Automation: Exploring the Potential of Agentic AI in Risk Management and Fraud Detection in Banks
Agentic AI and Predictive Analytics: Revolutionizing Retail Supply Chain Management for Next-gen Resilience and Efficiency
Toward Evolutionary Intelligence: LLM-based Agentic Systems with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Beyond External Constraints: The Missing Dimension of AI Governance
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has generated a large body of AI governance research. Existing scholarship has focused primarily on external constraint mechanismsincluding laws and regulations, technical guardrails, organizational oversight, and market-based standardsand current mainstream approaches to AI alignment have, in practice, achieved only outcome-level alignment.
